title: [Testcase Refactoring] Decouple test_aot_inductor_package.py from CUDA-specific
body:
## Summary
This PR add `privateuseone` to accelerator test cases just with `cuda` so out-of-tree accelerator backends can run these tests, hardware classify and instantiate device-specific test classes.

## Changes
- Add `privateuseone` to accelerator test cases just with `cuda`.
- Instantiate device-agnostic test templates as device-specific test classes for multiple differrent device backends.
- Add `HardwareClassification.GENERIC|ACCELERATOR|CPU|CUDA|XXX` to tests class.

`torch.cuda` and `torch.xpu` only recognizes CUDA and XPU. New accelerators (e.g., `PrivateUse1`-based out-of-tree backends) are silently skipped even when enough devices are available. A generic decorator lets inductor tests adapt to any accelerator supported by `torch.accelerator`.

- Verified test cases correctly on CPU, GPU, and XPU.

title: [MPS] Fix silent corruption in bmm for non-contiguous inputs > 2**32 elements
body:
Fixes #197636.

### Description
This PR addresses a critical bug in the MPS backend where `bmm` silently returns corrupted outputs (and corrupted gradients on the backward pass) when the output exceeds 2**32 elements and the inputs are non-contiguous views (e.g., in eager attention `q @ k.transpose()`). 

**Root Cause:**
When inputs cross the 2**32 element threshold, `bmm_out_mps_impl` routes them to `tiled_bmm_out_mps_impl`. However, `tiled_bmm_out_mps_impl` passes the raw `MTLBuffer` objects directly to `MPSNDArrayDescriptor` without accounting for memory strides. For transposed or sliced inputs, the Metal kernel blindly reads the memory sequentially, causing complete math corruption. 

Because the backward pass calculates gradients using `bmm(G, b.transpose(-1, -2))`, this lack of a `.contiguous()` check also silently corrupts the backward gradients even when the forward pass inputs were perfectly contiguous.

**Fix:**
We explicitly enforce `.contiguous()` on both `batch1` and `batch2` immediately before routing to the `tiled_bmm_out_mps_impl` function. This forces PyTorch to pack the memory into a row-major layout, allowing the Metal tiled kernel to read the correct values safely and resolving both the forward and backward pass corruptions.

### Testing
- Relying on PyTorch CI for MPS regression test suites.
- Resolves the exact reproduction harness outlined in Issue #197636.

title: [distributed] Tear down NCCL timeout tests explicitly
body:
### Problem

`test_set_nccl_pg_timeout` and `test_extend_nccl_pg_timeout` spin up a process group and return without tearing it down, so cleanup falls to the destructor while the interpreter is already shutting down. The nccl2 watchdog keeps polling once a second, and if it checks an event after CUDA has started unloading, that `driver shutting down` error gets recorded as a work failure. The watchdog then kills the process thinking a real operation failed (or the collective just hangs). Legacy has no watchdog thread, so only the `backend0` parametrization flakes (see #195724).

### Fix

Call `dist.destroy_process_group()` at the end of both tests, so teardown goes through `finalize()`. The watchdog is stopped first, work queue drained cleanly, all before anything starts unloading.

### Test Plan

1. `python test/distributed/test_c10d_nccl.py --use-pytest -vv -p no:xdist --pytest-single-test test/distributed/test_c10d_nccl.py::ProcessGroupNCCLGroupTest::test_set_nccl_pg_timeout_backend0`
2. `python test/distributed/test_c10d_nccl.py --use-pytest -vv -p no:xdist --pytest-single-test test/distributed/test_c10d_nccl.py::ProcessGroupNCCLGroupTest::test_extend_nccl_pg_timeout_backend0`

Both pass on 8 GPUs (7.3s / 17.2s).


Follows the test-stabilization approach in #194954. Related: #195724.

- Bitwise and comparison ops on lazy constants realize and install value guards

title: [benchmarks/dynamo] Use small-output accuracy policy for SigLIP
body:
## Summary
The next Triton pin bump will include https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/11189, which updates Triton’s bundled CUDA libdevice. This change is not included in PyTorch's current Triton pin. 

In particular, the Triton PR changes the implementation used for float32 `erf` (`__nv_erff`). On A10G, we observed that the updated `__nv_erff` changes GELU rounding in `vit_base_patch16_siglip_256`. This causes the benchmark’s synthetic training loss to fail its accuracy check:
  - Failing test: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/35206051520/job/105174646954
  - Eager RMSE against FP64: 0.13545
  - Compiled RMSE against FP64: 0.47106
  - Ratio: 3.48×
  - Current limit: 3×

We isolated the failure to the updated `__nv_erff`; when we restored only its previous implementation, the accuracy failure disappeared. We also verified that the updated implementation remains within 1 ULP of correctly rounded FP64 (while CUDA permits up to 2 ULP) so this is expected numerical variation from the new implementation.

The failure is limited to the synthetic scalar loss that the benchmark creates to run backward. Inference and all other training results still pass with the existing thresholds.

This PR adds SigLIP to the existing small-output policy similar to what has been previously done (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/177042 for example) to allow a larger multiplier for small tensors.

## Test plan
  - Both affected A10G TIMM shards pass with this change:
    https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/35167626498
  - `erff` accuracy sweep:
    https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/34736991855
  - Nonscalar training results pass:
    https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/34738810460

title: [Lint] Add TEST_LINTER linter for testcase linter checks
body:
## Summary

Add a new `TEST_LINTER` linter that ensures every `TestCase` subclass satisfy the test case requirements.

This linter enforces test case requirements, including hardware classification declaration, test instantiation patterns, test method signatures, and supported decorators.



## Rules

All test classes inheriting from `TestCase` must first declare a valid `hw_classification` attribute. Supported values are `GENERIC`, `ACCELERATOR`,`CPU`, `CUDA`, `MPS`, and `XPU`.

The requirements for each `hw_classification` are summarized below:

GENERIC:

   - Class must not be used with instantiate_device_type_tests.
   - Test methods must not accept device/devices parameter.

ACCELERATOR:

   - Class must be used with instantiate_device_type_tests.
   - Every test method must accept device/devices parameter.
   - Test methods must not use `@only*` decorators (except @onlyAccelerator).
   - instantiate_device_type_tests must not use only_for (use except_for as a blacklist approach instead).

CPU / CUDA / MPS / XPU (device-specific):

   - Class must be used with instantiate_device_type_tests.
   - Every test method must accept device/devices parameter.
   - instantiate_device_type_tests must use only_for matching the device (e.g. only_for='cuda').
   - instantiate_device_type_tests must not use except_for.



## Changes

- `.lintrunner.toml`: register `TEST_LINTER` linter for `test/**/test_*.py` and `test/**/*_test.py`, excluding openreg and cpython tests.
- `tools/linter/adapters/test_linter.py`: the linter script.
- `tools/linter/adapters/test_linter_allowlist.json`: allowlist of files not yet classified (1191 entries covering all current test files).
- `tools/test/test_test_linter.py`: unit tests covering missing/invalid/`GENERIC`/`ACCELERATOR`/`CUDA`/non-test scenarios.



## Test Plan

`pytest tools/test/test_test_linter.py -vvv -s -x : 54 passed in 0.18s`

title: Avoid hint guards in symbolic expand fast paths

`SymIntArrayRef::equals` can specialize backed symbolic dimensions from their hints in optional expand fast paths. Use `TORCH_GUARD_OR_FALSE(c10::sym_equals(...))` in both `expand_outplace` overloads so an unproven equality falls through to general broadcasting without installing a guard.

Add focused coverage for binary `logical_and` and tensor-list `broadcast_tensors`, asserting that a hint-1 dimension remains symbolic and that `ShapeEnv` records no guards. Remove the now-stale `nn.functional.cosine_similarity` unbacked xfail shared by the base tensor and DTensor suites.

title: [FSDP2] Prepare nonzero-dimension shard copies in C++
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.15.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #197701
* #198058
* #197204

what if we do view and metadata manipulation at cpp level ?

> AI-assisted implementation and summary prepared with Codex. The question above is the author's request motivating this follow-up to #197204.
>
> The opt-in nonzero-dimension shard callbacks create one Python Tensor view per contiguous prefix. For Shard(1) over [N, F, D], that CPU work can outweigh the faster GPU copies: at N=128, the Python-view path takes 334 us for eager all-gather copy-out, versus 181 us for the default reorder path.
>
> Pass the original tensors and prefix metadata to private native operators instead. CUDA builds pointer/size descriptors directly and reuses the existing copy kernels. Reduce-scatter accepts an internal preparation result without expanding gradients into Python views; custom callbacks returning padded sizes remain supported. Preserve version counters, dtype conversion, padding, and composite fallbacks.
>
> On B200 with 224 MiB BF16 input, eight shards, and FP32 reduction, N=128 eager all-gather falls from 334 to 104 us. N=2 remains about 104 us. CUDA kernel counts and temporary allocation peaks match the Python-view path. Keep opt-in: at N=8192, native all-gather takes 302 us versus 264 us for the default path, although it improves on Python views' 17.74 ms.
>
> Test Plan:
> ```bash
> CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=5 python test/test_prefix_copy.py -v
> CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,2 python test/distributed/_composable/fsdp/test_fully_shard_training.py \
>   TestFullyShard1DTrainingCore.test_train_parity_single_group_shard_dim0 \
>   TestFullyShard1DTrainingCore.test_train_parity_single_group_shard_largest_dim \
>   TestFullyShardShardPlacementFnMultiProcess.test_train_parity_shard_placement_fn_shard_largest_dim \
>   TestFullyShardShardPlacementFnMultiThread.test_shard_placement_fn_contiguous_params_grads -v
> lintrunner -a
> git diff --check
> ```
> Passed 184 native CPU/CUDA cases (2 expected skips) and all four FSDP training tests. Coverage includes mixed shard dimensions/dtypes, noncontiguous fallback, inference/version counters, functionalization, and CUDA graph replay. A separate two-rank [2,14336,4096] W13 forward/backward run preserved exact loss and gradients and improved about 10% versus the default copy path.

title: [c10d] Allow CPU device_id in init_process_group
body:
_new_process_group_helper rejected any CPU device_id, even one with a valid index (e.g. cpu:0), raising ValueError: init_process_group device_id parameter must be an accelerator with an index. This made it impossible to use device_id with the GLOO backend on CPU, despite init_process_group itself already treating CPU device_id as a valid case (it skips the accelerator-matching checks specifically for CPU, at line ~2513).

The restriction traces back to when device_id was CUDA-only, added to support NCCL's early-connect optimization (ncclCommSplit). A later commit (#143735) generalized the check to also allow XPU, but the CPU exclusion was carried forward unchanged rather than reconsidered.

This relaxes the check to only require a valid index, regardless of device type, and updates the error message and docstring to match. Tested manually with a two-rank torch.multiprocessing.spawn GLOO group confirming dist.barrier() succeeds across both ranks with device_id=torch.device("cpu:0"), not just single-rank initialization. Added test_device_id_cpu (confirms the fix) and test_device_id_cpu_no_index (confirms a missing index still correctly raises) to test_c10d_gloo.py.

Note: could not verify backend/device-type mismatch handling (e.g. nccl + cpu) since NCCL isn't compiled on this machine (Apple Silicon has no CUDA); confirmed the attempt still fails, but at a different point (RuntimeError: Distributed package doesn't have NCCL built in), before any real semantic check would run. Would appreciate a maintainer with GPU access double-checking that specific combination.

Also ran the full test_c10d_gloo.py suite: 48 pre-existing failures in ProcessGroupGlooLazyInitTest, unrelated to this change — confirmed via git stash that they fail identically without this fix applied.

Fixes #160731

title: [Auto] Fix #152893: DISABLED test_comprehensive_nn_functional_conv3d_cuda_float16 (__main__.TestIndu
body:
Human direction from @mlazos:

> "go ahead and do all of the updates, I'll review on github independently"

> **AI-assisted draft for that independent GitHub review:**
>
> ## Summary
>
> Recover cached, statically launchable Triton kernels when their emitted GPU binary is missing or corrupted. Loading has three explicit outcomes. A digest-valid payload already retained by a launcher is accepted. If retained bytes are absent, loading selects an exact bundle payload, or a digest-valid local payload when the bundle omits it; if both copies are absent, the cached static autotuner is not registered and the normal source-compilation cache-miss path runs. A validation failure in the candidate selected under those precedence rules forces recompilation. Ambiguous bundled candidates also force recompilation when no digest-valid retained payload exists.
>
> This allows the disabled `nn.functional.conv3d` float16 Inductor OpInfo case to pass without source compilation when a digest-valid retained or bundled payload is available.
>
> Fixes #152893
>
> ## Root cause
>
> Static autotuners normally omit their own raw GPU binary bytes and rely on files emitted from the Triton bundle. Although the bundle retained the exact bytes, loading did not reattach them to the deserialized launchers. A file removed after validation therefore caused the later-device launch to fail before native loading, while a truncated file produced a native loader error instead of using the retained payload.
>
> Dynamic reduction-block scaling can add a compile result after the first launcher set is built. Capturing the static autotuner before that step serialized stale candidates, so the final selected launcher could lack matching provenance in the bundle. With raw retention enabled, waiting until after launcher construction also requires preserving each candidate's bytes across native loading rather than rereading a cache pathname that may disappear concurrently.
>
> The bundle-to-launcher lookup also needs more identity than a hash and filename. Device-specific entries with the same hash and filename must not select another device's bytes, while a device-agnostic compile result may use a bundled payload only when all matching device entries agree. When a launcher has no retained bytes, a valid local cache file can supply them if the bundle has no matching payload, but conflicting bundled payloads are ambiguous and must not be selected.
>
> Conflict detection must happen before bundle emission. Otherwise a complete conflicting artifact group can populate Triton's disk cache even though static registration later forces recompilation when the launcher has no valid retained payload. Omitting the group preserves local cache integrity. Bundle emission must also be best-effort: a read-only cache cannot prevent independently verified retained bytes from loading in memory.
>
> An already-retained binary has to be authoritative before native loading, not only after an invalid-image error. A different but valid, ABI-compatible cubin can load successfully and execute the wrong kernel, leaving no loader failure from which to recover. Native file-not-found errors also have to remain classified as missing-artifact failures when another writer recreates the pathname before Python examines it.
>
> ## Fix
>
> Build one nested index of bundled GPU binaries keyed by `(hash, filename)` and then device. A shared `StaticTritonCompileResult` helper derives that same identity for both bundle matching and cache-path reconstruction. Each compile result also preserves the SHA-256 digest of the binary it produced before optional raw-byte removal. Device-specific results use their exact device key. Device-agnostic results accept a payload only when every matching device entry contains the same bytes, and every selected bundle or local payload must match the persisted digest. Duplicate exact keys retain all distinct payloads so malformed conflicting entries cannot be silently collapsed. One prevalidation pass resolves the candidates and digest-checks each uniquely selected payload once; bundle emission and static-autotuner loading consume the same trusted-payload decision.
>
> There are three binary representations: retained bytes on the launcher (`cubin_raw`), serialized bytes in a bundle artifact, and the canonical local Triton cache file. Loading applies three distinct branches. First, digest-valid retained launcher bytes are authoritative even if a separate bundle candidate is rejected; a mismatched retained payload instead forces recompilation. Second, when retained bytes are absent, loading prefers one exact, unambiguous bundle artifact, or a digest-matching local snapshot only when the bundle omits the binary. A rejected bundle selection forces recompilation; after bundle omission, a mismatched selected local snapshot does the same because a merely loadable local binary cannot authenticate graph semantics. Third, when bundle and local payloads are both absent, the cached static autotuner is not registered and ordinary cache-miss compilation handles the miss. Native CUDA, HIP, and XPU bindings load accepted retained bytes directly in memory, so a concurrent writer changing the local cache file cannot substitute a different but loadable module and no writable temporary directory is required. Conflicting or digest-invalid bundle groups are omitted from emission. Filesystem emission is best-effort on `OSError`, after which verified retained bytes can still load.
>
> Register the static autotuner only after launcher construction and dynamic reduction-block scaling, so serialization includes the post-scaling compile-result set and its provenance. When raw retention is enabled, preserve those bytes across native launcher construction; no later cache-file read is needed. The native byte-loading entry point is declared in the Python API source stub for typed callers.
>
> When retained bytes are available, the native loader consumes that immutable payload rather than reopening a pathname. Cold deserialization leaves pre-existing nonempty cache groups untouched. The artifact-recovery layer does not intercept unrelated loader errors or rewrite the cache; existing autotuner retry policies still apply. During initial/precompile-time loading, a native invalid-image rejection is classified as an invalid cache artifact and routed through the existing one-time source fallback in `StaticAutotunerFuture`; a later-device load from `run()` propagates that error. The callback always loads and precompiles in the parent process—even when the original compile used a worker pool—and uses Triton's supported `TRITON_ALWAYS_COMPILE` mode under Dynamo's compile lock. Only forced source recompilation may replace a bad artifact through Triton's atomic cache writer. CUDA, ROCm, and XPU static launchers share the native byte-loading API.
>
> Keep native module ownership guarded until symbol lookup, post-load validation, and Python result construction succeed. CUDA and ROCm unload a newly created module if any later check throws. After XPU's `_createKernel` takes ownership of the Level Zero module, its failure cleanup guards destroy that module or the raw kernel if subsequent construction fails. The XPU Python capsule is itself held by an owning Python smart pointer until tuple construction succeeds, so its destructor is reachable on both success and failure. A per-launcher lock serializes the first check/load/publication for each device, preventing two concurrent callers from creating a module whose handle is overwritten before cleanup can see it. Successful loads retain the existing launcher ownership behavior.
>
> ## Architecture
>
> Applicability: Applicable
>
> Description: `TritonBundler.read_and_emit()` owns serialized artifact selection, builds one nested payload index, resolves trust once, rejects ambiguous or mismatched device/hash groups before filesystem emission, and passes those same resolutions to `load_autotuners()`. Missing or empty cache groups are staged in a temporary directory, replaced atomically on POSIX and under a file lock on Windows; pre-existing nonempty groups and groups that raise `OSError` are skipped. `StaticTritonCompileResult` owns the canonical artifact identity and reconstructs a filesystem path only for disk-backed loading. Digest-valid retained launcher bytes are authoritative. When retained bytes are absent, one unambiguous bundle artifact is primary, or a stable local snapshot is used only when the bundle has none. A mismatched retained payload forces recompilation; a rejected bundle does so only when no valid retained payload exists. `StaticallyLaunchedTritonKernel` passes retained bytes directly to the backend-native API, classifies backend-specific missing/invalid images, and serializes first load per launcher. Native CUDA, ROCm, and XPU loaders guard module ownership through Python result construction; the XPU capsule transfers the final kernel lifetime into Python. Source fallback remains in `StaticAutotunerFuture` at the existing initial/precompile boundary, while retained-byte launches require no temporary binary or post-load disk I/O.
>
> Examples: A compile-on-one-rank graph can load its device-agnostic cubin on CUDA device 0, lose or truncate the emitted file, and then run on device 1 directly from retained bytes without invoking Triton. A device-specific launcher chooses only the payload for its own device even if another bundle entry has the same hash and filename. When retained bytes are absent, conflicting complete bundle entries are omitted before either can populate a cold Triton cache; the static future then forces source recompilation without loading any pre-existing local binary. Retained launcher bytes remain authoritative when the separate bundled artifact is corrupt, ambiguous, or a valid same-ABI implementation of a different operation. They also remain authoritative when an alternate binary is written to the local cache file after `read_and_emit()`. A mismatched retained payload instead forces recompilation. A bundle missing its binary can still use and retain an existing valid local file; conversely, an invalid readable local file can fall back to the bundle's valid image without invoking the compiler. Two threads that first use the same device share one loaded module instead of racing to publish separate handles.
>
> ## Example
>
> Before: deserialize a bundled static launcher with `keep_static_cubin_raw=False`, load it on CUDA device 0, then delete or truncate its emitted binary before running on device 1. Despite the graph bundle retaining the exact bytes, deletion caused a missing-binary launch failure and truncation caused a native loader error.
>
> After: bundle loading selects the exact candidate bytes and native loading consumes them directly in memory. Deleting or truncating the emitted file after device 0 loads no longer affects device 1 because the launcher retains the trusted bytes and performs no post-load disk access.
>
> Additional cases:
>
> - A writer that replaces the canonical cache path with another valid same-symbol cubin cannot change the already-selected retained payload.
> - A dynamically scaled reduction serializes its post-scaling candidates. With no retained payload, substituting a same-named binary from another graph is rejected and a forced-recompile future produces the expected result.
> - With no retained payload, an invalid or conflicting bundle is never replaced by unauthenticated local bytes; it registers a future that forces source recompilation. A digest-valid retained payload remains authoritative despite a separately damaged bundle, while a mismatched retained payload forces recompilation.
> - When both bundle and local bytes are missing, the cached static autotuner is not registered and ordinary cache-miss compilation handles the kernel. The artifact-recovery layer does not rewrite the local cache for unrelated loader errors; existing autotuner retry policies remain in effect.
>
> ## Testing
>
> The final tests use real bundle data, filesystem damage, Triton compilation, CUDA execution, a malformed bundled payload, a real missing-symbol driver error, and a real excessive-shared-memory error; no new mocks were added. The concurrency regression requires two GPUs. The native ownership guards were independently source-reviewed because CUDA does not expose a stable module-count assertion here. ROCm and XPU ownership and error-code branches are source-verified but were not built or executed on their hardware. The local execution results below are author-reported; raw runner logs are not attached to this PR.
>
> The focused FX graph cache suite passed 33/33. The dynamic reduction-block regression passed on an NVIDIA H100; removing only its production fix made all 8,192 outputs differ, and restoring the fix made the same test pass. Coverage is grouped as follows:
>
> - Artifact validation: same- and cross-device conflicts, corrupt and valid-but-wrong same-ABI payloads, digest mismatches in bundled, retained, and local binaries, retained-payload precedence, dynamic reduction-block provenance, and suppression of rejected bundle groups before emission.
> - Filesystem recovery: missing and truncated files, read-only empty and nonempty cache groups, a pre-existing invalid local group, bundle recovery from a corrupt local file, and bundle omission recovered from a valid local file.
> - Device and concurrency behavior: fixed-device and device-agnostic launchers, second-device recovery, candidate replacement before first load, and serialized concurrent first load.
> - Cleanup and errors: initial-load fallback with one and two compile threads, unrelated shared-memory errors with present and missing canonical files, missing-symbol classification, and device-1 partial-load cleanup while device 0 is current.

title: [ROCm] Always eagerly allocate hipBLAS(Lt) workspaces
body:
## Summary

- Make per-operation BLAS workspaces the default on ROCm, as they are on CUDA since #194311. ATen's hipBLAS and hipBLASLt operations allocate their workspace from the HIP caching allocator for each operation, so during capture it comes from the graph's memory pool. `TORCH_CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CACHE=1` keeps the previous persistent workspace cache.
- Run ATen's rocBLAS operations on internal per-thread handles that release the arena rocBLAS allocates when it creates a handle. Binding a workspace makes rocBLAS free that arena, and the free is illegal under stream capture.
- Give each (thread, stream) its own public handle, the one `torch.cuda.current_blas_handle()` and `at::cuda::getCurrentCUDABlasHandle()` return. ATen never binds a workspace to it, so it keeps its rocBLAS arena, and a workspace a caller binds stays bound. `capture_begin` keeps one spare, so the first request on a capture stream does not create a handle during capture.
- Route TunableOp's rocBLAS GEMMs and solution listing through the internal handle and its per-operation workspace, and give its hipBLASLt GEMMs the per-operation hipBLASLt workspace.
- Enable the existing eager-workspace tests on ROCm, add a C++ handle-pool test and ROCm graph-capture tests, isolate the FSDP2 MemTracker tests from BLAS workspaces, and document the ROCm behaviour in the HIP notes.

## Motivation

A persistently cached workspace is shared by every graph captured on the same handle and stream, so replaying one graph can overwrite a workspace another graph still uses. A per-operation workspace allocated during capture comes from that graph's pool, so no two graphs share one. `test_graph_capture_cublas_workspace_separate_graphs` catches this: with `TORCH_CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CACHE=1` it faults on SM90 and gfx90a and corrupts its canary on gfx950 (MI355X) and gfx942 (MI308X), and it passes with per-operation workspaces.

## Why ROCm needs a public handle per stream

cuBLAS resets a handle to its default workspace pool on every `cublasSetStream`, and that pool is guarded against concurrent use ([cuBLAS documentation](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cublas/index.html#cublassetworkspace)). rocBLAS has neither: a handle's arena is one buffer, and `rocblas_set_stream` keeps whatever workspace is bound and does not wait for the old stream. A public handle shared by a thread's streams could therefore run GEMMs on two streams in the same arena at once, so on ROCm each stream gets its own.

## Behaviour for callers of the public handle on ROCm

- `torch.cuda.current_blas_handle()` returns a different handle on each stream. A caller that keeps a handle and moves it to another stream with `rocblas_set_stream` must synchronize the old stream first, as rocBLAS requires.
- A workspace bound with `rocblas_set_workspace` stays bound, even after the buffer is freed and after the thread exits and the handle passes to another thread. Unbind it with `rocblas_set_workspace(handle, nullptr, 0)` before freeing the buffer. The handle then has no workspace of its own: its GEMMs use kernels that need none, and other calls make rocBLAS allocate one, which capture does not allow.
- `HIPBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:0:0` makes rocBLAS GEMMs use kernels that need no workspace, but other rocBLAS calls such as `torch.dot` then allocate their own, so they cannot be captured.

The first rocBLAS use on a thread cannot be captured, in cached or eager mode, and this PR does not change that. On MI308X, capturing `torch.dot` on a new thread whose earlier GEMMs all went to hipBLASLt fails at the merge base and with this PR alike. Handle initialization and TunableOp tuning must happen before capture. This is tracked by [ROCm/rocm-libraries#11838](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-libraries/issues/11838).

## Cost

- Each public handle keeps the arena rocBLAS allocates when it creates the handle, outside the caching allocator. On MI355X a new public handle took 162 MiB outside the caching allocator, 128 MiB of it the arena. The arena size depends on the GPU and the rocBLAS version.
- There is one public handle per (thread, stream) that requests it, plus one spare once a capture has begun on a device where a public handle was requested. Handles are never destroyed, and an exited thread's handles pass to other threads and streams, so this memory stays allocated for the life of the process.
- ATen's own rocBLAS operations use the internal handles, which hold no arena, so a process that never requests the public handle pays none of this. Two ATen paths still request it and so create a public handle on each stream they run on: MAGMA queue creation and the batched BLAS3 LU kernel.
- Per-operation workspaces cost a caching-allocator allocation per operation; see Performance.

## Validation

MI355X (gfx950) and MI308X (gfx942), same results on both:

- `hip_cublas_handle_pool_test`: 6 pass and 1 skips; with `TORCH_CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CACHE=1`, 2 pass and the eager-only tests skip.
- `test/test_cuda.py -k cublas -k workspace -k blas_handle`: 22 tests pass, 3 skip. With `TORCH_CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CACHE=1`, `test_cublaslt_workspace_eager_resize_and_zero` and both shapes of `test_graph_capture_cublas_workspace_separate_graphs` fail, as expected; the separate-graphs test fails in each of three runs and passes in each of three runs without it.
- `test_graph_capture_tunableop_cublas_workspace` passes and replays a rocBLAS solution; it skips when TunableOp picks none.
- A TunableOp GEMM on a new stream no longer creates a public handle: 0 MiB outside the caching allocator, down from 162 MiB (MI355X).
- On MI355X, the 43 `test/test_linalg.py` TunableOp tests, each in its own process, give the same results at the merge base and with this PR.
- FSDP2 MemTracker tests pass with per-operation workspaces and with `TORCH_CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CACHE=1`.
- Bounded workspace OOM tests raise a normal `OutOfMemoryError` and recover, for rocBLAS (128 MiB workspace) and hipBLASLt (80 MiB), in both modes.

## Performance

Following #194311: BF16 `torch.mm`, synchronized `torch.utils.benchmark.Timer.blocked_autorange(min_run_time=2.0)`, shapes labelled `(M,N,K)`, and one process per (mode, backend) because the caching mode latches into a function-local static on first use.

Two adjustments were needed for the numbers to be stable on these parts.

First, the dominant noise term is a per-process offset, not within-process jitter: the spread of per-process medians reached 4.3 us while the within-process Timer IQR is 0.01-0.8 us. So the run uses **20 alternating-order trials** and reports a **paired** statistic - `eager - cached` within a single trial - with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval and the per-trial sign count. Raising `min_run_time` does not help, since it only shrinks the term that was already small.

Second, that offset was tracked to CPU socket placement. The `gfx950` host is dual-socket with the GPU on one socket's PCIe root; at 11-17 us these GEMMs are dispatch-bound, so the measurement is dominated by host-side launch traffic, and a process scheduled onto the far socket pays an interconnect hop on every launch. Five pinned processes per socket measured +0.6 us for the far socket, and pinning collapsed the per-process spread from 1.95 us to 0.39 us. Both arms are therefore pinned to the GPU-local CPU list. The `gfx942` numbers are unpinned but do not need this: their same-mode control is 0.023 us median / 0.156 us worst case.

The control referred to above is a same-mode null - splitting one mode's own trials in half and differencing them, where the true answer is zero by construction, so the result is the noise floor of the instrument. Two further checks on the protocol: a negative delta is not physically possible here, since eager performs strictly more allocator work than cached, so any negative row indicates drift rather than a speedup; and the eager path was confirmed active in each binary by measuring per-operation workspace scratch after a warmup GEMM, 76-80 MiB in eager mode against 0 in cached mode.

### MI355X (`gfx950`)

Both arms pinned to the GPU-local socket.

| Backend | Shape (M,N,K) | Cached | Eager | Delta | Paired median | 95% CI | Eager slower |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| rocBLAS | (64,64,64) | 12.182 us | 12.337 us | +0.155 us / +1.28% | +0.208 us | [+0.080, +0.352] | 15/20 |
| rocBLAS | (256,256,256) | 12.035 us | 12.169 us | +0.134 us / +1.11% | +0.119 us | [+0.048, +0.164] | 14/20 |
| rocBLAS | (1024,1024,1024) | 11.186 us | 11.351 us | +0.165 us / +1.47% | +0.174 us | [+0.072, +0.368] | 14/20 |
| rocBLAS | (32,2048,10944) | 16.613 us | 16.790 us | +0.177 us / +1.07% | +0.290 us | [+0.004, +0.590] | 14/20 |
| hipBLASLt | (64,64,64) | 12.169 us | 12.297 us | +0.127 us / +1.05% | +0.114 us | [-0.140, +0.392] | 12/20 |
| hipBLASLt | (256,256,256) | 11.964 us | 12.152 us | +0.188 us / +1.57% | +0.285 us | [-0.014, +0.326] | 14/20 |
| hipBLASLt | (1024,1024,1024) | 11.114 us | 11.335 us | +0.221 us / +1.99% | +0.153 us | [-0.125, +0.326] | 14/20 |
| hipBLASLt | (32,2048,10944) | 16.612 us | 16.653 us | +0.041 us / +0.25% | +0.158 us | [-0.212, +0.550] | 12/20 |

Every shape here completes in 11-17 us, so all rows are launch-bound, and the cost is uniform across them at roughly +0.16 us: every delta is positive, every paired median is positive, four of the eight intervals exclude zero, and pooled over all 160 paired samples the median is +0.159 us with a 95% interval of [+0.110, +0.237]. The same-mode control on this part is 0.132 us median / 0.356 us worst case, so the pooled effect sits above the noise floor while no individual row is resolved much below it.

For reference, the unpinned version of this same run put four of the eight rows at a negative delta, down to -0.714 us, with every interval crossing zero and a same-mode control of 0.737 us median / 1.612 us worst case - larger than any delta in the table. Those negative rows were socket-assignment artifacts, not speedups.

### MI308X (`gfx942`)

| Backend | Shape (M,N,K) | Cached | Eager | Delta | Paired median | 95% CI | Eager slower |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| rocBLAS | (64,64,64) | 11.145 us | 11.472 us | +0.327 us / +2.93% | +0.306 us | [+0.281, +0.379] | 19/20 |
| rocBLAS | (256,256,256) | 11.195 us | 11.488 us | +0.292 us / +2.61% | +0.328 us | [+0.230, +0.372] | 19/20 |
| rocBLAS | (1024,1024,1024) | 55.440 us | 55.435 us | -0.005 us / -0.01% | -0.001 us | [-0.006, +0.007] | 8/20 |
| rocBLAS | (32,2048,10944) | 484.504 us | 484.493 us | -0.011 us / -0.00% | -0.024 us | [-0.048, +0.031] | 8/20 |
| hipBLASLt | (64,64,64) | 18.512 us | 18.753 us | +0.241 us / +1.30% | +0.259 us | [-0.050, +0.329] | 13/20 |
| hipBLASLt | (256,256,256) | 18.312 us | 18.464 us | +0.152 us / +0.83% | +0.127 us | [+0.061, +0.206] | 15/20 |
| hipBLASLt | (1024,1024,1024) | 24.419 us | 24.420 us | +0.001 us / +0.00% | -0.000 us | [-0.003, +0.003] | 10/20 |
| hipBLASLt | (32,2048,10944) | 34.160 us | 34.141 us | -0.019 us / -0.06% | -0.015 us | [-0.065, +0.020] | 8/20 |

This part carries the least per-process drift of the two, and unlike gfx950 it spans both duration regimes, so the rows are bimodal by operation duration:

- **Short, launch-bound** (11-19 us; the 64^3 and 256^3 shapes) - eager costs +0.13 to +0.33 us, three of four significant, worst relative case +2.93%.
- **Long, GPU-bound** (24-484 us; the 1024^3 and large-K shapes) - -0.02 to +0.00 us, none significant, and the intervals exclude +0.3 us, so the cost is absent rather than merely unresolvable.

The two regimes are not averaged together here, since a pooled figure would mix a real +0.3 us against four rows pinned at zero.

### Interpretation

The eager cost is CPU-side caching-allocator bookkeeping, and `torch.mm` is asynchronous. On a long GEMM that work overlaps GPU execution of the preceding operation and is free; on a short one, dispatch is the critical path and it shows up in full. The two parts agree on this: every gfx950 shape is launch-bound and all eight carry the cost at +0.16 us, while on gfx942 only the launch-bound rows carry it, at +0.13 to +0.33 us, and the GPU-bound rows are pinned at zero with intervals that exclude +0.3 us. So the data is consistent with a fixed per-operation cost of roughly 0.15-0.35 us, worth at most a few percent on operations short enough that launch overhead already dominates, and absent on any GEMM doing substantial work.

That is the same order as CUDA PR #194311 (0.07-0.85 us / 0.5-5.1%), and below it in absolute terms, despite the hipBLASLt workspace being 76-80 MiB against cuBLASLt's 1 MiB - the caching allocator returns the same block on every call, so workspace size does not enter the per-operation cost.

title: [FSDP] Stabilize fully_shard overlap timing test
body:
The overlap test emulates compute and communication with fixed-cycle GPU sleeps. DVFS and device contention can change their wall-clock duration between separate single-shot measurements, causing false failures under load.

Interleave reference and test measurements and compare their least-perturbed samples. This only improves timing stability; it does not relax assertions or tolerances, change emulated sleep durations, or add conditional retries or skips.

title: Prevent saving mutated grad inputs in AOT min-cut
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #185876

AOTAutograd clones data-mutated grad inputs in the joint trace so the
backward graph can read their pre-mutation values. For mutations replayed by
the runtime epilogue, the original primal placeholder is not a valid saved
activation: it aliases the user's input and is mutated after the AOT forward
returns, so backward can observe a bumped version counter.

Mark only grad-requiring primal inputs whose data mutation is
`MUTATED_OUT_GRAPH`, and make min-cut treat those placeholders as unsaveable.
Mutations kept inside the graph, including conservative hidden mutations from
custom Triton kernels, remain valid saved inputs. This distinction fixes the
original failure without making such graphs produce an infeasible min-cut.
The zero-budget input-only fast path remains in place unless an out-of-graph
mutation needs a safe cut.

Catching the resulting `NetworkXUnbounded` or suppressing its visualization
would only mask the incorrect constraint, so the fix narrows the mutation
classification at its source.

Fixes #185497

title: [Dynamo] Detect tensor mutations when reconstructing generators
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #185920

Dynamo reconstructs returned local generators by exhausting the remaining generator body during bytecode generation. Existing generator reconstruction side-effect checks rejected Python object mutations, but two paths still missed tensor data mutation: direct generator returns exhausted the generator without entering the reconstruction guard, and tensor writes were represented as FX tensor operations rather than normal SideEffects mutations.

This wraps direct returned-generator exhaustion in the generator reconstruction guard and teaches tensor operation paths to reject tensor writes while that guard is active. The detection covers mutating tensor methods, torch function schemas that write the first tensor argument, out= tensors, in-place builtin operators such as +=, and version-change based in-place mutations.

I considered relying only on fake tensor version changes after tracing, but some paths need to stop before graph insertion or before fake propagation mutates out= metadata. The schema checks keep the rejection close to each mutating entry point while still using the existing SideEffects error path.

Fixes #146628

title: [FSDP2] Separate sharded and unsharded gradient dtypes
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.15.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #194434

Fixes #170648. Based on #172074 by @arkadip-maitra.

> Authored with Codex.
>
> Preserve each parameter's pre-FSDP grad_dtype policy on reduced shards. The unsharded leaf uses an explicit MixedPrecisionPolicy.reduce_dtype, otherwise the parameter's explicit grad_dtype (including None); parameters without an override use the original parameter dtype `P`, independently of `MixedPrecisionPolicy.param_dtype`. Defaulting unconditionally to compute dtype discarded explicit gradient precision: BF16 parameters with FP32 grad_dtype accumulated 256 + 1 - 256 as 0 instead of 1. Preserving the gradient policy keeps this accumulation in FP32.
>
> Reduce gradients in groups with the same actual dtype while retaining the existing all-gather grouping. Retain every HSDP all-reduce buffer until completion, and preserve higher-precision partial gradients if an unrestricted policy produces a different dtype later. Reduction casts outputs to each shard's dtype, using a flat cast for uniform policies and grouped foreach copies otherwise. Including unused parameters in reduction requires an explicit reduce_dtype when grad_dtype is explicitly None, so every rank can construct compatible zero gradients.
>
> Capture the policy at fully_shard(), including explicit None. Default policies follow parameter dtype changes, while explicit overrides survive conversion and load_state_dict(assign=True) replacement. Direct grad_dtype edits afterward, including before lazy initialization, are intentionally unsupported and raise at the next FSDP boundary. A code comment and API documentation state this limit.
>
> Keep native gradient owners separate: unreduced accumulation stays on the unsharded parameter's .grad, reduced history stays on the sharded parameter's .grad, and HSDP retains local reduction buffers until all-reduce completes. Combining FP32 reduced history with BF16 pending accumulation would lose information: 256 synchronized, then 1 without synchronization, then -256 synchronized must produce 1. HSDP retains per-parameter views so later microbatches can use different parameter subsets without confusing packed offsets.
>
> Start review with dtype initialization and reduction output casts, then native accumulation ownership and gradient clearing. In the sharded state, model.parameters() exposes sharded parameters and their reduced .grad. In the unsharded state, it exposes unsharded parameters and their accumulation .grad. HSDP partial reduction buffers remain internal. Integer reshard_after_forward retains its existing temporary parameter layout without gradients. With CPU offload, unreduced gradients stay on the compute device and reduced shards are offloaded.
>
> Ordinary nn.Module.zero_grad() clears only the currently registered parameters. Clearing sharded gradients preserves hidden unsharded accumulation; clearing unsharded gradients preserves reduced history and internal HSDP partials. Gradient reduction consumes the unsharded .grad and sets it to None, while HSDP retains partial buffers until all-reduce completes. synchronize_gradients() completes pending reductions before global clipping or optimizer updates; callers retaining unsharded parameters also reshard before updating them. Conversion checks preserve native buffers on no-op conversions and explain how to complete reduction, reshard, and clear gradients before incompatible conversions. Pending gradients must be consumed or cleared on their actual owners before changing reduction policy.
>
> **Sharded gradient dtype:**
>
> These three rows fully determine `self.sharded_grad_dtype`. Neither mixed-precision field nor `self.unsharded_grad_dtype` changes this stored policy.
>
> | 1. Model parameter dtype before `fully_shard` | 2. Model parameter `grad_dtype` before `fully_shard` | 3. `self.sharded_grad_dtype` | 4. BC-breaking? Reason |
> | --- | --- | --- | --- |
> | `P` | Not set | `P` | **No.** Sharded dtype unchanged |
> | `P` | Explicit `G` | `G` | **Yes.** Sharded dtype follows `G` |
> | `P` | Explicit `None` | `None` | **Yes.** Fixed shard cast removed |
>
> **Unsharded gradient dtype and reduction:**
>
> Without an explicit `reduce_dtype`, `self.unsharded_grad_dtype` follows `self.sharded_grad_dtype`, independently of `param_dtype`. `Not set` and explicit `G=P` both resolve to `P`, including when `param_dtype=M`.
>
> For any actual parameter dtype `P`, all 12 combinations are listed below: three input gradient policies, two `param_dtype` choices, and two `reduce_dtype` choices. The BC column here covers only unsharded accumulation and reduction; sharded policy changes are covered above.
>
> | 1. Model parameter dtype before `fully_shard` | 2. Model parameter `grad_dtype` before `fully_shard` | 3. `mp_policy.param_dtype` | 4. `mp_policy.reduce_dtype` | 5. `self.unsharded_grad_dtype` | 6. BC-breaking? Reason |
> | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
> | `P` | Not set | Explicit `None` / not set (resolves to `P`) | Explicit `None` / not set (resolves to `P`) | `P` | **No.** Accumulation and reduction unchanged |
> | `P` | Not set | Explicit `None` / not set (resolves to `P`) | Explicit `R` | `R` | **Yes.** Autograd accumulation uses `R` |
> | `P` | Not set | Explicit `M` | Explicit `None` / not set (resolves to `P`) | `P` | **Yes.** Accumulation and reduction use `P` |
> | `P` | Not set | Explicit `M` | Explicit `R` | `R` | **Yes.** Autograd accumulation uses `R` |
> | `P` | Explicit `G` | Explicit `None` / not set (resolves to `P`) | Explicit `None` / not set (resolves to `G`) | `G` | **Yes.** Accumulation and reduction use `G` |
> | `P` | Explicit `G` | Explicit `None` / not set (resolves to `P`) | Explicit `R` | `R` | **Yes.** Autograd accumulation uses `R` |
> | `P` | Explicit `G` | Explicit `M` | Explicit `None` / not set (resolves to `G`) | `G` | **Yes.** Accumulation and reduction use `G` |
> | `P` | Explicit `G` | Explicit `M` | Explicit `R` | `R` | **Yes.** Autograd accumulation uses `R` |
> | `P` | Explicit `None` | Explicit `None` / not set (resolves to `P`) | Explicit `None` / not set (resolves to actual gradient dtype) | `None` | **Yes.** Reduction follows actual gradient dtype |
> | `P` | Explicit `None` | Explicit `None` / not set (resolves to `P`) | Explicit `R` | `R` | **Yes.** Autograd accumulation uses `R` |
> | `P` | Explicit `None` | Explicit `M` | Explicit `None` / not set (resolves to actual gradient dtype) | `None` | **Yes.** Reduction follows actual gradient dtype |
> | `P` | Explicit `None` | Explicit `M` | Explicit `R` | `R` | **Yes.** Autograd accumulation uses `R` |
>
> Test Plan
>
> All 52 focused tests pass: 16 CPU/CUDA accumulation and unrestricted-policy cases, 23 mixed-precision cases, 12 HSDP pending-gradient cases, and one two-rank unused-parameter case. These exercise cancellation, per-parameter gradient dtypes, explicit reduction overrides, changing incoming gradient dtypes, partial-only synchronization, changing parameter subsets, and CPU offload. The new FP32 cancellation regression fails on the previous implementation. Lint and whitespace checks pass.

> CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=4,5,6,7 /home/weif/.conda/envs/code-review/bin/python test/distributed/_composable/fsdp/test_fully_shard_pending_grad.py -k test_grad_dtype_pending_reductions -k test_native_partial_ownership -v

title: [dynamo] Lower the backward eagerly under the multi-graph capture config
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #198217
* #198227
* #198138
* #198216
* #198137
* __->__ #198215
* #198136
* #198214
* #198243
* #198135
* #198213
* #197993
* #198284
* #198283
* #198223
* #198211

**Problem.** `_capture_config` only forced the backward to lower eagerly for `training=True`, but AOTAutograd does not save a grad-enabled graph to the bundled cache until its backward has been lowered, so an ordinary inference capture made outside `torch.no_grad()` compiled fine and then had nothing to put in the artifact.

**Fix.** Set `force_non_lazy_backward_lowering` unconditionally in the capture config and drop the `training` parameter it used to gate on.

**Summary.** `_capture_config(training)` added `force_non_lazy_backward_lowering` to its functorch patch only when `training=True`, leaving inference captures with AOTAutograd's default of lowering a graph's backward lazily on the first `.backward()`. The cache entry the bundled artifact is built from is saved only once the backward has been lowered, so a graph compiled with grad enabled whose backward was never lowered records no backend at all -- and that is the ordinary inference case, a capture made outside `torch.no_grad()` on a model whose parameters require grad. The flag is now set unconditionally, so a graph compiled with grad enabled carries its backward into the artifact, and a call served under that grad mode returns outputs with a `grad_fn` as eager does. A call made under `torch.no_grad()` still compiles an inference graph, because the flag only changes when a backward that AOTAutograd would build anyway gets lowered, not whether one exists. With nothing left for it to select, the `training` parameter goes, and the two `_capture_config` tests pin the unconditional flag and its scoping.

## Where this fits

The stack replaces the callable `torch.compiler.precompile(fn, *example_inputs)` (trace once on inputs passed up front, pair returned in memory) with a caller-driven context manager: `capture(fn, artifact_path=, cache_path=)` is entered with a `with` block, the caller calls it on as many example inputs as they like (each graph break and recompiled variant is folded in), the `(python_code, cache)` pair is written to the two files on exit, and `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` serves it in a fresh process. The end-to-end example and the PR-by-PR map live in #197993's "The new API, end to end" section. This PR is plumbing for the multi-call `DynamoTracer` capture (#198138): the capture config always lowers the backward eagerly, so a grad-enabled call records its artifact.

## The patch dict, before and after

The parent built the functorch patch and then appended the eager-lowering flag under a condition:

```python
# parent: torch/_dynamo/precompile_package.py
@contextlib.contextmanager
def _capture_config(training: bool) -> Iterator[None]:
    functorch_patch = {
        "bundled_autograd_cache": True,
        "bypass_autograd_cache_key": True,
    }
    if training:
        functorch_patch["force_non_lazy_backward_lowering"] = True
    ...
```

Now the flag is part of the dict itself and the parameter is gone:

```python
# now
@contextlib.contextmanager
def _capture_config() -> Iterator[None]:
    functorch_patch = {
        "bundled_autograd_cache": True,
        "force_non_lazy_backward_lowering": True,
        "bypass_autograd_cache_key": True,
    }
    ...
```

The rest of the scope is unchanged: `strict_autograd_cache` still follows `torch._dynamo.config.strict_precompile`, `allow_empty_graphs` is still patched on, and `force_disable_caches` still raises `PackageError` up front. The docstring now says why the backward lowers eagerly for every capture: a graph compiled with grad enabled whose backward was never lowered is never saved, so a capture that never makes one -- a training step, or an inference call made outside `torch.no_grad()` -- would record no backend at all.

## Why an inference capture was affected

AOTAutograd lowers a graph's backward lazily, on the first `.backward()`, and the bundled cache entry is saved only once that has happened. A capture that only runs forwards never triggers the lowering:

```python
model = torch.nn.Linear(4, 4)          # parameters require grad
with _capture_config(training=False):  # parent: no eager lowering
    compiled(model, x)                 # grad enabled -> joint graph, backward deferred
# parent: no .backward() ever ran, so the entry was never saved -> no backend in the artifact
# now:    the backward is lowered at compile time, the entry is saved, the artifact has a backend
```

Under `torch.no_grad()` there is no backward to lower, so that path compiles an inference graph exactly as before.

## Tests

Both `_capture_config` tests move to the parameterless call and pin the flag as unconditional. `test_capture_config_is_scoped_per_entry_and_per_thread` reads the four patched flags in order (`bundled_autograd_cache`, `bypass_autograd_cache_key`, `force_non_lazy_backward_lowering`, `allow_empty_graphs`) from an all-`False` ambient:

```python
# parent
with _capture_config(training=False):
    self.assertEqual(flags(), (True, True, False, True))
    with _capture_config(training=True):
        self.assertEqual(flags(), (True, True, True, True))
    self.assertEqual(flags(), (True, True, False, True))

# now
with _capture_config():
    self.assertEqual(flags(), (True, True, True, True))
    with _capture_config():
        self.assertEqual(flags(), (True, True, True, True))
    self.assertEqual(flags(), (True, True, True, True))
self.assertEqual(flags(), ambient)
```

The same test still checks that an exception inside the scope restores the ambient flags, and that a worker thread holding its own `_capture_config()` scope sees `(True, True, True, True)` while the main thread's flags are untouched. `test_capture_config_refuses_disabled_caches_and_honours_strict` keeps its `force_disable_caches` refusal and its `strict_precompile` -> `strict_autograd_cache` checks, now written as `with _capture_config():`.

Test Plan:

python test/dynamo/test_precompile_package.py
lintrunner -a torch/_dynamo/precompile_package.py test/dynamo/test_precompile_package.py
```

title: [Dynamo] route PrivateUse1 autocast classes
body:
Dynamo recognizes the built-in autocast context managers, but an autocast
  subclass exposed by a registered PrivateUse1 device module can otherwise fall
  through to the user-defined class path. This prevents the context manager from
  being represented as an AutocastModeVariable during tracing.

  This change resolves `torch.<registered_backend>.amp.autocast` through the
  registered device module and routes the exact registered class through
  `TorchCtxManagerClassVariable`.

  The lookup first rejects ordinary functions and unrelated classes before
  accessing the registered device module. Class matching uses identity only;
  there is no source-file or qualified-name fallback.

  When reconstructing the context:

  - `device_type` is supplied from the registered backend only when the wrapper
    signature does not expose it.
  - An explicitly supplied `device_type` is preserved.
  - Missing `dtype`, `enabled`, and `cache_enabled` values use the base autocast
    defaults instead of raising an internal `KeyError`.

  The open registration tests exercise the actual `torch.compile(fullgraph=True)`
  routing path. Reduced-signature behavior is covered by a temporary registered

  This does not add a `DeviceInterface` slot, backend-specific metadata, or a new

title: [dynamo] Add PrecompileSession, the caller-driven multi-graph capture
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #198217
* #198227
* #198138
* #198216
* __->__ #198137
* #198215
* #198136
* #198214
* #198243
* #198135
* #198213
* #197993
* #198284
* #198283
* #198223
* #198211

**Problem.** `torch/_dynamo/precompile_package.py` held the pieces of a multi-graph capture -- the guard filter, the compiler configuration, the guard classification, the summary builder -- but nothing drove them, so no caller could record a function's compiled variants.

**Fix.** Add `PrecompileSession`, a context manager that compiles the function into a fresh `CompilePackage` under a recording guard filter and reports what the calls covered as a `PrecompileSummary`, with `precompile_capture(fn, *, backend, guard_filter_fn, recompile_limit, dynamic)` as its entry point.

**Summary.** The module had `default_guard_filter_fn`, `_capture_config`, the guard classification and `_summarize`, but no driver, so nothing under `torch/` could capture a function's variants. `PrecompileSession` is that driver: entering it compiles `fn` through `torch._dynamo.optimize` with a fresh `CompilePackage`, a filter that records every kept and dropped guard slot, the caller's `dynamic` and `recompile_limit`, and `isolate_recompiles=True`, and hands back a callable whose calls run under `_capture_config`. That callable records any exception a call raised for the summary and, after every call, takes the bundled AOTAutograd artifacts filed under its backend ids out of `PrecompileContext` with the new `take_artifact`, so another capture's `clear()` between calls cannot lose them. The key constraint is that the filter runs once per compilation, spells every slot through `_normalize` so the kept, dropped and risky sets and the facts compare with each other, and keys its `GuardFact` set by the code object the new `CompilePackage.current_entry` property names, which lets `summary()` report a dropped slot whose source held different values across a frame's variants as risky. Rendering the session as an artifact behind the coverage and guard gates is the next PR; the guard-drop invariance policy, the drift probe and the installed serving mode of the reference stack are out by design, and `truncated` is always empty.

## Where this fits

The stack replaces the callable `torch.compiler.precompile(fn, *example_inputs)` (trace once on inputs passed up front, pair returned in memory) with a caller-driven context manager: `capture(fn, artifact_path=, cache_path=)` is entered with a `with` block, the caller calls it on as many example inputs as they like (each graph break and recompiled variant is folded in), the `(python_code, cache)` pair is written to the two files on exit, and `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` serves it in a fresh process. The end-to-end example and the PR-by-PR map live in #197993's "The new API, end to end" section. This PR adds `PrecompileSession`, the multi-graph capture that the multi-call `DynamoTracer` front-end of `capture()` (#198138) is built on.

## Entering a session

The new test drives a graph-breaking step at two shapes and reads the summary inside the block:

```python
from torch._dynamo.precompile_package import precompile_capture

def step(model, x):
    y = model(x)
    torch._dynamo.graph_break()
    return y.sum(dim=0) + y.shape[0]

model = torch.nn.Linear(4, 4)
x2, x3 = torch.ones(2, 4), torch.ones(3, 4)
session = precompile_capture(step, backend="eager")
with session as call:
    call(model, x2)   # compiles step and its graph-break continuation
    call(model, x3)   # recompiles both for the second shape
    summary = session.summary()
call(model, x2)       # PackageError: "PrecompileSession is not active"
```

`__enter__` does one thing:

```python
self._compiled = torch._dynamo.optimize(
    self._backend,
    package=self._package,              # a fresh CompilePackage(fn)
    guard_filter_fn=self._guard_filter_fn,
    dynamic=self._dynamic,
    recompile_limit=self._recompile_limit,
    isolate_recompiles=True,
)(self._fn)
return self._call
```

`isolate_recompiles=True` gives the package its own cache region: a function captured (or compiled) earlier in the process would otherwise serve its existing cache entries and this package would record nothing. The test pins this by opening a `second` session on the same `step` after the first and checking `second.summary().guarded_codes >= 2`. A session cannot be re-entered: the test re-enters the finished `session` and expects `PackageError` ("cannot be re-entered; start a new capture").

## Each call runs under the capture configuration

The configuration is per call, not per block, so user code between calls (`optimizer.step`, data loading, a later `save()`) runs in the ambient configuration:

```python
def _call(self, *args, **kwargs):
    if self._compiled is None or self._finished:
        raise PackageError("PrecompileSession is not active")
    limit = max(self._recompile_limit, torch._dynamo.config.accumulated_recompile_limit)
    try:
        with _capture_config(), torch._dynamo.config.patch(accumulated_recompile_limit=limit):
            return self._compiled(*args, **kwargs)
    except Exception as e:
        message = f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"
        if message not in self._capture_errors:
            self._capture_errors.append(message)
        raise
    finally:
        self._take_backend_artifacts()
```

The ambient `accumulated_recompile_limit` is raised to at least the per-frame limit so the explicit `recompile_limit` is the effective one. An `Exception` is recorded once (deduplicated by message) and re-raised; a `BaseException` such as `KeyboardInterrupt` is not a capture error and propagates unrecorded. Either way the `finally` takes the call's backend artifacts (see "Taking the backend artifacts after every call" below). The test calls `call(model, torch.ones(2, 5))` on a `Linear(4, 4)`, catches the `RuntimeError`, and checks `failed.summary().complete` is false with exactly one `capture_errors` entry.

## The recording guard filter

A dropped guard does not fail at serving time; it silently widens what a graph is reused for, so the drops have to be inspectable. The session wraps `default_guard_filter_fn` (or the caller's filter) and, per compilation, records the decision for every `(guard_type, source)` slot:

```python
decisions = list(inner(entries))
default_kept = default_guard_filter_fn(entries) if self._custom_guard_filter else decisions
for keep, by_default, entry in zip(decisions, default_kept, entries):
    slot = (entry.guard_type, _normalize(strip_local_scope(entry.name)))
    enforced = keep or (_is_noop_guard_type(entry.guard_type) and global_state_kept)
    if enforced:
        self._kept_guards.add(slot)
    else:
        self._dropped_guards.add(slot)
        if rendered := " ; ".join(_render_code(entry.code_parts)):
            self._dropped_guard_code.setdefault(slot, rendered)
        if by_default or _is_risky_drop(entry, namespaces):
            self._risky_dropped_guards.add(slot)
    if entry.guard_type not in _UNMODELLED_GUARD_TYPES:
        facts.add(_GuardFact(guard_type=..., source=slot[1], code=..., value=_value_fingerprint(entry), enforced=enforced))
```

Every slot is normalized once, and `GuardFact.source` reuses `slot[1]`, so the dropped, risky and kept sets and the per-variant facts share one spelling and compare as equals. A dropped slot's rendered code is recorded only when it renders to something. A no-op guard type counts as enforced when `GLOBAL_STATE` is kept, since that is where its check lives. A drop the default filter would not have made (`by_default` true under a custom filter) is risky by construction: nothing here can say what the caller gave up. The test pins this with a custom filter that drops every `TENSOR_MATCH`:

```python
custom = precompile_capture(step, backend="eager",
                            guard_filter_fn=lambda es: [e.guard_type != "TENSOR_MATCH" for e in es])
with custom as call:
    call(model, x2)
("TENSOR_MATCH", "x") in custom.summary().risky_dropped_guards   # True
``` Unmodelled guard types are never compared, so they contribute no fact. One filter call is one compilation, and the package knows which frame is being compiled, so the fact set is filed under that frame:

```python
current = self._package.current_entry          # new property on CompilePackage
code = current.python_code
key = (code.co_name, code.co_filename, code.co_firstlineno)   # else ("<unknown>", "<unknown>", 0)
self._guard_sets.setdefault(key, []).append(frozenset(facts))
```

## `summary()`

`summary()` feeds the recorded sets to the landed `_summarize`, adding one more risk rule first: a dropped slot whose source held different values across a frame's variants is risky, because that guard was what told the variants apart and cannot pick between them at serve time. Merely being absent from one variant (a `MODULE_MATCH` a branch does not touch) is not. `test_a_dropped_guard_that_tells_variants_apart_is_risky` pins the rule: it rebinds the same-file global def `_act` (whose `CLOSURE_MATCH` the default filter drops) between two `dynamic=False` calls of `_through_act`, and `("CLOSURE_MATCH", "G['_act']")` is reported risky only when the def changed between the variants; it fails with the rule removed.

```python
risky = set(self._risky_dropped_guards)
for variants in self._guard_sets.values():
    values = {}
    for facts in variants:
        for f in facts:
            if not f.enforced:
                values.setdefault((f.guard_type, f.source), set()).add(f.value)
    risky |= {slot for slot, seen in values.items() if len(seen) > 1}
return _summarize(self._package.cache_entry(), dropped=..., kept=..., policy_dropped=set(),
                  risky=risky, truncated=frozenset(), capture_errors=..., guard_sets=..., dropped_code=...)
```

For the two-shape capture above the test checks:

```python
summary.complete                                  # True
(summary.frames, summary.resume_functions)        # (2, 1): step and its continuation
summary.guarded_codes >= 3                        # recompiled for the second shape
"MODULE_MATCH" in summary.dropped_guard_types     # the default filter's drop
("CLOSURE_MATCH", "G['torch']._dynamo.graph_break") in summary.dropped_guards
summary.kept_guards                               # non-empty
summary.risky_dropped_guards                      # ()
```

## Taking the backend artifacts after every call

The AOTAutograd cache records a bundled entry under each graph's backend id as the graph compiles, into a process-global list on `PrecompileContext`. After every call, in `_call`'s `finally`, the session moves this package's entries out of that list through the new `take_artifact`, a `pop` next to `serialize_artifact_by_key`; `__exit__` only marks the session finished and drops the compiled callable:

```python
@classmethod
def take_artifact(cls, key: str) -> BackendCacheArtifact[Any] | None:
    return cls._backend_artifacts_by_key.pop(_BackendId(key), None)

# PrecompileSession._take_backend_artifacts
for backend_id in self._package.cache_entry().backend_ids:
    if backend_id not in self._backend_artifacts:
        artifact = PrecompileContext.take_artifact(backend_id)
        if artifact is not None:
            self._backend_artifacts[backend_id] = artifact
```

Taking them as the capture goes keeps another capture's `PrecompileContext.clear()` between calls from losing them. Ownership moves to the session: once taken, an id is no longer found by `serialize_artifact_by_key`, as the `take_artifact` docstring says.

## `precompile_capture` and what it refuses

`precompile_capture` builds the session after three up-front refusals, each pinned by the test:

```python
precompile_capture(functools.partial(step, model))   # PackageError: "... cannot capture a partial ..."
precompile_capture(model)                            # PackageError: "... capture the function that CALLS the model ..."
precompile_capture(model.forward)                    # PackageError: "... cannot capture a bound method ..."
```

A `functools.partial` is refused because its bound arguments are not on the code object. A bare `nn.Module` is refused because Dynamo compiles it through its own wrapper frame, whose graphs close over the module, which a standalone artifact cannot rebuild; the message suggests a module-level `def step(model, x): return model(x)`. A bound method (`types.MethodType`) is refused because the artifact rebuilds `fn` from its code object, whose first parameter is the receiver: a captured `model.forward` would be served as `f(model, x)` instead of `f(x)`, so the message points at a module-level function that takes the receiver as an argument. `recompile_limit` defaults to 256, well above Dynamo's usual 8, because a precompile deliberately wants one compiled variant per condition, whereas the normal limit exists to catch runaway recompilation. Runtime guards stay intact during capture: `guard_filter_fn` applies only to the serialized guard state, so every call observes the same recompilation behavior as ordinary `torch.compile`.

## Scope

Rendering the session as an artifact, behind the coverage and guard gates, is the next commit (#198216). Not here, by design: the guard-drop invariance policy, the drift probe and the installed serving mode of the reference stack; `truncated` is always empty. `test_precompile_session_captures_variants_and_summarizes` pins everything above except the varied-value rule, which `test_a_dropped_guard_that_tells_variants_apart_is_risky` pins.

Test Plan:

`test_precompile_session_captures_variants_and_summarizes` captures a graph-breaking step at two shapes and checks the summary (frames, continuation, variants, dropped and kept slots), the inactive-session and re-entry refusals, a call that raised, a second session on the same function, a custom filter's drop reported risky, and the partial/module/bound-method refusals. `test_a_dropped_guard_that_tells_variants_apart_is_risky` rebinds a same-file global def between two static-shape calls and checks the dropped slot is reported risky only when the def changed (it fails with the varied-value rule removed).

```
python test/dynamo/test_precompile_package.py
python test/dynamo/test_package.py
lintrunner -a torch/_dynamo/precompile_package.py torch/_dynamo/precompile_context.py torch/_dynamo/package.py test/dynamo/test_precompile_package.py
```

title: [dynamo] Validate getattr arguments before dispatch
body:
## Summary

Part of #195901.

`GetAttrBuiltinVariable` accessed positional arguments before validating `getattr()` calls. Too few arguments could raise an internal `IndexError`, excess arguments could be silently ignored, and keyword arguments were not rejected before dispatch. Non-string attribute names could also surface as internal Dynamo errors.

This change uses `no_keywords` and `check_positional` to match CPython’s argument validation, validates attribute names before generic lookup, adds focused regression coverage for invalid calls, and removes the CPython 3.13 expected-failure marker for `BuiltinTest.test_getattr`.
