title: [functorch] Decouple AOTDispatch tests from hardware-specific execution
body:
I reviewed the implementation and the AI-generated description below. It accurately describes the hardware-decoupling goal, the constrained class split, and the preservation of existing test coverage.

> ## Summary
>
> This PR hardware-decouples `test_aotdispatch.py` so that its generic and accelerator-wide AOTDispatch coverage can be reused by registered out-of-tree backends.
>
> It classifies the existing test classes as generic, CPU-specific, CUDA-specific, or accelerator-wide, and moves hardware-specific test methods into dedicated device-test templates. Eligible accelerator tests use an exclusion list instead of a device allowlist, allowing registered PrivateUse1 backends to participate without adding backend names to this file.
>
> ## Motivation
>
> The standard hardware-decoupling pattern is to split tests into hardware-homogeneous classes, add hardware-classification labels, instantiate device-generic classes, and rely on the capability-registration infrastructure for backend participation.
>
> `test_aotdispatch.py` cannot apply that pattern as a simple class split. Its main AOTAutograd suite is reused by Dynamo and cache variants through inheritance, and those variants also depend on `xfail_inherited_tests` and overridden execution helpers. In addition, device-test instantiation only materializes the test entries exposed by each template class. A direct split or ordinary inheritance-based decomposition would therefore risk changing test discovery, inherited expected-failure behavior, or which `run_autograd` and verification implementation executes.
>
> This change uses a constrained split:
>
> - The existing public generic classes and their shared helper methods remain in place.
> - Only tests with hardware-specific proof goals move into dedicated CUDA or accelerator classes.
> - Small private bases reuse the existing AOTAutograd, Dynamo, cache, partitioning, and module-simplified execution paths.
> - Explicit Dynamo and cache accelerator variants preserve the original overridden execution and inherited-xfail behavior.
> - Pure CPU classes remain CPU-specific and are not admitted to PrivateUse1.
>
> This keeps the existing mechanisms intact while separating hardware policy from the generic test suites.
>
> Capability registration is not needed here. The refactor is constrained by test discovery, inherited xfail behavior, and Dynamo/cache helper selection, none of which capability gates control. After splitting, device eligibility is fully determined by the device matrix and existing skips; there are no optional runtime capability consumers.
>
> ## Changes
>
> - Add `HardwareClassification` metadata to the existing generic and CPU-specific test classes.
> - Split CUDA-only AOTAutograd, partitioning, and module-simplified tests into CUDA-classified classes.
> - Split CPU-plus-accelerator tests into accelerator-classified device-test templates.
> - Preserve the existing Dynamo and cache execution paths for the split AOTAutograd tests.
> - Replace accelerator allowlisting with backend exclusions, currently retaining the existing HPU exclusion.
> - Add the PrivateUse1 autocast dispatch registration needed by the accelerator-wide autocast tests.
>
> Existing test coverage and test behavior for CPU, CUDA/ROCm, MPS, XPU, HPU, and the other previously covered devices are unchanged. No existing test is removed from its applicable hardware scope. The only coverage expansion is admission of eligible registered PrivateUse1 backends.
>
> #198365 extracts the class split and hw_classification labels from this PR as a separate structural change. After #198365 lands, rebase this PR on it so the device parameterization and Triton admission changes can be reviewed here on their own.
>
> ## Test Plan
>

> python3 -m py_compile test/functorch/test_aotdispatch.py

title: [precompile] Add DynamoTracer and serve its captures through capture()
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #198217
* #198227
* __->__ #198138
* #198216
* #198137
* #198215
* #198136
* #198214
* #198243
* #198135
* #198213
* #197993
* #198284
* #198283
* #198223
* #198211

**Problem.** `torch.compiler.precompile.capture()` only took a `MakeFxTracer`: one positional call, one ATen trace, no graph breaks, no recompiled variants, no keyword arguments. The `PrecompileSession` of the previous commits can record all of those, but nothing in the public module reached it.

**Fix.** Add `DynamoTracer`, the multi-graph front-end passed as `tracer=`, and `_DynamoCapture`, the `Capture` that drives a `PrecompileSession` across as many calls as the block makes and writes the standalone artifact on a clean exit, so `load()` serves it in a fresh process.

**Summary.** `capture()` accepted a `MakeFxTracer` and nothing else, so a function with a graph break, a shape-dependent branch or a keyword argument could not be precompiled through `torch.compiler.precompile` even though `PrecompileSession` and `snapshot_artifact` could already record and render such captures. This commit adds `DynamoTracer(guard_filter_fn, recompile_limit, dynamic, require_complete, require_no_risky_drops, require_no_dropped_guards)` beside `MakeFxTracer`, and `_DynamoCapture`, which enters the session under a fresh `CacheArtifactManager` cache so the inductor bundle in the cache half holds only this capture's compiles (the swap spans the whole block, which the `capture()` docstring now states), counts attempted calls so a block whose calls all raised gets the `require_complete` report rather than "nothing was captured", refuses a recursive re-entry, and on a clean exit renders the pair behind the three `require_*` gates and writes it, while a block that raised writes nothing and a gate refusal is raised after teardown with nothing written. The artifact is standalone, so `fn` must be a module-level function of an importable module, an artifact whose capture graph-broke cannot load beside the live compile that captured it (the continuation names collide, and `load` says so), and it is locked to the producing Python version and torch build. A Dynamo capture runs every call in the caller's grad mode and lowers a backward whenever grad is enabled, so a training step that calls `.backward()` captures its compiled backward and the served artifact accumulates `.grad` like eager, which a fresh-process test checks on both backends. `MakeFxTracer` stays the default for two more commits, package and recompile errors surface as `PrecompileError`, and mid-block `save()` checkpoints and `summary()` are the next commit's, so `save()` on this tracer raises a `PrecompileError` saying its artifact is written when the block exits.

## Where this fits

The stack replaces the callable `torch.compiler.precompile(fn, *example_inputs)` (trace once on inputs passed up front, pair returned in memory) with a caller-driven context manager: `capture(fn, artifact_path=, cache_path=)` is entered with a `with` block, the caller calls it on as many example inputs as they like (each graph break and recompiled variant is folded in), the `(python_code, cache)` pair is written to the two files on exit, and `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` serves it in a fresh process. The end-to-end example and the PR-by-PR map live in #197993's "The new API, end to end" section. This PR is where `capture()` becomes multi-call: `DynamoTracer` takes as many calls as the caller makes and folds every graph break and recompile they exercise into one artifact. It becomes the default tracer in #198217.

## The golden path

The new tests write a module with a graph-breaking step, capture it over two shapes and a keyword default, and serve it in a fresh process:

```python
# precompile_golden_<uuid>.py, importable from sys.path
def step(model, x, *, scale=1.0):
    y = model(x) * scale * SCALE
    torch._dynamo.graph_break()
    if y.shape[0] > 2:
        y = y + 1
    return y.sum(dim=0)
```

```python
from torch.compiler.precompile import capture, DynamoTracer, load

with capture(step, artifact_path="m.py", cache_path="m.cache", tracer=DynamoTracer(), backend="inductor") as cap:
    y2 = cap(model, x2)               # step and its graph-break continuation
    y3 = cap(model, x3, scale=0.5)    # the branch recompiles the continuation; the keyword is a second entry variant
# exit: TRACER = "dynamo", SERVING_MODE = "standalone", FN_NAME = 'step' in m.py

load("m.py", "m.cache")               # in this process: PrecompileError, the message says to use a fresh process
```

```python
# a fresh process
f = torch.compiler.precompile.load("m.py", "m.cache")
f(model, x2)                          # == y2
f(model, x3, scale=0.5)               # == y3
f(model, x2.double())                 # PrecompileError: no captured variant
```

The last line is the standalone contract: there is no compiler behind a source artifact, so a call no variant covers raises rather than silently serving. `test_graph_breaks_and_recompiles_round_trip_in_a_fresh_process` pins this on both backends, including the in-process collision refusal; `test_a_single_graph_serves_in_process` pins the no-graph-break case, where `load` works in the capturing process, `f.installed` is false, `with f:` and `f.unload()` are no-ops, a second `Model()` swaps weights in, and `f(model, x3)` after a shape-2 capture raises `no captured variant`.

## `DynamoTracer` carries the multi-graph knobs

```python
@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True)
class DynamoTracer:
    guard_filter_fn: Callable[[Sequence[Any]], Sequence[bool]] | None = None
    recompile_limit: int = 256
    dynamic: bool | None = None
    require_complete: bool = True
    require_no_risky_drops: bool = True
    require_no_dropped_guards: bool = False
```

`guard_filter_fn` filters the guards kept in the serialized artifact (runtime capture guards are always retained; the default drops only what cannot be serialized), `recompile_limit` caps recompilations per frame, and `dynamic` forces dynamic shapes as `torch.compile(dynamic=)` does. The `require_*` gates refuse, at write time, an artifact with a coverage gap (`require_complete`: a bypassed or uncovered frame, a call that raised), one whose dropped guards told captured variants apart or hang off a configuration-chosen slot (`require_no_risky_drops`), or one that dropped any guard at all (`require_no_dropped_guards`, off by default since every model drops identity guards that cannot be serialized). The docstring names what `guard_filter_fn` receives: the `GuardFilterEntry` records (`guard_type`, `name`, ...), returning one keep flag per entry. The annotation stays `Sequence[Any]` rather than naming `GuardFilterEntry`, because torch/compiler/precompile.py resolves the re-homed classes' annotations with `typing.get_type_hints` at import.

`test_the_tracer_knobs_reach_the_session` pins that the knobs get through to the session: a `DynamoTracer(dynamic=True)` capture of `single` on `x2` serves `x3` too, and a `guard_filter_fn` that drops the guard on `x` on top of `default_guard_filter_fn` (dropping what tells the shapes apart) is refused by `require_no_risky_drops` (`can affect dispatch`), while the same filter with `require_no_risky_drops=False` writes an artifact that loads. `DynamoTracer(dynamic=False, recompile_limit=1)` called on `x2` then `x3` keeps only the first shape's variant, so the served artifact refuses `x3` with `no captured variant`. `test_the_strict_gate_refuses_dropped_guards` shows the default capture of `single` listing `['MODULE_MATCH', ...` in the artifact's dropped guards, and `DynamoTracer(require_no_dropped_guards=True)` refusing the same capture with a `dropped ... guard` error.

## `capture()` dispatches on the tracer

```python
tracer: MakeFxTracer | DynamoTracer = MakeFxTracer()
...
if isinstance(tracer, MakeFxTracer):
    return _MakeFxCapture(fn, artifact_path, cache_path, backend=backend, decompositions=tracer.decompositions)
if not isinstance(tracer, DynamoTracer):
    raise TypeError("precompile.capture tracer must be a MakeFxTracer or DynamoTracer, got ...")
if backend not in ("inductor", "eager"):
    raise ValueError(f"precompile backend must be 'inductor' or 'eager', got {backend!r}.")
try:
    session = precompile_capture(fn, backend=backend, guard_filter_fn=tracer.guard_filter_fn, recompile_limit=tracer.recompile_limit, dynamic=tracer.dynamic)
except PackageError as e:
    raise PrecompileError(str(e)) from e
return _DynamoCapture(session, artifact_path, cache_path, require_complete=..., require_no_risky_drops=..., require_no_dropped_guards=...)
```

The make_fx front-end validates `backend` when it builds its `PrecompiledModule`; the Dynamo front-end builds none, so `capture()` checks it before creating the session. `precompile_capture`'s up-front refusals now surface as `PrecompileError`, which `test_entries_a_standalone_artifact_cannot_rebuild_are_refused` pins: a bare `nn.Module` (`CALLS the model`: Dynamo compiles its wrapper frame, whose graphs close over the module) and a closure entry (`closes over`), since a code object cannot rebuild what the closure captured. A `functools.partial` never reaches the tracer: `capture()` itself refuses it with a `TypeError` (`takes the function itself, not a functools.partial`) before dispatching, and the same test asserts that `TypeError`. `_MakeFxCapture`'s two refusals (a keyword argument, a second call) now point at `tracer=DynamoTracer()` instead of just explaining themselves.

## `_DynamoCapture` drives the session

Entering the block opens a fresh cache before the session, and undoes it if the session refuses to enter:

```python
def __enter__(self):
    with self._lock:
        if self._call is not None or self._exited:
            raise PrecompileError("this capture has already been entered; capture() returns a fresh capture per call.")
        self._fresh_cache = CacheArtifactManager.with_fresh_cache()
        self._fresh_cache.__enter__()
        try:
            self._call = self._map(self._session.__enter__)
        except BaseException:
            self._fresh_cache.__exit__(None, None, None)
            self._fresh_cache = None
            raise
    return self
```

The capture's compiles record into the process-global cache-artifact list, which the cache half of the artifact bundles to prime the kernel caches on load; a fresh one means the bundle holds only this capture's compiles. The swap spans the whole `with` block, not just the calls, so anything else compiled inside the block records into the same list; the `capture()` docstring now says a `DynamoTracer` capture records the kernel-cache artifacts of everything compiled inside the block, so compile nothing else there and do not overlap two such captures. `_map` is the one place `PackageError` and `RecompileError` become `PrecompileError`. Each call is serialized under an `RLock`, refuses a call before `__enter__` or after `__exit__` (`capture is not active`), refuses `fn` calling the capture it is being captured through (`re-entered recursively`), and counts the call before it runs:

```python
def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs):
    with self._lock:
        ...
        self._in_call = True
        # Counted before the call: a call that raised is for the session's
        # require_complete gate to report, not "nothing was captured".
        self._calls += 1
        try:
            return self._map(self._call, *args, **kwargs)
        finally:
            self._in_call = False
```

Counting attempts rather than successes matters for a block whose only calls raised: it made calls, so exit goes on to `snapshot_artifact`, and the session's `require_complete` report lists the capture errors instead of the misleading `nothing was captured`.

Exit writes on a clean block only, and holds a gate refusal until the session and cache are torn down:

```python
def __exit__(self, *exc):
    with self._lock:
        error = None
        try:
            if exc[0] is None:
                try:
                    if self._calls == 0:
                        raise PrecompileError("nothing was captured: call the capture with your example arguments inside the `with` block.")
                    self._write()        # snapshot_artifact(**gates) then _write_artifact(...)
                except BaseException as e:
                    error = e
            self._exited = True
            try:
                self._map(self._session.__exit__, *exc)
            except BaseException as e:
                if error is None:
                    raise
                raise e from error
        finally:
            if self._fresh_cache is not None:
                self._fresh_cache.__exit__(None, None, None)
                self._fresh_cache = None
    if exc[0] is None and error is not None:
        raise error
```

A teardown error that follows a gate refusal is raised `from` the refusal, so the refusal is not lost, and the fresh cache is always exited with `(None, None, None)` rather than with the in-flight exception. `_write` renders through `self._session.snapshot_artifact(**self._gates)` and hands the pair to `_write_artifact`; an `OSError` there becomes a `PrecompileError` (`precompile could not write the artifact`), and since `_write_artifact` leaves the previous pair in place the last good pair is still loadable. `test_a_raised_call_is_refused_at_exit_and_writes_nothing` pins the gate: a second call with `torch.randn(2, 5)` into a `Linear(4, 4)` raises `RuntimeError` inside the block, the block itself runs to completion, exit raises `PrecompileError` (`captured call raised`) through `require_complete`, and neither `m.py` nor `m.cache` exists afterwards. The same test covers a block whose only call raised, which reaches the same `captured call raised` gate rather than `nothing was captured`, and `DynamoTracer(require_complete=False)`, which writes the partial artifact instead.

`test_misuse_is_refused` pins the rest of the lifecycle: a bad backend (`backend="aot_eager"`) raises `ValueError`, an unknown tracer (`tracer=object()`) raises `TypeError` (`tracer must be`), a call before the block raises `not active`, an empty block raises `nothing was captured`, a second `with` on the same capture raises `already been entered`, a call after it raises `not active` again, a `Reentrant` module whose `forward` calls the capture raises `re-entered recursively`, a block raising its own `KeyError` propagates it unchanged and writes nothing, and a mocked `_write_artifact` raising `OSError` surfaces as `PrecompileError` (`could not write`).

## Grad mode and the training step

`capture()` has no grad-mode flag. A Dynamo capture runs every call in the caller's own grad mode and lowers a backward whenever grad is enabled: a `.backward()` in `fn` graph-breaks and re-runs at serve time through the live autograd engine, accumulating `.grad` like eager, so a training step is captured like any other call, and the artifact should be served under the grad mode it was captured in.

```python
def train_step(model, x):
    model(x).sum().backward()

with capture(train_step, ..., tracer=DynamoTracer(), backend=backend) as cap:   # backend: "inductor" or "eager"
    cap(model, x2)                    # returns None; model.lin.weight.grad matches an eager step

# a fresh process, model reloaded from the pre-step state dict
f = torch.compiler.precompile.load("m.py", "m.cache")
f(model, x2)                          # returns None; every parameter's .grad matches the eager step
```

`test_training_step_grads_match_eager_in_a_fresh_process`, parametrized over `inductor` and `eager`, is what pins the claim that the served artifact accumulates `.grad` like eager: it runs an eager step on a `Model` loaded from the same state dict, checks the capture's `lin.weight` grad against it, restores the pre-step weights, and serves the artifact in a fresh process, asserting each parameter's `.grad` against the eager one.

## The artifact does not mix with a make_fx pair

`test_a_dynamo_pair_does_not_mix_with_a_make_fx_pair` captures `single` once with `DynamoTracer()` and once with `MakeFxTracer()` into two pairs; `load` of the Dynamo artifact with the make_fx cache raises `PrecompileError` mentioning `tracer`, and the reverse raises `tracer` or `does not match`. `load`'s docstring now says a Dynamo artifact takes keyword arguments, that entering and unloading it are no-ops, that it re-seeds the names Dynamo minted into the captured module, and that an artifact whose capture graph-broke must be loaded in a fresh process.

## Exports, docs and scope

`DynamoTracer` joins `torch.compiler.precompile.__all__`, the `__module__` re-homing loop, the public-members test, and the API reference (`.. autoclass:: torch.compiler.precompile.DynamoTracer` in docs/source/torch.compiler_api.md). `MakeFxTracer` stays the default for two more commits; the tests pass `tracer=DynamoTracer()` explicitly through `_capture`. Mid-block `save()` checkpoints and the `summary()` report are the next commit's (#198227), so `_DynamoCapture.save()` raises `PrecompileError` (`save() is not supported on a DynamoTracer capture yet: its artifact is written when the block exits.`) rather than the base class's bare `NotImplementedError`. The module Note's `tracer:` paragraph now describes both tracers (`MakeFxTracer` the default, `DynamoTracer` standalone and version-locked, refusing uncovered calls through its guards and listing the guards it could not serialize as `DROPPED_GUARDS`) instead of saying `dynamo` raises `NotImplementedError`. Deliberately absent, as follow-ups: the installed serving mode (`load(fn=)`), the rendered-as-source subgraphs, the invariants report and the per-frame drift probe. The fresh-process tests are skipped under the crossref harness, whose active dispatch mode Dynamo guards on and a fresh process lacks.

Test Plan:

title: Preserve input aliases for multi-output view returns
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #186503

AOTAutograd classified differentiable multi-output views of graph inputs as
non-alias outputs. All siblings then shared one `CompiledFunctionBackward`, so
backward on the first output freed saved state required by later outputs.

This change keeps those results as input aliases and reconstructs their eager
view graph outside the compiled autograd function. To avoid quadratic replay, it
groups outputs by the exact shared autograd view node, finds the last
multi-output operation in each chain, replays that operation once, and applies
each sibling's own suffix views. The implementation supports both saved
functionalization `ViewMeta` recipes and autograd `ViewFunc` chains, including
prefixes, heterogeneous multi-operation suffixes, reordered/subset results, and
independent identical calls.

Symbolic view recipes may be removed before cache serialization, so trace-time
lazy conjugate/negative metadata is retained and restored with differentiable
view operations during fallback. When synthetic bases replace input views, stale
recipes relative to the pre-merge input are discarded. Metadata mutations retain
their logical version ordering so regenerated views remain valid, while inference
tensors and failed compiled calls preserve their expected version behavior.

The existing optimization for views of computed intermediates remains intact.
Nested multi-output chains batch their last shared operation; fully memoizing
earlier multi-output prefixes across independent inner groups is intentionally
left as a broader optimization.

Fixes #118739

title: Preserve SymInt bindings in dynamic-shape minifier repros
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #186520

Dynamic-shape FX graphs can have SymInt placeholders whose only purpose is
to bind a symbol used by FakeTensor metadata. The minifier's unused-input
cleanup only looked at graph users, so it could erase one of these otherwise
unused SymInt placeholders while leaving tensor metadata that still referenced
the symbol. That produced invalid minified graphs with free symbols and no
binding node.

Fix this by treating symbol-binding placeholders as live when remaining node
metadata still references their symbol and no other remaining node binds it.
This keeps the minifier's graph/input invariant intact without preserving
unrelated unused inputs.

The generated after-aot repro path had the same class of metadata loss: when
called with concrete integer args for a graph whose placeholder metadata was
symbolic, it serialized the SymInt as a plain int and selected real tracing.
Use matching symbolic placeholder metadata for concrete int args, and select
symbolic tracing when graph metadata contains free symbols.

An existing local PR candidate, #185473, was checked and skipped as a duplicate:
it fixes AOTAutograd partitioner / Inductor backward SymInt binding propagation,
not fx_minifier input pruning or after_aot repro serialization.

Fixes #114296

title: Fix reinplace alias checks for index_put
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #185450

Inductor's reinplace pass can rewrite functional index_put into its in-place variant when the destination has no later observable uses. That check was only reasoning about later uses of the destination tensor. It did not account for operands that index_put reads during the operation.

When self aliases either the values tensor or a tensor entry in the indices list, rewriting aten.index_put.default to aten.index_put_.default changes a functional update into an in-place read/write overlap. That is unsafe: eager either needs functional clone semantics or raises the usual overlap error for the in-place form. The same hazard applies to the _unsafe_index_put mapping, and the extra_check hook also has to handle with_effects nodes where inner op arguments are shifted by the token and op operands.

This adds an index_put-specific reinplace eligibility check that rejects overlap between self and all read tensor operands: values plus every tensor nested in indices. The check is shared by aten.index_put.default and aten._unsafe_index_put.default, and it accounts for with_effects positional argument offsets.

An older abandoned draft PR for #156786 only checked the last positional argument, which misses schemas with an accumulate argument and does not cover indices. This version keys off the operator schema positions instead.

Fixes #156786

title: Make FX traceback preserve state thread-local
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #184917

FX traceback stored preservation flags and metadata in module globals. A
preserve_node_meta or sequence-number context in one thread therefore changed
what concurrent tracing work observed, leaking metadata across threads.

Move the state behind one Python thread-local object while preserving the
existing mutable current_meta interface and boolean behavior. Python TLS alone
is not captured by autograd's C++ ThreadLocalState, so publish the caller's
live state through ThreadLocalPythonObjects while a preservation context is
active. This lets a GraphTask snapshot see metadata updates made after context
entry.

A native snapshot initially shares its Python object with the caller. Lazily
copy and re-stash the state on the first mutable access whose GraphTask ID does
not match its marker. GraphTask.thread_locals_ retains the original seed, so
the engine reinstalls a mismatching seed for each NodeTask and each NodeTask
gets a private copy. Reentrant GraphTasks similarly fork from the active outer
state. ThreadLocalStateGuard restores the prior native object on success or
exception and keeps posthook metadata alive through InputBuffer.add. This also
isolates mutations from tensor or user prehooks that run before the AOT
traceback prehook.

Ordinary caller tracing skips native object-map probes when no GraphTask is
active, and TracerBase.create_node snapshots the combined state once to avoid
repeated TLS lookups on the FX hot path. The process-global callback_set
workaround is removed because native TLS restoration now owns cleanup and the
global set was itself racy.

Fixes #173816

title: [dynamo] Add `DELETE_GLOBAL` handler
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #197057
* __->__ #197056

### Summary

Dynamo had no `DELETE_GLOBAL` handler, so `del some_global` was unsupported: under
`fullgraph=True` it raised `Unsupported: Missing bytecode handler`, and otherwise it
graph-broke. This adds the handler for the root frame and for inlined cross-module
frames. （#195901）

### Design

Both handlers share one `_check_global_delete` helper that decides, once, whether the
name is bound while tracing:

- unbound, and nothing in this trace bound it -> `raise_name_error`;
- an earlier `del` in this trace already removed it -> `raise_name_error`;
- a `STORE_GLOBAL` earlier in this trace created it -> the delete cancels that pending
  store, so nothing is replayed;
- otherwise -> record the delete.

That decision is baked into the generated code, so a `DICT_CONTAINS` /
`DICT_NOT_CONTAINS` guard is installed on the globals dict itself
(`_install_globals_membership_guard`): a name that later appears or disappears forces a
recompile instead of reusing a stale artifact.

Replay: the root frame emits `DELETE_GLOBAL`. For a module `__dict__`, the new
`AttrMutationKind.GLOBAL_DELETE` plus `utils.delete_global_from_module` delete the dict
entry directly, preserving `NameError` semantics. Deleting a tensor-valued global drops
the last reference, so `_maybe_emit_sync_dealloc` is called as `DELETE_FAST` does.
Inlined functions whose globals dict is not a registered module `__dict__` graph-break
(`GB4909`).

`SideEffects.discard_attr_mutation` drops a recorded mutation that replayed as a no-op;
`track_global_existing` returns the variable it already built for a sentinel, so repeated
`STORE_GLOBAL` to one name no longer orphans a `NewGlobalVariable` per store.

title: [inductor] Fold small-row expanded bmm to mm in post-grad
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #185404

A dynamic linear on batch-first transposed activations can reach post-grad as
an expanded batched matmul:

    [T, B, K] @ expand([K, N], [T, K, N])

For small B this produces many small-row GEMMs. On CUDA fp16 this path can be
much slower than flattening the transposed activation to [T * B, K] and using
one mm. The issue shows up in AOTInductor autocast because the fp16 cast drops
requires_grad, so the existing matmul folding heuristic no longer takes the
requires_grad escape hatch that the fp32 graph happened to use.

Add a post-grad Inductor pattern for the specific expanded-bmm shape generated
by transposed linear. This keeps eager and general decomposition stride behavior
unchanged, addressing the concern from the abandoned decomposition-only PR. The
pattern is deliberately narrow: GPU fp16/bf16/fp32, batch-first transpose
layout, large T/K/N, and B <= 64. Dynamic dimensions are checked with guards so
cache reuse is stable: large batches keep the original bmm path, while small
batches compile to the mm path.

I considered a runtime torch.cond between bmm and mm, but tracing cond inside
this post-grad replacement currently nests torch.compile and trips Inductor's
compile event stack. Guarded specialization is the simpler established path and
keeps large-batch behavior on the original implementation.

Benchmark Results:
On NVIDIA B200, fp16, T=1000, K=2048, N=6144, max_autotune_gemm_backends=ATEN,
5 warmup iterations and 20 timed CUDA-event iterations:

Before:
- B=1: current bmm 0.0721 ms, manual folded mm 0.0724 ms
- B=2: current bmm 1.3912 ms, manual folded mm 0.0841 ms
- B=4: current bmm 1.4169 ms, manual folded mm 0.1524 ms

After:
- generated code uses mm for the small-batch guarded graph
- B=1: 0.0772 ms
- B=2: 0.0903 ms
- B=4: 0.1531 ms

title: [CPU] Add RVV vectorized kernel for FusedAdam (float/double)
body:
## Motivation

CPU FusedAdam expresses its math through `at::vec::Vectorized`, which has no RVV backend: on riscv64 the generic `Vectorized<T>` degrades to element-wise scalar loops, and the `blendv`-based lerp in `adam_math` blocks even compiler autovectorization. This patch adds a kernel-local RVV implementation following the pattern of the previously merged DepthwiseConvKernel RVV kernel ([PR #127867](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/127867)). Because the new code is guarded by `__riscv_v_intrinsic >= 12000`, default riscv64 builds (rv64gc, no V) and all other platforms compile it out with zero impact — upstream CI stays green.

## Build & Test Environment

```bash
# build
export USE_CUDA=0
export USE_DISTRIBUTED=0
export USE_MKLDNN=0
export MAX_JOBS=32
export CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++
export CMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang
export CMAKE_C_FLAGS=-march=rv64gcv
export CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS=-march=rv64gcv
pip3 install --upgrade typing_extensions scikit-build-core
pip3 install --no-build-isolation -v -e .

# full-fused sweep (all 94 cases)
python3 -m pytest test/test_optim.py -k "fused" -q
```

title: [precompile] Serve the continuations Dynamo never traced as plain Python
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #198217
* #198227
* #198138
* #198216
* #198137
* #198215
* #198136
* __->__ #198214
* #198243
* #198135
* #198213
* #197993
* #198284
* #198283
* #198223
* #198211

**Problem.** When a captured step ends in `.backward()`, Dynamo compiles nothing of the continuation it resumes after that call: `convert_frame` skips it when no tensor reaches it (`return None`), and it traces no ops in it (`SkipFrame`) when one does (`return loss`). Either way the continuation runs as plain Python during capture, and its record still exists (the frame ahead names it by resume name) but has no variant, so a standalone artifact treated it as a coverage gap: `_serving_mode` sent the capture to installed serving and the driver bound a refusal under the resume name.

**Fix.** The record now says `trivial` for a code entry with no guarded code that was not bypassed, `_serving_mode` counts such a non-entry frame as covered when reached and harmless when not, and the driver rebuilds it as a plain function over its code object in the captured module's scope, so the frame runs at serve time exactly as it ran during capture.

**Summary.** A standalone multi-graph artifact rebuilds each captured frame from its record, and a continuation with no variant used to be read as a frame the artifact could not serve. That was wrong for the continuation after a trailing `.backward()`: whether Dynamo skipped it before tracing or traced it and found no ops, it ran eager during capture, and yet the capture was sent to installed serving while a call reaching the frame in a standalone rebuild would have raised. `_multigraph_frames` now records `trivial = not code.guarded_codes and not code.bypassed`, `_serving_mode` treats a trivial non-entry frame as covered, and `_build_multigraph_forward` binds such a frame as a `types.FunctionType` over its code object in the captured module's scope (a factory over the closure tuple when it has free variables, the way Dynamo binds one). The design constraint is that the entry never qualifies and a bypassed frame never does, because a trivial entry means the whole capture ran eager and a bypassed frame's variants were dropped rather than never made. A bypassed continuation is unchanged: it still sends the capture to installing and still refuses at the call that reaches it.

## Where this fits

The stack replaces the callable `torch.compiler.precompile(fn, *example_inputs)` (trace once on inputs passed up front, pair returned in memory) with a caller-driven context manager: `capture(fn, artifact_path=, cache_path=)` is entered with a `with` block, the caller calls it on as many example inputs as they like (each graph break and recompiled variant is folded in), the `(python_code, cache)` pair is written to the two files on exit, and `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` serves it in a fresh process. The end-to-end example and the PR-by-PR map live in #197993's "The new API, end to end" section. This PR is plumbing for the multi-call `DynamoTracer` capture (#198138): continuation frames Dynamo compiled nothing of are served as plain functions.

## The frames Dynamo compiled nothing of

The new test is parametrized over three steps whose continuation after `.backward()` gets no variant:

```python
def no_tensor(model, x):          # continuation reaches no tensor: skipped before tracing
    (model(x) * _MULTIGRAPH_SCALE).sum().backward()

def no_ops(model, x):             # continuation traced, no ops found: SkipFrame
    loss = (model(x) * _MULTIGRAPH_SCALE).sum()
    loss.backward()
    return loss

def _closure_step(model, x):      # module-level; continuation has free variables
    loss = (model(x) * _MULTIGRAPH_SCALE).sum()
    loss.backward()
    get = lambda: loss
    return get()

package = CompilePackage(step)
compiled = torch._dynamo.optimize(backend="eager", package=package, guard_filter_fn=default_guard_filter_fn)(step)
compiled(model, x)
frames = _multigraph_frames(package.cache_entry())
```

`.backward()` is a graph break, so Dynamo mints a resume function for the rest of the step. In `no_tensor` that continuation only returns `None`, so `convert_frame` skips it before compiling. In `no_ops` the loss reaches it, Dynamo enters it, finds no ops and raises `SkipFrame("No ops traced")`, so its record has `has_compile_id` set but still no guarded code; `closure` also hands the loss to its continuation, which builds and calls the lambda without keeping any guarded code. In all three the continuation runs as plain Python during capture, and it is not bypassed. The records now read:

```python
[f["trivial"] for f in frames[:2]]        # [False, True]
[len(f["variants"]) for f in frames[:2]]  # [1, 0]
all(f["trivial"] for f in frames[1:])     # True: in "closure" the lambda's frame is recorded too
```

The parent produced the same records minus the `trivial` key, and the continuation -- reachable from the entry's bytecode, no variant -- was indistinguishable from a bypassed continuation.

## Recording `trivial`

```python
# torch/_precompile.py, _multigraph_frames
{
    "is_entry": i == 0,
    "bypassed": code.bypassed,
    # now: no variant and not bypassed -- Dynamo skipped the frame or traced
    # no ops in it, so it ran eager during capture and the driver runs it eager too
    "trivial": not code.guarded_codes and not code.bypassed,
    "code": code.python_code,
    ...
}
```

The key is the absence of guarded code, not the compile id. Keying on `has_compile_id` would miss the common `return loss` step (`no_ops` above), whose continuation Dynamo enters and then skips, so it has a compile id and no guarded code. A bypassed frame is excluded on purpose: its guarded codes are dead for a different reason (its guards could not be serialized, or a backend artifact was missing), and install keeps its binding but none of its codes.

## Counting it as covered

```python
# torch/_precompile.py, _serving_mode
reachable = _reachable_frames(frames)
# parent: covered = {i for i, frame in enumerate(frames) if frame["variants"]}
#         return "standalone" if covered == reachable else "installed"
compiled = {i for i, frame in enumerate(frames) if frame["variants"]}
trivial = {i for i, f in enumerate(frames) if f["trivial"] and not f["is_entry"]}
return "standalone" if compiled <= reachable <= compiled | trivial else "installed"
```

Every compiled frame must still be reachable (an unreachable one would run eager, giving up its variant), and every reachable frame must be compiled or trivial. A trivial frame that is not reached costs nothing, which is what the `closure` shape's recorded lambda needs. The entry is excluded because a trivial entry means the whole capture ran eager, which is not something an artifact should serve. The test pins both verdicts on the same records:

```python
_serving_mode(frames)                  # now: "standalone" (parent: "installed")
frames[1].update(trivial=False, bypassed=True)
_serving_mode(frames)                  # "installed": a bypassed continuation is still a gap
```

## Rebuilding it as plain Python

```python
# torch/_precompile_driver.py, _make_dispatcher
if frame["trivial"] and not is_entry:
    scope = _scope(frame)

    def _plain(closure):
        return types.FunctionType(target, scope, target.co_name, None, closure)

    if target.co_freevars:
        return _plain
    return _plain(None)
if not frame["variants"]:
    ... # parent: this branch bound a refusal under the resume name
```

The branch sits ahead of the existing no-variant refusal, so a trivial continuation never reaches it. `_scope(frame)` opens the captured module so the bytecode's `LOAD_GLOBAL`s read the module's live dict, the same scope a compiled variant is bound over; the driver's module-scope comment now says a module is opened only for a frame the driver serves, and a dead record never imports its module. When the code object closes over locals (the `closure` shape), Dynamo binds the continuation as a factory taking the closure tuple and the frame ahead passes one, so the driver returns `_plain` itself in that case and a bound function otherwise -- mirroring the `factory` / `dispatch` split the compiled path already uses. The resume-name collision pre-check in `_build_multigraph_forward` now opens the module of every frame `_make_dispatcher` opens a scope for (`variants`, or `trivial` and not the entry), so a trivial continuation recorded under another module under `config.nested_graph_breaks` has its resume names checked too.

The refusal branch that remains now covers a bypassed frame, and for a frame that is not bypassed it is reached only by the entry: every non-bypassed non-entry frame without variants is trivial and takes the branch above. A bypassed continuation still binds its resume names in a standalone artifact, so its refusal is deferred to a call; a no-variant entry raises directly instead of binding a refusal.

## Tests

`test_trivial_continuation_is_served_as_plain_python`, parametrized over `no_tensor`, `no_ops` and `closure`, captures the step, checks the `[False, True]` / `[1, 0]` records (and that every frame past the entry is trivial), checks the `_serving_mode` verdict before and after modelling the continuation as bypassed (`trivial=False, bypassed=True`), then rebuilds the driver from the records in this process -- `exec` of `_build_multigraph_forward`'s source over the pickled frames and backends, with the captured module aliased into `sys.modules` -- and serves the step on a fresh `Linear` loaded from the captured model's state dict, comparing its return value, `weight.grad` and `bias.grad` with an eager run of the step.

Test Plan:

`test_trivial_continuation_is_served_as_plain_python` captures a step whose continuation after `.backward()` reaches no tensor, one that returns the loss, and one whose continuation closes over a cell of the frame ahead (the factory path), checks the record and both `_serving_mode` verdicts, rebuilds the driver from the records and serves the step in this process, comparing the runtime model's grads with eager.

```
python test/test_precompile.py
lintrunner -a torch/_precompile.py torch/_precompile_driver.py test/test_precompile.py
```

title: [precompile] Apply a make_fx capture's in-place updates once
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #198217
* #198227
* #198138
* #198216
* #198137
* #198215
* #198136
* #198214
* __->__ #198243
* #198135
* #198213
* #197993
* #198284
* #198283
* #198223
* #198211

**Problem.** A make_fx capture ran the caller's `fn` twice, once to trace it and once to serve the rendered artifact. Every in-place update in `fn`, such as a BatchNorm's running stats or an `x.add_(1)`, landed twice. The hazard comes from the commit directly below, which added `capture()` and its serve; the two land together.

**Fix.** Restore the buffers and tensor inputs the trace changed, so the serve is the one execution the caller sees. Refuse a `fn` that updates a parameter in place, detected from the traced graph.

**Summary.** `_MakeFxCapture.__call__` traces `fn` with make_fx, then serves the freshly rendered artifact on the real arguments so the caller gets exactly what serving returns. A static trace runs on the real example tensors, though, so one captured call of a training-mode BatchNorm left `num_batches_tracked == 2` and a `x.add_(1)` added 2. The trace now snapshots the modules' buffers and the tensor arguments, and after tracing copies back any value that changed, the same treatment `_capture` already gives `.grad`; changed values are found by comparing values, because under make_fx the batch-norm kernel's running-stat update does not bump the buffer's version. Parameters are not snapshotted, because that would clone every parameter up front, so a `fn` that updates one in place (an optimizer step) is refused with a `PrecompileError`, found by scanning the traced graph for a write into a parameter placeholder rather than by version counter, which a write through `p.data` does not bump. An unbacked (`mark_unbacked`) capture traces on fake tensors, so it skips the snapshot and the scan entirely.

## Where this fits

The stack replaces the callable `torch.compiler.precompile(fn, *example_inputs)` (trace once on inputs passed up front, pair returned in memory) with a caller-driven context manager: `capture(fn, artifact_path=, cache_path=)` is entered with a `with` block, the caller calls it on as many example inputs as they like (each graph break and recompiled variant is folded in), the `(python_code, cache)` pair is written to the two files on exit, and `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` serves it in a fresh process. The end-to-end example and the PR-by-PR map live in #197993's "The new API, end to end" section. This PR fixes the `MakeFxTracer` capture from #198135 so in-place updates in `fn` land once, not twice.

## Before and after

```python
import torch
from torch.compiler.precompile import capture, MakeFxTracer

def step(m, x):
    y = m(x)
    x.add_(1)
    return y.sum()

m = torch.nn.BatchNorm1d(4).train()
x = torch.zeros(3, 4)
with capture(step, artifact_path="a.py", cache_path="a.cache", tracer=MakeFxTracer()) as cap:
    cap(m, x)

m.num_batches_tracked   # parent: 2   now: 1
x[0, 0]                 # parent: 2.0 now: 1.0
```

Measured on both `backend="eager"` and `backend="inductor"`, with the same numbers on each.

## How the trace is kept side-effect free

```python
def _trace_without_side_effects(self, args):
    if _has_unbacked_marks(args):
        self._module._compile(args)          # traces on fakes; only the serve touches the reals
        return
    mods = [a for a in args if isinstance(a, torch.nn.Module)]
    leaves = pytree.tree_leaves(args)
    # a parameter also passed as a plain argument is snapshotted like any input
    params = {id(p) for m in mods for p in m.parameters()} - {id(t) for t in leaves}
    tensors = [*(b for m in mods for b in m.buffers()), *leaves]
    saved = {id(t): (t, t.detach().clone()) for t in tensors
             if isinstance(t, torch.Tensor) and id(t) not in params}
    try:
        self._module._compile(args)          # the make_fx trace
    finally:
        with torch.no_grad():
            for t, value in saved.values():
                if not torch.equal(t, value):  # by value: BN does not bump _version
                    t.copy_(value)
    if _writes_a_parameter(self._module._gm, len(self._module._param_names)):
        raise PrecompileError("MakeFxTracer cannot capture a fn that updates a parameter in place ...")
```

The restore runs in `finally`, so a trace that raises also leaves the caller's buffers and inputs as they were.

A parameter passed to `fn` both inside its module and as a plain tensor argument (`cap(model, model.lin.weight, x)`) is traced as that user input, so the parameter scan below would not see a write to it. It is therefore left out of `params` and snapshotted and restored by value like any other input, and the serve applies its update once.

## How a parameter write is detected

The params are the first `len(_param_names)` placeholders of the traced graph. `_writes_a_parameter` looks for an op whose schema marks an argument `alias_info.is_write`, and walks that argument back to its base through `_aliased_input`:

```python
# A write can reach a parameter placeholder in several graph shapes:
w.add_(1)                                  # add_ directly on the placeholder
w.data.add_(1)                             # add_ on aten.alias(placeholder)
w.chunk(2)[0].add_(1)                      # add_ on getitem(split(placeholder))
for row in w.unbind(0): row.mul_(0.9)      # mul_ on getitem(unbind(placeholder))
torch._foreach_add_(list(m.parameters()), 1)  # a Tensor(a!)[] argument, walked per element
```

`_aliased_input` steps through `operator.getitem` to the list it indexes. For a schema op it follows the argument whose alias set matches the return's, so an `out=` overload walks to `out`, not to its first argument; `torch.mul(w.detach(), 2, out=buf).add_(1)` with `buf` an input still captures. `split`/`unbind`, whose alias set sits on the list elements, follow their one aliased argument.

The graph is used rather than `p._version` because a write through `.data` bumps no counter the parameter shares: with a version check, `p.data.add_(1)` in `fn` was captured silently and the weight ended up +2. Checking fake-tensor storage (`StorageWeakRef` on each node's `meta["val"]`) was also tried and rejected: in a real-mode trace a view's fake value does not share its placeholder's storage, so `.data`, `chunk` and `unbind` writes were missed. `p.data = new` (a rebind) leaves no op in the graph at all; that is a pre-existing make_fx limitation this PR does not change.

```python
def step(model, x):
    with torch.no_grad():
        model.lin.weight.add_(1)   # an optimizer-style in-place update
    return model(x)

with capture(step, ..., backend="eager") as cap:
    cap(model, x)
# PrecompileError: MakeFxTracer cannot capture a fn that updates a parameter in place
# (e.g. an optimizer step): serving the capture would apply the update a second time,
# and the trace has already applied it once. Step the optimizer outside the captured fn.
```

## Alternatives rejected

- **Return the trace's own outputs and drop the serve.** An unbacked capture traces on fake tensors and has no real output to return, and `.grad` reaches the caller's model only through the served artifact.
- **Document the double update.** That would leave the default MakeFxTracer silently wrong for any model with batch norm.
- **Snapshot and restore parameters too.** That clones every parameter up front on every capture; the refusal costs nothing on the common path.

## Tests

| Test | Pins |
|---|---|
| `test_a_capture_applies_in_place_updates_once` (inductor, eager) | result, `num_batches_tracked`, running mean and `x` match a single eager step |
| `test_a_capture_refuses_an_in_place_parameter_update` (direct, `.data`, `chunk`, `unbind`, `_foreach_add_`; inductor, eager) | the refusal, and that no artifact is written |
| `test_a_parameter_passed_as_an_argument_is_updated_once` (inductor, eager) | a parameter also passed as a plain argument is updated once, not refused |
| `test_a_trace_that_raises_leaves_buffers_and_inputs_as_they_were` | the restore runs when `fn` raises, and nothing is written |

Test Plan:

`test_a_capture_applies_in_place_updates_once` (both backends) captures a BatchNorm step that also does `x.add_(1)`, and checks the result, `num_batches_tracked`, the running mean and `x` against a single eager step. `test_a_capture_refuses_an_in_place_parameter_update` pins the refusal, for a direct write, a write through `.data`, a write through a `chunk` or `unbind` piece, and a `_foreach_add_` over the parameters, on both backends, and checks that nothing is written. `test_a_parameter_passed_as_an_argument_is_updated_once` covers a parameter that `fn` also receives as a plain tensor argument: it is snapshotted with the inputs, so the serve applies its update once. `test_a_trace_that_raises_leaves_buffers_and_inputs_as_they_were` checks the restore also runs when `fn` raises.

title: [dynamo] Add testcases for DELETE_GLOBAL handler
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #197057
* #197056

### Summary

Stacked on #197056. Test-only PR: exercises the new `DELETE_GLOBAL` handler with
eager CPython as the specification for every case.

The handler's decision table is branchy (name present vs. created during the trace
vs. already deleted; root frame vs. inlined cross-module frame; plus the membership
guard and the side-effect replay), so the tests are grouped by the branch they pin.

### Coverage

| Behavior | Test |
| --- | --- |
| `del g` on a pre-existing global | `test_delete_global` |
| `del g` when `g` is unbound: observed exception under `fullgraph=True`, and the real `NameError` when a graph break falls back to eager; also when the `try/except` sits in the caller | `test_delete_missing_global`, `test_delete_missing_global_caught_by_caller` |
| Deleting a name created earlier in the same trace cancels the pending `STORE_GLOBAL`, so nothing is replayed (`side_effect_replay_policy="error"`) | `test_delete_global_created_then_deleted`, `test_delete_global_crossfile_created_then_deleted` |
| Double delete raises `NameError`, including when the first delete cancelled a store | `test_delete_global_twice`, `test_delete_global_created_then_deleted_twice` |
| `del g; g = 7`: the replayed delete precedes the store, so the name lands at the end of the module `__dict__` exactly as eager does | `test_delete_global_then_store`, `test_delete_global_then_store_order`, `test_delete_global_crossfile_then_store_order` |
| Deleting a tensor-valued global drops the last reference | `test_delete_tensor_global` |
| Multi-stream semantics: deleted across streams emits `sync_dealloc` + `record_event`, deleted on the same stream emits no `sync_dealloc` | `test_del_global_multi_stream_sync_dealloc`, `test_del_global_same_stream_no_sync_dealloc`, `test_del_global_crossfile_multi_stream_sync_dealloc` |
| Inlined cross-module delete replays against the callee module `__dict__` (`AttrMutationKind.GLOBAL_DELETE`) | `test_delete_global_crossfile_inline` |
| Inlined function whose globals are not a registered module `__dict__` graph-breaks (`GB4909`) and falls back to eager | `test_delete_global_in_unregistered_importlib_module` |
| The membership guard forces a recompile when the name's presence flips between calls | `test_delete_global_presence_flip` |

### Files

- `test/dynamo/test_global.py`: new `TestDeleteGlobal` (14 tests), plus the `_ABSENT`,
  `temp_globals` and `crossfile_globals` helpers. `_assert_delete_missing_global` pins
  both compile modes for an unguarded delete: `fullgraph=True` reports
  `Unsupported: Observed exception`, without `fullgraph` the graph break lets eager
  raise the real `NameError`.
- `test/dynamo/test_streams.py`: three device-generic `TestStreams` tests (CUDA/XPU).
- `test/dynamo/mock_store_global_crossfile_inline.py`: the cross-module callees used by
  the inline tests (`delete_value_fn`, `store_then_delete_missing_fn`,
  `delete_then_store_value_fn`, `store_then_delete_multi_stream_tensor_fn`).

### Test plan
```
python test/dynamo/test_global.py
python test/dynamo/test_streams.py -k del_global
```

title: [FSDP2] Add gradient accumulation finalization API
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.15.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #196727
* #196726
* #196963
* #196725
* #196724
* __->__ #196640
* #196641

Add a public FSDPModule method, `finalize_gradient_accumulation`, that completes deferred gradient reduction on the caller thread. It reshards parameters and reduces the accumulated gradients into sharded `.grad`.

The autograd final callback runs on the autograd thread, so its stream waits cannot be captured in a CUDA graph. Reuse its cleanup on the caller thread, but track deferred reduction explicitly so finalization does not rerun post-backward or reduce zero gradients after a synchronized backward. Temporarily override gradient synchronization, all-reduce, reshard, and last-backward settings, then restore them.

A separate callback would duplicate iteration cleanup. The deferred-work flag keeps one cleanup path while gating the reduction. HSDP all-reduce-only deferral requires a separate collective and gradient view-out path, so reject it explicitly instead of silently skipping gradients.

Test Plan:

```bash
python3 test/distributed/_composable/fsdp/test_fully_shard_training.py TestFullyShardGradientAccumulation.test_finalize_gradient_accumulation
python3 test/distributed/_composable/fsdp/test_fully_shard_training.py TestFullyShardGradientAccumulation.test_finalize_gradient_accumulation_rejects_partial_all_reduce
python3 test/distributed/_composable/fsdp/test_fully_shard_training.py TestFullyShardCudaGraph.test_finalize_gradient_accumulation_cudagraph
UV_NO_CONFIG=1 lintrunner -a
```

title: [ROCm][UT] Fix runOnRocmArch used in boolean context in test_cublas_baddbmm_large_input
body:
Fixes https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/196572

## Summary

`runOnRocmArch()` is a decorator factory. It returns a function, which is
always truthy. In `test_cublas_baddbmm_large_input`:

```python
if runOnRocmArch(MI200_ARCH) and dtype == torch.float16:
```

The arch check is discarded and the condition reduces to
`dtype == torch.float16`. The relaxed MI200 tolerance was therefore applied on
every platform, including CUDA, and the strict `else` branch was unreachable
for fp16.

Use `TEST_WITH_ROCM` and `isRocmArchAnyOf(MI200_ARCH)`, the form already used in
this file for the Navi guard in `test_cublas_addmm`.

Scope of the behaviour change is narrow: `_DTYPE_PRECISIONS[torch.float16]` is
`(0.001, 1e-5)`, so both code paths use `rtol=1e-3` and the only difference is
atol, `1e-4` -> `1e-5`. MI200 is unaffected: it takes the relaxed path before
and after. Non-MI200 ROCm and NVIDIA fp16 move to the default atol.

## Validation

The identity matmul under test (linear and baddbmm) is bitwise
exact, `max_abs = max_rel = 0.0`, on gfx1100 and gfx1200 for
`N in {100, 1000, 10000}` across fp16/bf16/fp32, so the tightened atol has
ample headroom on RDNA. `test_matmul_cuda` passes 12/12 on both GPUs.

MI200, MI300, MI350 and NVIDIA hardware were not available locally; please run
`ciflow/rocm-mi200` and `ciflow/trunk` jobs.

`test_2d_reductions_mixed_indexing` is skipped on ROCm by

```python

```

The decorator was added by #185013, a bulk pass that inlined CI bot disable
entries as decorators. The auto-disable behind it, #158328, was raised for

title: [Inductor][ROCm] Keep NVIDIA communication model off HIP
body:
## Summary

`comm_analysis.py` contains an analytical model calibrated for NVIDIA GPU
generations, NCCL protocols and NVLink/InfiniBand topologies. On ROCm it
interprets HIP capability numbers as NVIDIA compute capabilities and treats
peer accessibility as evidence of NVLink.

On two gfx1200 GPUs this selects `BLACKWELL` and `NVLINK_B200`, with an
intra-node bandwidth of 720 GB/s. The measured PCIe peer-to-peer bandwidth is
approximately 54.5 GB/s.

HIP devices no longer enter this NVIDIA model. Their NVIDIA GPU type is
unavailable, their interconnect is reported as unknown, and analytical
bandwidth, runtime and saturation estimates return zero. The existing
backend-native RCCL estimator is unchanged and remains available where the
process group supports it.

Zero means that no calibrated analytical estimate is available. It does not
affect collective execution, but heuristic scheduling may be conservative when
the RCCL estimator is unavailable. This change does not attempt to model PCIe
or xGMI bandwidth.

## Validation

Current-main reproducer on two gfx1200 GPUs:

| GPU type | NVLink | Interconnect | Modelled bandwidth | Measured P2P |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| `BLACKWELL` | `True` | `NVLINK_B200` | 720 GB/s | ~54.5 GB/s |

Patched result:

| Device | GPU type | Interconnect | Analytical bandwidth | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| gfx1100 | unavailable | `UNKNOWN` | 0 | pass |
| gfx1151 | unavailable | `UNKNOWN` | 0 | pass |
| gfx1200 | unavailable | `UNKNOWN` | 0 | pass |

A new synthetic regression test patches `torch.version.hip` and verifies that
HIP returns no NVIDIA GPU type, reports no NVLink, selects `UNKNOWN`
interconnect and returns no analytical bandwidth estimate. It fails on current
main and passes with this change.

The existing analytical-fallback and saturation tests were updated for the
neutral ROCm result and pass. The native RCCL estimator was also verified on
two gfx1200 GPUs and returned a nonzero estimate.

Validation is limited to RDNA hardware.

title: [ROCm] Read maximum clock rate from HIP
body:
## Summary

On ROCm, `max_clock_rate()` returns a value from a hardcoded table keyed by `gfx`
prefix. The table reports 1700 MHz for gfx1100, gfx1151 and gfx1200, which does
not match the peak clock reported by HIP on any of those devices.

HIP exposes the device peak clock through `clock_rate` in kHz. Replace the
table with that runtime property and convert it to the MHz returned by
`max_clock_rate()`.

The `clock_rate` binding reads the current device rather than the device
described by the properties object, so the requested device is made current
while reading the property. If HIP reports zero, the function logs a warning
and returns zero instead of substituting a guessed clock. The NVIDIA path is
unchanged.

## Validation

HIP's property matches the AMD SMI peak clock on all tested devices:

| Device | Hardcoded value | HIP `clock_rate` | Returned value |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| gfx1100 | 1700 MHz | 1760000 kHz | 1760 MHz |
| gfx1151 | 1700 MHz | 2900000 kHz | 2900 MHz |
| gfx1200 | 1700 MHz | 2670000 kHz | 2670 MHz |

The existing `test_max_clock_rate_uses_current_rocm_device` test now supplies a
runtime `clock_rate` value rather than a gfx name. It continues to verify
current-device resolution and also pins the kHz-to-MHz conversion. All three
`max_clock_rate` tests pass on gfx1100, gfx1151 and gfx1200.

On a two-GPU gfx1100 host, both device indices are read and cached separately.
Both cards are the same model and report 1760 MHz.

This work is scoped to RDNA. ROCm CI should cover MI architectures.

title: [Inductor][ROCm] Fall back for BF16 atomic accumulation
body:
## Summary

`needs_fallback_due_to_atomic_add_limitations()` uses an NVIDIA capability
comparison for BF16 atomics. On ROCm, gfx1100 reports `(11, 0)`, gfx1151
reports `(11, 5)` and gfx1200 reports `(12, 0)`, so all three are treated as
SM90-or-newer and skip the existing fallback.

With repeated indices, the generated BF16 atomic path rounds after each update
and accumulation stops advancing at 256. Eager `index_put_` returns 1000 for
the same 1000 additions.

Make HIP use the existing fallback for BF16 atomic accumulation. The NVIDIA
SM90 predicate and XPU behavior are unchanged.

This applies to all HIP devices, including MI/CDNA. Native BF16 atomic support
alone is not sufficient to preserve eager behavior: gfx1200 has native BF16
atomics and still reproduces the mismatch. This work is validated on RDNA;
ROCm CI should cover MI correctness and performance.

## Validation

The existing `test_index_put_duplicate_indices_accumulate` test is extended
with 1000 repeated BF16 updates. It is the reproducer and regression guard; it
compares compiled output against eager output and does not mock the fallback
predicate.

| Device | Eager | Current main | With this change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| gfx1100 | 1000 | 256 | 1000 |
| gfx1151 | 1000 | 256 | 1000 |
| gfx1200 | 1000 | 256 | 1000 |

The test fails before the fix and passes afterward on all three devices. Its
existing float32 case remains unchanged.

Other helper consumers retain eager parity after the change:

| Operation | Eager | Compiled |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `index_put` | 1000 | 1000 |
| `scatter_add` | 256 | 256 |
| `index_reduce(mean)` | 1 | 1 |

The added BF16 case also runs in NVIDIA CUDA CI, while the production NVIDIA
predicate remains unchanged.

title: [ROCm] Expose shared_memory_per_block_optin
body:
## Summary

`torch.cuda.get_device_properties()` exposes
`shared_memory_per_block_optin` on NVIDIA, but the binding is excluded from
ROCm builds. HIP provides the same limit as
`hipDeviceProp_t::sharedMemPerBlockOptin`.

Expose the property on ROCm 6.0 and newer, where the field is present in the
HIP device-properties structure. Older ROCm builds remain unchanged.

Remove comments that describe the property as NVIDIA-only. Inductor's existing
property check is unchanged; once the binding is available, it naturally reads
the opt-in limit on ROCm. The profiler export can also include the value through
its existing `hasattr()` guard.

This PR only exposes the property. Replacing hardcoded shared-memory limits in
downstream consumers is a separate follow-up.

## Validation

`test_cuda_shared_memory_per_block_optin` is the regression guard. On current
main it fails on ROCm because the property is missing. With this change it is
present and no smaller than the default per-block limit.

| Device | Base limit | Opt-in limit |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| gfx1100 | 65536 | 65536 |
| gfx1151 | 65536 | 65536 |
| gfx1200 | 65536 | 65536 |

An independent HIP probe also confirmed that
`hipDeviceProp_t::sharedMemPerBlockOptin` matches
`hipDeviceAttributeSharedMemPerBlockOptin` on all three devices.

The test skips ROCm versions older than 6.0, matching the source guard. This
work is scoped to RDNA; ROCm CI should cover MI architectures.

title: [ROCm] Clamp nearest2d backward launch grid
body:
## Summary

The contiguous `upsample_nearest2d_backward` path derives its launch grid from
`grad_input.numel() / nbatch`. Large inputs can make
`gridDim.x * blockDim.x` exceed HIP's `UINT32_MAX` x-dimension work-size limit,
causing the launch to fail with `hipErrorInvalidConfiguration`.

Clamp the launch grid to the device limit and HIP's work-size limit. When the
full grid cannot be launched, the kernel uses a grid-stride loop to cover the
remaining output. A compile-time flag preserves the existing one-element-per-
thread path for normal-sized inputs.

The batch offset is applied at the output store so the grid-stride cursor is
not modified inside the batch loop. This completes the backward-path TODO from
#180310.

## Validation

`test_upsamplingNearest2d_backward_hip_grid_limit` is the reproducer and
regression guard. It calls the backward operator directly with a
`(1, 1, 65536, 65536)` FP16 input shape, reaching the `2^32` launch boundary
while keeping `grad_output` small.

| Device | Current main | With this change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| gfx1100 | `hipErrorInvalidConfiguration` | passes |
| gfx1151 | `hipErrorInvalidConfiguration` | passes |
| gfx1200 | `hipErrorInvalidConfiguration` | passes |

The test checks the output shape, total gradient and individual positions, so
it verifies grid-stride indexing rather than only checking that the launch
succeeds.

This work is scoped to RDNA. ROCm CI should cover MI architectures.

title: [Inductor][ROCm] Keep NVIDIA reduction thresholds off HIP
body:
## Summary

Two reduction heuristics use the device major version as an NVIDIA SM version:

- the inner-reduction no-split threshold selects GB200 values for `major >= 10`
- the `R0_BLOCK` architecture cap selects the B200 value for `major >= 10`

ROCm reports the `gfx` major in the same field, so gfx1100, gfx1151 and gfx1200
are incorrectly treated as SM100+ hardware.

Limit the no-split thresholds to normalized `DeviceProperties.type == "cuda"`.
For `R0_BLOCK`, keep the NVIDIA condition in the base heuristic and override
only the architecture cap in `ROCmReductionHeuristic`. Workload-specific caps
remain unchanged.

The strided-block test helper now constructs the `DeviceProperties` type
required by the threshold function instead of passing raw CUDA properties.

## Validation

The two regression tests use synthetic `DeviceProperties`, following the
existing reduction-heuristic test style.

`test_inner_reduction_no_split_threshold_is_nvidia_only` checks:

- HIP major 12 returns the default 8192
- CUDA major 12 retains 32768/40960
- a missing major returns 8192

`test_reduction_r0_block_cap_is_nvidia_only` checks:

- CUDA major 8 returns 2048
- CUDA major 10 returns the B200 cap of 1024
- ROCm major 12 returns 2048
- ROCm major 9 remains 2048

On current main, the HIP no-split assertion returns 32768 instead of 8192 and
the ROCm major-12 R0 assertion returns 1024 instead of 2048. Both tests pass
after the change and run without requiring ROCm hardware.

Separate real-device probes confirmed the same values:

| Device | Value | Current main | With this change |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| gfx1100 | no-split threshold | 32768 | 8192 |
| gfx1100 | first `R0_BLOCK` | 1024 | 2048 |
| gfx1151 | no-split threshold | 32768 | 8192 |
| gfx1151 | first `R0_BLOCK` | 1024 | 2048 |
| gfx1200 | no-split threshold | 32768 | 8192 |
| gfx1200 | first `R0_BLOCK` | 1024 | 2048 |

This work is scoped to RDNA. ROCm CI should cover MI architectures.

title: [Inductor][ROCm] Restrict scaled-MM filtering to gfx950
body:
## Summary

The scaled-MM heuristic removes configurations with `BLOCK_K <= 64` when
`get_device_capability() >= (9, 5)`. This restriction targets gfx950, but ROCm
capability tuples contain the `gfx` major and minor rather than an ordered
feature level. The predicate also matches gfx1100, gfx1151 and gfx1200. The normal scaled-MM
path is confirmed reachable on gfx1200, where valid configurations are removed;
the gfx1100 and gfx1151 checks exercise the heuristic directly.

Move the restriction into the ROCm scaled-MM heuristic and match `gfx950`
directly with `rocm_gfx_arch()`. Other ROCm architectures retain their
`BLOCK_K=32` and `BLOCK_K=64` configurations. Other backends are unchanged.

## Validation

`test_scaled_mm_block_k_pruning_is_limited_to_gfx950` is a table-driven
regression test. It patches the reported ROCm architecture and checks the
filtered `BLOCK_K` values:

| Architecture | Expected `BLOCK_K` values |
| --- | --- |
| gfx1100 | `[32, 64, 128]` |
| gfx1151 | `[32, 64, 128]` |
| gfx1200 | `[32, 64, 128]` |
| gfx950 | `[128]` |

On current main, the three RDNA subcases fail because 32 and 64 are pruned;
the gfx950 case passes. All four cases pass after the change. The test runs
without requiring ROCm hardware.

Separate real-device probes confirmed the before/after behavior:

| Device | Current main | With this change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| gfx1100 | `[128]` | `[32, 64, 128]` |
| gfx1151 | `[128]` | `[32, 64, 128]` |
| gfx1200 | `[128]` | `[32, 64, 128]` |

The normal scaled-MM path is confirmed reachable on gfx1200. The gfx1100 and
gfx1151 probes exercise the heuristic directly.

This work is scoped to RDNA. The gfx950 restriction is preserved by exact
architecture matching and should be covered by ROCm CI.

title: [ROCm] Return power_draw in milliwatts
body:
## Summary

`torch.cuda.power_draw()` returns milliwatts on NVIDIA, where it forwards
`nvmlDeviceGetPowerUsage()`, and watts on ROCm, where it forwards the AMD SMI
socket power reading unchanged. The docstring documents milliwatts, so the ROCm
result is 1000x too small.

Documenting the difference instead is not an option: it is one public function
and a caller cannot branch on the backend to learn the unit. So the ROCm path
converts, and both backends now agree with the documented unit.

The conversion covers both AMD SMI readings, the average socket power and the
current-power fallback used when the average is unavailable. The path where
neither is available is untouched and still returns 0, and no caller
compensated for the watts value, so nothing else in tree changes.

## Validation

`power_draw()` against the AMD SMI reading taken at the same moment:

| Device | AMD SMI | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| gfx1100 | 54 W | 54 | 54000 mW |
| gfx1151 | 29 W | 29 | 29000 mW |
| gfx1200 | 14 W | 14 | 14000 mW |

Each row is a pair read back to back, and five consecutive samples per device
gave exactly 1000x.

`test_power_draw` only asserts a non-negative result, which passes either way,
so a new test mocks AMD SMI to pin the unit: average power available, average
unavailable with the current-power fallback, and neither available. Passes on
all three devices.

MI hardware is out of my scope, so please run ROCm CI for MI coverage.

title: [ROCm] Calibrate GPU sleep delays in stream tests
body:
## Summary

The stream-synchronization tests in `test/test_autograd.py` keep a producer's
backward pass busy while the consumer starts, and they ask for that delay as a
fixed number of GPU cycles, `NUM_GPU_CYCLES_IN_ONE_SEC // 2`, meaning 0.5 s.

A cycle count is not a duration. `spin_kernel` counts ticks from
`wall_clock64()` on gfx11 and from `clock64()` everywhere else, and
`wall_clock64()` runs at a fixed 100 MHz. On gfx1100 and gfx1151 the delay is
therefore 10 s instead of 0.5 s. Windows terminates a GPU task that runs longer
than two seconds, which resets the device, so every test that follows in the
same process fails while setting up. On gfx1200 the same count reads the shader
clock and gives 0.3-0.4 s depending on how busy the GPU is, too short to keep
the producer busy.

The five affected tests now compute the count with `get_cycles_per_ms()`. That
call is made in the test body rather than inside `backward()`, because it
synchronizes and would otherwise interfere with the stream ordering being
tested. No assertions change.

## Validation

Measured tick rate, and what the tests' 1e9-tick request actually slept:

| Device | clock read | rate | actual sleep |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| gfx1100 | `wall_clock64()` | 100 MHz, fixed | 10.02 s |
| gfx1151 | `wall_clock64()` | 100 MHz, fixed | 10.02 s |
| gfx1200 | `clock64()` | 2.5 GHz idle, 3.2 GHz loaded | 0.32-0.40 s |

`wall_clock64()` is a constant-rate counter, so the gfx11 figures reproduce
exactly: 99,774 and 99,858 cycles/ms on two different machines. `clock64()`
counts shader cycles, so on gfx1200 the rate is whatever the engine clock is
doing: it rose from 2.49 to 3.16 GHz under load, tracking the reported engine
clock up to 3442 MHz. No constant can express a duration against that.

Runtime before and after:

| Test | gfx1100 | gfx1151 | gfx1200 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `test_consumer_to_single_producer_case_2_correctness` | 20.7 → 1.8 s | 20.5 → 1.6 s | 1.25 → 1.45 s |
| `test_side_stream_backward_overlap` | 30.7 → 2.3 s | 30.5 → 2.1 s | 1.48 → 1.77 s |

gfx1200 takes slightly longer now because its delay rises to the intended 0.5 s.
Both tests passed 30 out of 30 fresh-process runs on each device. The remaining
three tests need two GPUs and pass on a two-GPU gfx1100, dropping from
20.8–40.8 s to 1.9–2.9 s. This removes the condition that trips Windows, since 0.5 s is well under the two-second limit. Validation ran on Linux, where the only symptom is slow
tests, so the Windows path is unverified.

cc @jeffdaily @sunway513 @jithunnair-amd @pruthvistony @ROCmSupport @jataylo @hongxiayang @naromero77amd @pragupta @jerrymannil @xinyazhang

title: [ROCm] Fix get_rotating_buffer_size() docstring units
body:
## Summary

`get_rotating_buffer_size()` documents its return value in kilobytes:

```python
r"""Get the rotating buffer size in kilobytes."""
```

The binding returns bytes. `TuningContext::GetRotatingBufferSize()` returns
either `l2CacheSize` or the value stored by `SetRotatingBufferSize(size)`,
which is `size * 1024 * 1024`. The setter already documents MB, so only the
getter docstring was wrong.

## Validation

On gfx1100, gfx1151 and gfx1200 the default equals the reported `L2_cache_size`
(6291456, 2097152 and 4194304 bytes), and `set_rotating_buffer_size(1)` returns
1048576 on all three.

`test_rotating_buffer_tunableop` already pins the byte semantics, so no new
test is added.

title: Delay RNN graph break until module call
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #186614

Dynamo intentionally graph breaks on nn.RNN, nn.GRU, and nn.LSTM when
allow_rnn is disabled. The old implementation raised the unsupported error
while wrapping the recurrent module attribute. For LOAD_ATTR/LOAD_METHOD
bytecode this goes through the generic step graph-break path, which can
compile the prefix but cannot build a continuation for the call site, so the
rest of the frame runs eagerly and post-RNN code is never compiled.

Return a DelayGraphBreakVariable for unsupported recurrent modules instead.
This keeps the attribute load traceable enough to reach the CALL instruction,
where Dynamo's regular call graph-break handling can run the recurrent module
eagerly and resume tracing the continuation. This matches the existing delayed
break pattern used for disabled optimized modules and avoids changing the
experimental allow_rnn=True behavior.

Add regression coverage for RNN, GRU, and LSTM modules that verifies Dynamo
compiles both the pre-recurrent and post-recurrent regions.

Fixes #141184
Generated by my agent

Test Plan:
- python test/dynamo/test_modules.py -k test_rnn_graph_break_resumes_after_call
- python test/export/test_export.py -k test_export_dynamo_config
- python test/dynamo/test_modules.py -k unsupportedmodule
- lintrunner -a
