title: [ROCm][UT] Run test_scaled_mm_deepseek_error_messages on RDNA4
body:
## Summary

`test_scaled_mm_deepseek_error_messages` is gated to MI350 only via
`@runOnRocmArch(MI350_ARCH)`. gfx1200 supports the MX path and passes the
test, so `NAVI4_ARCH` is added to the allowlist.

Widening the allowlist cannot wrongly enable the test on other RDNA parts:
gfx1100 and gfx1151 still skip through the existing `PLATFORM_SUPPORTS_MX_GEMM`
gate. I confirmed this by running with the allowlist removed entirely — both
still skipped.

`NAVI4_ARCH` covers gfx1200 and gfx1201, and I only tested it on gfx1200.
The two behave the same here by construction: `PLATFORM_SUPPORTS_FP8` matches
them with the same `gfx120` prefix, and the `NotImplementedError` this test
asserts is raised from a `#ifndef USE_ROCM` branch in `ScaledBlas.cpp` that
has no arch dependence.

## Validation

gfx1200, HIP `7.16.26320`. The test expands to six parametrizations, and all
six pass, repeated across runs with no failures:

```
test/test_scaled_matmul_cuda.py::TestFP8MatmulCUDA::test_scaled_mm_deepseek_error_messages_bfloat16_lhs_block_1_rhs_block_1_M_256_N_256_K_256_cuda PASSED
test/test_scaled_matmul_cuda.py::TestFP8MatmulCUDA::test_scaled_mm_deepseek_error_messages_bfloat16_lhs_block_1_rhs_block_1_M_256_N_256_K_512_cuda PASSED
test/test_scaled_matmul_cuda.py::TestFP8MatmulCUDA::test_scaled_mm_deepseek_error_messages_bfloat16_lhs_block_1_rhs_block_128_M_256_N_256_K_256_cuda PASSED
test/test_scaled_matmul_cuda.py::TestFP8MatmulCUDA::test_scaled_mm_deepseek_error_messages_bfloat16_lhs_block_1_rhs_block_128_M_256_N_256_K_512_cuda PASSED
test/test_scaled_matmul_cuda.py::TestFP8MatmulCUDA::test_scaled_mm_deepseek_error_messages_bfloat16_lhs_block_128_rhs_block_1_M_256_N_256_K_256_cuda PASSED
test/test_scaled_matmul_cuda.py::TestFP8MatmulCUDA::test_scaled_mm_deepseek_error_messages_bfloat16_lhs_block_128_rhs_block_1_M_256_N_256_K_512_cuda PASSED
```

Confirmed still skipped on gfx1100 and gfx1151 with the patch applied:
`PLATFORM_SUPPORTS_MX_GEMM` gates them out, so widening the allowlist cannot
wrongly enable the test there.

Also checked on legacy ROCm: I built this branch's base against ROCm 7.2.1 and

title: Fix symbolic stride-order sorting without explicit ShapeEnv
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #185871

Inductor stride-order computation was only symbolic-aware when callers explicitly passed a ShapeEnv into get_stride_order/get_fill_order. Some lowering paths call get_stride_order with symbolic strides while an Inductor graph is active but without passing shape_env. That made get_fill_order fall back to the generic argsort helper, and Python sorting then tried to truth-test SymPy relationals such as 1 < s53.

Recover a ShapeEnv from SymInt stride values or from the active V.graph before sorting symbolic strides, so the existing argsort_sym path handles these comparisons with ShapeEnv guards/hints. This keeps the fast plain argsort path for fully static stride lists, and uses the already-established symbolic comparator instead of introducing a separate stride-specific ordering rule.

The alternative was to thread shape_env through every current and future get_stride_order caller. That would be more invasive and would still leave this helper fragile for missed call sites, so the fix centralizes the fallback at the symbolic sort boundary.

Benchmark Results:

A focused timeit benchmark for the four-stride helper showed static old behavior median 759.17 ns/call and static new behavior median 1235.47 ns/call. For symbolic [s, 1, s, s], explicit shape_env median was 90308.02 ns/call and the new implicit V.graph fallback median was 92420.08 ns/call. Before this fix, the implicit symbolic path crashed with TypeError: cannot determine truth value of Relational: 1 < s53, so no runtime was available for that failing case.

title: Fix ModuleTracker with Dynamo runtime modules
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #186431

ModuleTracker maintains its hierarchy with global module hooks. Under Dynamo,
those hooks also run on compiler-owned modules during backend compilation and
compiled execution. Recording those modules as user hierarchy installs backward
hooks for compiler artifacts and corrupts the parent set seen by user hooks.

Carry weak references to exact runtime module identities in a nested
thread-local context. The collector follows explicit roots, compiler-created
GraphModule get_attr subgraphs, and internal wrappers that explicitly declare
their runtime values, while leaving ordinary user call_module children visible.
Dynamo activates this context at backend compile/runtime, correctness
verification, specialization, AOT flattening and boxed/restored calls, DDP
submodule compilation and fake execution, and compiled-autograd boundaries.
ModuleTracker resolves and caches the checker lazily through sys.modules so
eager-only users do not import Dynamo.

AOTAutograd now scopes forward, inference, and lazy backward compiler calls and
their returned callables centrally. This covers compiler-time GraphModule calls,
lazy backward lowering, and backend fallbacks without relying on every compiler
adapter to remember the protocol. The wrapper preserves the boxed calling
convention and bypasses tracking work when no global module hook is installed.

That observational wrapper initially obscured the capture placeholder identity
used by standalone AOT source composition. The composer then mistook an inner
tensor-subclass wrapper for an outer orchestration wrapper and reversed their
call order. Tracking wrappers now expose their immediate inner callable, and
the composer peels only a marker authenticated by that wrapper's own
__wrapped__ link. This retains semantic decorators that merely inherited the
marker through functools.update_wrapper.

Compile packages recompute runtime identities after backend deserialization.
Serializable eager callables expose their owned GraphModule through an explicit
internal provider interface, and RegionalOutputCode rebuilds weak references
after bundled-cache deserialization. This avoids serializing weak references
while making both ordinary and forced-autograd-cache package reloads correct.

A permanent per-instance flag or process-wide registry would misclassify a
backend module when the same object is later called by user code. Recursively
walking arbitrary closures or all GraphModule children could likewise hide
user-owned modules. Generic callable unwrapping could erase behaviorful backend
decorators. The scoped, explicit identity protocol and authenticated wrapper
marker preserve those role distinctions without extending module lifetimes.

Fixes #127112

title: [DCP] Optimize FsspecReader with Batched cat_ranges and Async Prefetching
body:
## Problem
When loading distributed checkpoints (e.g., FSDP or Model Parallel) from object storage backends (like gcsfs or s3fs), the current `FsspecReader` processes byte intervals individually in a strictly sequential, single-threaded loop. This exposes several performance bottlenecks:
1. **Request Serialization**: Issuing thousands of individual HTTP range requests creates massive connection and latency overhead.
2. **Synchronous Starvation**: Because network I/O, `torch.load` unpickling, and tensor slicing occur sequentially on the main thread, the network stream is routinely starved while waiting for CPU deserialization.

## Solution
This PR introduces a concurrent, double-buffered pipeline and native batch range reading for `FsspecReader`:
- **Batched cat_ranges**:
  - Replaces per-item single range reads with a single `fs.cat_ranges(paths, starts, ends)` call per batch.
  - Range coalescing policy is left entirely to the storage backend. `FsspecReader` passes only paths, starts and ends, so backends that coalesce may do so under their own policy, and backends that do not are unaffected. No capability probing or argument-level fallback is required.
- **Double-Buffered Async Prefetching**:
  - Decouples network I/O from CPU deserialization: a dedicated single-threaded prefetch executor fetches batch k+1 while a multi-worker CPU thread pool deserializes batch k in parallel.
- **Configurable Batching & Concurrency**:
  - Exposes `max_batch_size` (default 64) to bound transient memory and `cpu_workers` to maximize deserialization throughput.

## Benchmark Results

Timings measure `FsspecReader.read_data`.

**Setup:** 8 ranks on a single VM; a 44.88 GiB checkpoint on GCS standard bucket

| Strategy | Baseline | This PR | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| FSDP (sharded) | 520.56 s | 17.69 s | **29.43x (-96.6%)** |
| Model Parallel (sharded, TP=4, DP=2) | 563.85 s | 34.92 s | **16.15x (-93.8%)** |

title: [dtensor] fix conv1d output placement and group scaling
body:
Fixes DTensor dispatch for **depthwise** convolution (`groups == in_channels == out_channels`) when channels are sharded across the mesh — e.g. under FSDP or TP where the weight is `Shard(0)` and the input is `Shard(1)` on the channel dim. This is the layout used by GatedDeltaNet-style depthwise `Conv1d` in hybrid-attention models (Qwen3.5).

Depthwise conv treats each channel as an independent group, so channel-sharding requires no cross-rank communication — each rank computes its own channels locally. DTensor previously couldn't express or execute this, failing in both forward and backward.

## The bugs

1. **Wrong forward output placement.** `convolution_single_dim_strategy` only enumerated batch-dim sharding with a replicated weight. Channel-sharded input + out-channel-sharded weight matched no rule, so the propagator fell back to all-`Replicate`. The handler then ran on the still-sharded local tensors but labeled the result `Replicate` — so a 64-channel local output was tagged as the full 128-channel tensor. Downstream ops (e.g. `full_tensor()`) trusted the label and silently returned wrong data.

2. **Crash on `groups` (forward and backward).** `groups` is a plain int that isn't sharded. With a channel-sharded weight (128 → 64 local channels per rank), the local conv was still called with `groups=128`:

   ```
   RuntimeError: Given groups=128, expected weight to be at least 128 at dimension 0, but got weight of size [64, 1, 4]
   ```

   The backward path had the identical defect and crashed the same way; it had gone unnoticed because earlier validation only exercised the forward/inference path.

## The fix

Split across the two layers that own each concern, symmetric for forward and backward:

- **`_ops/_conv_ops.py` (sharding strategies)** — add a depthwise channel-sharding rule to both strategies, gated on `groups == in_channels == out_channels`:
  - forward: `[output=Shard(1), input=Shard(1), weight=Shard(0), (bias=Shard(0))]`
  - backward: `[grad_input=Shard(1), grad_weight=Shard(0), grad_bias=Shard(0), grad_output=Shard(1), input=Shard(1), weight=Shard(0)]`

  `grad_weight` / `grad_bias` are `Shard(0)` (per out-channel, no cross-rank sum), **not** `Partial`, because the groups are independent. The propagator now returns the correct `Shard(1)` / `Shard(0)` placements with no redistribution.

- **`_tp_conv.py` (local arg adjustment)** — strategies decide placements only; the local op still needs `groups` rescaled to the local weight shard (`groups * local_out_channels // global_out_channels`). This is factored into a shared `_scaled_local_conv_groups` helper, with a divisibility assertion guarding the even-sharding invariant, and is called from both `convolution_handler` and `convolution_backward_handler`.

Only depthwise conv is handled; regular (`groups=1`) and general grouped conv are untouched and fall through unchanged.

## Test

`test/distributed/tensor/test_convolution_ops.py::test_conv1d_channel_shard` — depthwise `Conv1d`, input `Shard(1)` + weight `Shard(0)`, asserts for **both forward and backward**:

- zero communication (`CommDebugMode`),
- correct `Shard(1)` output / gradient placement,
- `full_tensor()` bit-identical (max_diff 0.0) to a single-device reference.

Regression tests (`test_conv1d`, `test_conv1d_batch_shard`, `test_depthwise_convolution`) still pass. Validated across FSDP, TP, and FSDP+EP configs, and end-to-end on a hybrid-attention model (Qwen3.5) whose GatedDeltaNet layers use depthwise `Conv1d`.

title: Implement MKLGenerator
body:
This PR aims to fix the issue from #132395 by implementing a new `MKLGeneratorImpl` that stores a consistent, global `vslStream` for use in random numbers generation. This path was previously disabled due to a problem of repeating variates, caused by repeated reseeding of the MKL generator with variates from the `CPUGenerator`. This new implementation only seeds the `MKLGenerator` once using the `CPUGenerator`, and then keeps reusing the same `vslStream`, providing the full period of the RNG.

For the sake of reproducibility, the saving and restoring of the `MKLGenerator` has been linked to `CPUGenerator` state changes, and the former does not provide its own `get_state()` and `set_state()` functionality. The point was to keep the user experience identical to before -- they do not need to handle a separate `MKLGenerator` explicitly.

There already exists a test to check for repetition based on the script from #132395. It can be found `test_distribution.py` as `test_multinomial_sequential_draw()`. For the old (reseeded) implementation of the MKL `vslStream`, this test showed 21 repetitions. For this new implementation, the test gives 0 repetitions as expected.

title: [dynamo] Graph break on shape-changing differentiable Tensor.data assignment
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #186512

DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 style forward hooks gather partitioned parameters by
assigning a full-sized tensor to Parameter.data before a submodule runs,
then repartition the same parameter back to an empty tensor in a forward
hook. Dynamo traced those hook-side mutations into the same graph as the
module compute.

AOTAutograd builds backward graphs from the original metadata of differentiable
graph inputs. If a traced .data assignment changes an input's shape, later
forward operations can produce gradients with the replacement shape for an
input whose original shape is different, causing an invalid-gradient failure.
This invariant applies to ordinary differentiable tensors as well as Parameters.

Fix this by graph breaking before shape-changing .data mutations on
differentiable tensors. Fake shapes are compared with sym_eq and
statically_known_true, so symbolic equality is not guarded and unbacked SymInts
are not evaluated. If equality cannot be proven, Dynamo conservatively breaks;
provably same symbolic shapes and non-differentiable assignments remain
traceable. The check does not depend on ambient grad mode because a mutation
inside a local no_grad block can be followed by differentiable use.

A fully traced alternative would require AOTAutograd-safe semantics for changing
differentiable input metadata. This patch uses the narrower correctness
boundary and lets Dynamo resume on the tensor compute after the mutation.

Fixes #115484

title: Make SDPA backend checks safe for unbacked head dims
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #184983

`torch.export` can trace models that build repeat counts as tensors and
pass them to `repeat_interleave`. Without an explicit output size,
`repeat_interleave` creates unbacked symbolic sizes for the repeated K/V
head dimension. The fused SDPA backend selectors then used normal
`SymInt` comparisons such as `query_size_last == key_size_last`,
`head_dim <= max`, and alignment tests while deciding whether flash,
mem-efficient, or cuDNN kernels are viable. Those bool conversions guard
on the unbacked expressions before SDPA can fall back to math, producing
`GuardOnDataDependentSymNode` errors like `Eq(128, u0)`.

Switch those eligibility predicates to `sym_*` expressions evaluated with
`TORCH_GUARD_OR_FALSE`. Concrete and guardable symbolic inputs keep the
same result, while unbacked or unknown predicates conservatively reject
the fused backend and let the existing math fallback handle export. This
keeps the fix in backend selection instead of special-casing
`repeat_interleave` or SDPA export.

The main alternative would be requiring users to add `torch._check(...)`
for these repeated dimensions, but the backend picker only needs to know
whether a fused kernel is definitely legal. Treating unknown fused-kernel
preconditions as not viable is the narrower framework fix.

Fixes #170127

title: [inductor] Give the lerp decompositions eager's output strides
body:
Fixes #198343

With |weight| >= 0.5 the lerp decompositions from #176804 compute from `end`, so the result took end's strides where eager lays it out like `start`. `x.lerp_(end_t, 0.75); x.view(-1)` then fails to compile, and `torch.compile(torch.lerp)` returns other strides than eager.

This copies the result onto `empty_like(start)` when `start` has the output's shape, in `lerp.Scalar`, `lerp.Tensor` and both paths of `_foreach_lerp.Scalar`: start's strides, or dense in start's order when `start` has gaps. When the strides already match nothing changes. I didn't use `prims.copy_strided` to `compute_elementwise_output_strides` as `torch._refs.lerp` does, because that lowering hits #198332. The OpInfo samples of lerp only use 0.4 as a scalar weight, so test_torchinductor_opinfo doesn't reach this path.

Test plan: `test_lerp_output_strides_follow_eager` in test_torchinductor.py (`lerp_` with a scalar weight, `lerp` with a 0-dim weight, a dense `start` and one with gaps) and `test_foreach_lerp_output_strides_follow_eager` in test_foreach.py (float32 and bfloat16), which fail without the change. On 2.14 with CUDA (RTX 4070), with the change and without: test_torchinductor.py GPUTests on lerp, mutation, copies, views and strides (522), test_foreach.py (617), test_compiled_optimizers.py (808) and the lerp OpInfo tests in test_torchinductor_opinfo.py (6), with no new failure.

## Summary
Add `register_stream_variable_cls` so out-of-tree backends can register their `StreamVariable` subclass without editing upstream PyTorch source.

title: Fix no-tensor-aliasing recompile reason for stale sources
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #184793

NO_TENSOR_ALIASING guard failure reporting re-evaluates the tensor source
expressions recorded by the first compile. When a later invocation changes a
container that held tensors into a value such as None, sources like
L['data'][0] no longer evaluate. The guard had already failed correctly, but

reporting, while unavailable sources are included in a separate reason.
TypeError handling is limited to subscription/indexing failures so unrelated
evaluation bugs still propagate.

I considered only skipping failed sources, but reporting them keeps the
recompile reason actionable and preserves information about the stale guard
sources.

title: Add focal_loss ATen op
body:
## Summary
- Adds a multi-class `aten::focal_loss` composite: `-alpha * (1 - pt)^gamma * log(pt)` with `pt = softmax(self)[target]`, defaults `alpha=0.25`, `gamma=2.0`, mean / sum / none reduction.
- `self` must be floating point `[N, C]` and `target` int64 `[N]`; anything else is rejected with a message.
- Answers the open feature requests for focal loss (#146034) and more loss functions (#41142).
- No Python caller is in this pull request. Tests that call the new op are in a draft follow-up and should land only after this change has been in tree for the forward-compatibility window.

## Reproduced definition
Installed PyTorch does not contain this op yet, so the numbers below are the same formula the C++ composite implements, executed in PyTorch 2.11.0 on arm64.

Logits `[[2, 0.5, -1], [0.2, 0.1, 0.3]]`, target `[0, 2]`:

| reduction | value |
|---|---|
| none | `[0.00277319, 0.10031443]` |
| mean | `0.05154381` |
| sum | `0.10308762` |

With `gamma=0, alpha=1` the formula equals `cross_entropy` exactly on the same inputs. Gradient of the mean at the logits is about `[[-0.00341059, 0.00278841, 0.00062218], [0.03596719, 0.03254446, -0.06851166]]`.

## Test plan
- [ ] Confirm codegen accepts the `CompositeImplicitAutograd` entry
- [ ] After the forward-compatibility window, land the draft Python checks

title: [inductor] Include tensor pinned-ness in FX-graph cache key
body:
### Summary
Fixes #197519, the FX-graph cache key couldn't tell pinned apart from pageable, so same-values compiles shared one entry and the second compile got the wrong memory kind. 

### The fix
Two small moves in `codecache.py`: ask every constant once whether it's pinned, and staple the answer onto both key payloads, the inlined one and the frozen-param one. I left shared `TensorMetadata` alone and the fake-tensor path too. Since the key is just a hash, telling the two apart can only ever cost a recompile, never a wrong hit.

### Testing
- Two new tests: `test_pinned_affects_cache_key` covers both key paths at the pickler level, and `test_fx_graph_cache_key_distinguishes_pinned` runs both pin orders end to end through one shared cache dir (each order misses twice and hits zero, that's the split working). Also `test_parameter_constants` works with the new frozen-path payload.
- The repro on the issue fails both orders before the fix and passes both after. I also ran the e2e logic against main to make sure the test can actually catchs the bug.

### Note
Old cache entries won't match anymore, so expect a one-time recompile.

Related: #197211, #173939

title: [Fearure Refactoring] Decouple hardware-specific checks for NPU/PrivateUse1 support
body:
## Summary

Replace hardcoded device checks (`is_cuda`, `is_xpu`, `torch.xpu.is_available()`) in
two files with generic PyTorch APIs so PrivateUse1 backends (e.g. Ascend NPU) are
supported without touching core code again. This is part of the ongoing third-party
backend friendliness effort (RFC #174469, #185142).

## Changes

- **`torch/_dynamo/variables/optimizer.py`**
  - `safe_to_set_capturable`: replace `p.is_cuda or p.is_xpu` with
    `p.device.type in _get_capturable_supported_devices()`, reusing the existing
    device list that already includes the PrivateUse1 backend name. NPU now gets
    capturable optimization.

- **`torch/_inductor/kernel/flex/flex_decoding.py`**
  - `get_split_k`: replace hardcoded `torch.xpu.is_available()` / `torch.cuda`
    branch with `torch._C._accelerator_getAccelerator()`, dispatching by the
    current accelerator device type and falling back to a safe default (32) when
    device properties are unavailable. Prevents crash on NPU-only machines.

## Motivation

Previously, running Inductor/Dynamo on NPU-only systems could crash because
`get_split_k` unconditionally called `torch.cuda.get_device_properties()` when XPU
was unavailable, and `safe_to_set_capturable` excluded PrivateUse1 devices from
capturable support. Both changes are minimal, non-behavioral for existing
CUDA/XPU paths, and required for third-party backend enablement.

## Test Plan

- Existing CUDA/XPU behavior unchanged (device list in `_get_capturable_supported_devices`
  is a superset; accelerator device type preserves original branches).
- `python test/run_test.py -i test_optim --hardware-requirement DEVICE_GENERIC`
- `python test/run_test.py -i test_flex_attention --hardware-requirement DEVICE_GENERIC`
- Manual run on NPU (A2/A3/A5): confirm no crash in flex decode lowering and
  capturable enabled for optimizers.

## Notes

- This commit only addresses the low-risk decoupling points (no CUDA-only
  underlying dependencies). `_is_static_for_cudagraphs` and the full
  `cudagraph_trees.py` module are intentionally left unchanged: they are
  CUDA-specific by design (explicit `_CUDAGRAPH_SUPPORTED_DEVICE_TYPES` whitelist)
  and NPU has its own GraphCapture path.
- Follow-up: `flex_decoding.py` BLOCK_M lower bound still uses
  `torch.xpu.is_available()` (low risk, deferred).

title: [symm_mem] Reject alloc and first rendezvous during CUDA graph capture
body:
alloc() and a first-time rendezvous() block the host on the current stream (handle exchange, peer-table upload, stream synchronize). Doing either while the stream is capturing a CUDA graph previously failed with a bare cudaErrorStreamCaptureUnsupported raised from deep inside the driver call, with nothing pointing at the actual mistake.

Both paths now raise a TORCH_CHECK up front, naming the operation and telling the caller what to do instead: allocate with _symmetric_memory.empty() and run the first rendezvous eagerly before starting capture. Subsequent rendezvous calls on the same buffer hit the cache and remain capture-safe, and collectives on a rendezvoused buffer stay capturable after one eager run - each replay performs that rank's peer synchronization, so every rank must replay the same number of times. Docs for empty() and rendezvous() updated to state the contract.

Fixes #198140

title: [Testcase Refactoring] Decouple TestDeprecatedJitQuantized for out-of-tree backends
body:
## Background

Ascend for PyTorch community test-case decoupling task, issue Ascend/pytorch-ecosystem#18.

`test/quantization/jit/test_deprecated_jit_quant.py` gates test discovery on backend availability: `test_quantization_modules` is defined inside a class-body `if "fbgemm" in torch.backends.quantized.supported_engines:` branch. On any backend that does not provide FBGEMM the method is never defined, so the same file collects a different number of tests depending on the backend it runs on. That blocks device-agnostic scheduling of the community test suite.

## Changes

1. Import `HardwareClassification` from `torch.testing._internal.common_utils` and set `hw_classification = HardwareClassification.GENERIC` on `TestDeprecatedJitQuantized`. The class instantiates no device and contains no accelerator-specific logic, so it is device independent.
2. Remove the class-body `if "fbgemm" in torch.backends.quantized.supported_engines:` guard around `test_quantization_modules` and mark the method with `@skipIfNoFBGEMM`, the decorator already used by the other three tests in this file.

Test method names, inputs, assertions and execution order are unchanged; no test case is added or removed. Guard semantics for community-supported configurations are unchanged: with FBGEMM available the branch was always taken, so `test_quantization_modules` is still executed, in the same order, and the collected set is identical.

## Test Plan

- Local build: passed - the change is Python test code only; verified against a CPU-only PyTorch build.
- Unit tests: all executed
  - `python test/test_quantization.py TestDeprecatedJitQuantized -v` -> Ran 4 tests, OK
  - `python -m pytest test/quantization/jit/test_deprecated_jit_quant.py -vv -ra` -> 4 passed
- Functional verification: reproduced the reported scenario - with FBGEMM unavailable the method is now always defined, so the file collects 4 tests instead of 3 and the FBGEMM-dependent tests report a clean skip instead of disappearing from the collected set. With FBGEMM available the collected test names and order are identical to the baseline.
- Lint: `lintrunner` reports no issues for the changed file.
- CUDA: no CUDA-specific code path is touched; covered by the upstream CI CUDA jobs.

## Risks

None.

title: Dispatch `index_put_` to `index_fill_.Scalar` when possible
body:
This is a followup on #188330 and tries to dispatch `index_put_` to `index_fill_.Scalar` where possible - e.g. `gpu_tensor[indices] = 1.0` - instead of converting the scalar to a tensor first and dispatching to `index_put_`.

Compared to #188330 the current code already doesn't do a GPU/CPU sync, however I think it's still a good idea to remove the unneeded tensor creation.

/cc @jgong5 @mingfeima @XiaobingSuper @sanchitintel @ashokei @jingxu10 @aditew01 @ngimel @atalman

I benchmarked this on a A100 with the following small script:
```python
import torch
from torch.utils.benchmark import Compare, Timer

results = []
for device in ["cuda", "cpu"]:
    if device == "cuda" and not torch.cuda.is_available():
        continue
    for dtype in [torch.float32]:
        for tensor_size in [100_000, 500_000, 1_000_000, 5_000_000]:
            shapes = [(tensor_size,), (1000, tensor_size // 1000)]
            for shape in shapes:
                indexed_dim_size = shape[0]
                permutation = torch.randperm(indexed_dim_size, device=device)
                for index_ratio in [0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0]:
                    num_indices = round(indexed_dim_size * index_ratio)
                    index = permutation[:num_indices]
                    indices = [("1-D index", index), ("2-D contiguous index", index.reshape(1, -1))]
                    for index_description, shaped_index in indices:
                        a = torch.rand(shape, dtype=dtype, device=device)
                        flat_index = shaped_index.view(-1)
                        sub_label = (f"{shape}, {index_description}, selected {index_ratio}")
                        statements = ("a[shaped_index] = val", "a.index_fill_(0, flat_index, val)")
                        descriptions = (f"index, {device}", f"index_fill, {device}")
                        timers = [
                            Timer(
                                stmt=statement,
                                num_threads=10,
                                sub_label=sub_label,
                                label="Fill",
                                description=description,
                                globals={"a": a, "shaped_index": shaped_index, "flat_index": flat_index, "val": 1.0},
                            )
                            for statement, description in zip(statements, descriptions)
                        ]
                        for timer in timers:
                            results.append(timer.blocked_autorange())

Compare(results).print()
```

**Before:**

On GPU `index_fill` tends to have much lower overhead since we don't need create a new GPU tensor. However, on CPU the the `index_put_` path is sometimes faster for smaller or sparse workloads. My guess is that this is due to the [smaller tuned grain size](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/d31de0a6ee94769b1eec66bc3c81dfe1cf5c2d5b/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/IndexKernelUtils.h#L70-L73) allowing for more parallelism for smaller indexing whereas `index_fill` uses the much larger default grain size. Let me know if you think this is worth re-tuning, though I guess that might need a few more benchmarks.

title: [ROCm] Honor depthwise_kernel="native" where the native kernel applies
body:
torch.backends.cudnn.flags(depthwise_kernel=...) is only consulted inside use_cudnn_depthwise(), which returns false when cuDNN is absent. On ROCm _select_conv_backend then took the next branch and picked MiopenDepthwise for "auto", "cudnn" and "native" alike, so asking for the native depthwise kernel had no effect unless MIOpen was disabled altogether. That is also why test_Conv2d_depthwise_kernel_flag was skipped on ROCm: all three modes ran the same kernel, so the comparison was meaningless.

The MIOpen depthwise branch now goes through ConvParams::use_miopen_depthwise(), which skips MIOpen when the flag is NATIVE and the native kernel can actually serve the input. "auto" and "cudnn" keep MIOpen unchanged.

What the native kernel can serve is taken from that kernel rather than from cuDNN's predicate. It is 2-D only, so a 5-D depthwise convolution stays on MIOpen: conv_depthwise3d has never run for fp32, fp16 or bf16 on ROCm, carries tighter numel <= INT32_MAX limits, and stages its grad_weight block reduction in scalar_t after accumulating in accscalar_t. It also indexes with 32 bits, and the tensors it range-checks are the input and the output, not the weight, in all three directions: the forward checks input and output, grad_input checks grad_input and grad_output, and grad_weight checks input and grad_output. A channel multiplier makes the output k times the size of the input, so an input just under INT_MAX can produce an output over it; the guard therefore tests input, weight and output element counts, taking the output count from conv_output_size(). Element counts are sufficient here because the backend contiguous-ifies before the kernel runs. Finally, a channels-last input stays on MIOpen when MIOpen is the one asked to suggest NHWC.

The remaining conditions cuDNN applies are deliberately not mirrored. On CUDA the flag is consulted only inside kernel_cond, which additionally requires fp16, at least 32 channels, no dilation and a square or 1-D stride, because those are the shapes cuDNN has a depthwise kernel for. MIOpen serves every dtype use_miopen() accepts and the native kernel handles all of them correctly, so "native" is a wider switch on ROCm than on CUDA.

With the test comparing two different kernels, fp16 needs a wider tolerance on ROCm. For fp16 depthwise 3x3 MIOpen selects the Winograd solver ConvBinWinogradRxSf2x3, whose output against an exact fp64 reference is off by up to 4.1e-3 over 50 seeds (about two fp16 steps at these magnitudes), while the native kernel stays at 9.8e-4; that gap is the same on gfx950, gfx942 and gfx90a and is reported as ROCm/rocm-libraries#12334. Across 500 seeds the largest MIOpen-to-native difference was 5.9e-3, so the ROCm atol is 1e-2; CUDA keeps 1e-3.

The tolerance is not what makes the test meaningful. Comparing numerics alone cannot fail in the state the test exists to catch: when "native" is not honored, all three modes run the same deterministic MIOpen kernel and return bitwise identical tensors, which passes at any tolerance. The test now asserts the selected backend, and a second test covers the 2-D restriction.

Test Plan:

On gfx950 (MI355X, ROCm 10.0), 533 passed, 343 skipped, 24 xfailed:

```
python -m pytest test/nn/test_convolution.py -k "depthwise or Depthwise or conv_backend"
```

Backend selection on a 4-D contiguous input returns CudaDepthwise2d for "native" and MiopenDepthwise for "auto" and "cudnn". A 5-D input stays on MiopenDepthwise under "native". A channel multiplier whose output exceeds INT_MAX while its input does not stays on MiopenDepthwise and runs, where routing it to the native kernel instead fails that kernel's own canUse32BitIndexMath(input) && canUse32BitIndexMath(output) check. torch.compile(dynamic=True) with the flag set matches eager across several batch sizes.

The tolerance measurements above were repeated on gfx942 and gfx90a, where MIOpen picked the same Winograd solver with the same 4.12e-3 error, so the fp16 gap is a property of the solver rather than of one architecture. The backend-selection changes have been exercised on gfx950 only.

title: [dynamo] Fix random.shuffle/random.sample freezing across repeated compiled calls
body:
Fixes #197085

## Summary

Inside a `torch.compile`d function, module-level `random.shuffle`/`random.sample` returned the same result on every call after the first, instead of drawing fresh each call like eager and like the other supported `random.*` functions (`random()`, `randint()`, `randrange()`, `uniform()`) already do.

**Root cause:** `RandomVariable.shuffle`/`sample` computed the permutation against a trace-time-only `random.Random` snapshot and baked the result into the graph as a constant. The scalar random functions instead route through Dynamo's existing "recorded call, re-executed on every real invocation" mechanism (`tx.output.random_calls`, replayed via `_get_gen_rand_values_fn`), which `shuffle`/`sample` never used.

**Fix:** add a `GlobalRandomVariable(RandomVariable)` subclass, selected at construction time when the wrapped `random.Random` is the actual process-global instance (`random._inst`). It overrides `shuffle`, `sample`, `seed`, `setstate` and `_call_random` to route through the same `random_calls` replay mechanism, so real values are drawn fresh on every invocation instead of being frozen at trace time. Explicit `random.Random()` instances keep the prior trace-time-only behavior unchanged.

The runtime-replay path is restricted to populations that are fully constant-foldable and homogeneous in a runtime-primitive type (`bool`/`int`/`float`); anything else (tensors, strings, mixed non-numeric types) falls back to the original trace-time-only behavior. This avoids two failure modes found during review:

- A population with heterogeneous element types could have its trace-time-chosen and real-runtime-chosen types diverge at a given list position, and Dynamo skips the `TYPE_MATCH` guard for these sources, so a mismatch was reaching `torch.tensor()` uncaught (`TypeError: new(): invalid data type 'str'`).
- Treating a non-numeric runtime-replayed value as a plain `ConstantVariable` risks Dynamo elsewhere treating it as a genuine compile-time constant (e.g. for branching), when its real value can differ on every call.

The fallback path also records its own state-advancing closure into `random_calls` (rather than relying solely on the end-of-function side-effect mutation replay), since that mutation replay runs after `random_calls` is already replayed each invocation -- without this, a fallback shuffle/sample sharing a compiled function with any other `random_calls`-routed call (a plain `random()`, another `seed()`, etc.) would leave that other call frozen too.

## Test Plan

```
cd ~/pytorch && .venv312/bin/python -m unittest -v \
  test.dynamo.test_unspec.UnspecTests.test_random_object_shuffle \
  test.dynamo.test_unspec.UnspecTests.test_random_object_sample \
  test.dynamo.test_unspec.UnspecTests.test_random_object_sample_raises \
  test.dynamo.test_unspec.UnspecTests.test_random_module_shuffle_sample \
  test.dynamo.test_unspec.UnspecTests.test_random_module_shuffle_sample_tensor_list \
  test.dynamo.test_unspec.UnspecTests.test_random_module_shuffle_heterogeneous_list \
  test.dynamo.test_unspec.UnspecTests.test_random_module_shuffle_sample_nonnumeric_fallback \
  test.dynamo.test_unspec.UnspecTests.test_random_module_shuffle_sample_mixed_numeric_types_fallback \
  test.dynamo.test_unspec.UnspecTests.test_random_module_seed_shuffle \
  test.dynamo.test_unspec.UnspecTests.test_random_module_setstate_shuffle \
  test.dynamo.test_unspec.UnspecTests.test_random_values_with_graph_break \
  test.dynamo.test_unspec.UnspecTests.test_multiple_consecutive_random_calls_before_graph \
  test.dynamo.test_unspec.UnspecTests.test_compiled_random_calls_are_random \
  test.dynamo.test_unspec.UnspecTests.test_module_random_random_fullgraph \
  test.dynamo.test_unspec.UnspecTests.test_random_object_overridden_methods \
  test.dynamo.test_unspec.UnspecTests.test_random_in_dynamo
```

title: [export_python] inductor: readable wrapper launches each kernel with its compile-time autotuned config
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #193901
* #193900
* #193899
* #198257
* #198256
* #198255
* #198254
* #198253
* #198252
* #193898
* #198277
* #198276
* #198275
* #198247
* #198246
* #198245
* __->__ #198311
* #198274
* #193974
* #193973

**Problem.** A readable module is an artifact that gets committed and replayed, but each hoisted Triton kernel kept inductor's heuristics decorator, so it still autotuned on its first launch. The launch config decides a kernel's numerics (a reduction's block sizes set its summation order), so two cold starts of the same artifact could return different bits, and nothing in the file said which config ran.

**Fix.** Nothing autotunes at runtime any more. `readable_wrapper` requires `triton.autotune_at_compile_time` for Triton kernels (turning it on when it is unset), pins each hoisted kernel to the config that tuning picked, and lists those configs in a `KERNEL_CONFIGS` table at the top of the module.

**Summary.** Under the parent commits, a hoisted kernel's `@triton_heuristics.persistent_reduction(...)` (or `pointwise`, `reduction`, ...) decorator built a CachingAutotuner that benchmarked its candidate configs on first launch, and coordinate-descended under `coordinate_descent_tuning`. So the config, and with it the result of a reduction, was picked anew in every process that loaded the artifact. Now the root wrapper reads each kernel's one winning launcher out of the compile-time autotune block's namespace (`generate_and_run_autotune_block` returns it). It rewrites the kernel's decorator to `@triton_heuristics.fixed_config(config=KERNEL_CONFIGS[...], ...)` and emits the table as a deferred line in the root header. The key constraint is that subgraph kernels reach the root as finished text before the root autotunes, so only a table resolved at assembly time can hold their configs. For the same reason, `triton.multi_kernel` (supported by the parent commits) and user-defined kernels autotuned over several configs are now refused, and the default wrapper is unchanged.

## What the emitted module looks like

```python
# parent: the kernel tunes itself on first launch
@triton_heuristics.persistent_reduction(
    size_hints={'x': 64, 'r0_': 128},
    ...,
    inductor_meta={..., 'coordinate_descent_tuning': True, ...},
)
@triton.jit
def triton_per_fused__softmax_0(...):
    ...
```

```python
# now: one table at the top of the module...
# The launch config of each kernel below, chosen by autotuning at compile time.
# Kernels launch with exactly these and never retune at runtime.
KERNEL_CONFIGS = {
    'triton_per_fused__softmax_0': {'XBLOCK': 1, 'num_warps': 8, 'num_stages': 1},
    ...
}

# ...and each kernel launches with exactly its entry
@triton_heuristics.fixed_config(
    config=KERNEL_CONFIGS['triton_per_fused__softmax_0'],
    filename=__file__,
    triton_meta=...,
    inductor_meta={...},
)
@triton.jit
def triton_per_fused__softmax_0(...):
    ...
```

A FIXED autotuner has one config and is exempt from coordinate descent and from dynamic RBLOCK scaling, so its first launch compiles that config and runs it. The table is where a reader looks up, or edits, the config a kernel runs with. Template kernels are built with their one config and keep their decorator. The compile-time autotune block itself still execs the original heuristics, since that is where the tuning happens.

## Three keys are dropped from the pinned inductor_meta

```python
dropped = ("combo_tuning_groups", "coordinate_descent_tuning", "incremental_autotune")
entries = [
    f"{ast.get_source_segment(src_code, k)}: {ast.get_source_segment(src_code, v)}"
    for k, v in zip(meta.keys, meta.values)
    if not (isinstance(k, ast.Constant) and k.value in dropped)
]
```

`combo_tuning_groups` would make `CachingAutotuner.run` run sequential combo-kernel tuning on first launch. `coordinate_descent_tuning` is subtler: even with one config, it makes `cached_autotune` consult the autotune cache, and that cache's best config for this file would replace the pinned one. Keeping the key fails every case of the test below on the autotune-cache lookup. `incremental_autotune` makes `get_caching_autotuner_plugins` install a tuning plugin, so it goes too. The entries are filtered as source text rather than round-tripped through `ast.literal_eval`, because some values are not literals: a bucketize kernel's `inductor_meta` holds `'autotune_hints': (AutotuneHint.ONE_ELEMENT_PER_THREAD,)`, which `literal_eval` rejects. Template kernels keep their `@triton_heuristics.template(...)` decorator and their meta, which is safe because the template decorator is emitted without a `filename=`, and `check_autotune_cache` consults the cache only when there is a filename.

## Why a root-level table and not a per-kernel literal

```python
# define_subgraph_launcher_fn: the subgraph's text is final when it is spliced
self.subgraph_definitions.splice(subgraph_code.value)
```

The configs are only known after `generate_and_run_autotune_block` has run in the root, and by then every subgraph's kernels have already been spliced into the root as strings. A literal written into each decorator could not be filled in for those kernels. `_KernelConfigs` is a `DeferredLineBase` in the root header, resolved in `getvalue()` after tuning. It reads as absent to the preamble usage scan, and it emits nothing for a graph with no hoisted Triton kernels. `_ReadableSubgraphPythonWrapperCodegen` shares the root's `kernel_configs` dict, so a subgraph's kernels are recorded where the root resolves them.

## Configurations that are refused

`triton.autotune_at_compile_time` defaults to unset (`None`, from `TORCHINDUCTOR_AUTOTUNE_AT_COMPILE_TIME`). `compile_fx` turns it on under `readable_wrapper` when it is unset, before tracing, because decompositions read it too: `repeat_interleave_Tensor` is not decomposed under `autotune_at_compile_time`, since its data-dependent kernel would be run by the compile-time autotune block on generated inputs. `compile_fx_inner` applies the same default again, next to the cpp_wrapper patches, for a lazily compiled backward. So the bare flag (`TORCHINDUCTOR_READABLE_WRAPPER=1`) keeps working for GPU compiles. Only an explicit `False` is refused, and the check runs first in `emit_triton_kernel_definition`:

```python
with config.patch(readable_wrapper=True, **{"triton.autotune_at_compile_time": False}):
    torch.compile(_softmax)(x)
# RuntimeError: ... readable_wrapper pins each Triton kernel to the config chosen by
#               autotuning at compile time and requires triton.autotune_at_compile_time ...

with config.patch(readable_wrapper=True, **{"triton.multi_kernel": 1}):
    torch.compile(torch.relu)(x)
# RuntimeError: ... readable_wrapper does not choose kernels at runtime and is
#               incompatible with triton.multi_kernel ...
```

`MultiKernelCall` benchmarks its candidate kernels on first launch and keeps the fastest, which is choosing a kernel at runtime, so the parent's `test_multi_kernel_runs_standalone` is replaced by `test_multi_kernel_is_refused`. A user-defined `@triton.autotune` kernel with more than one config (`add_kernel_autotuned` in the test) stays an `async_compile.triton` source string whose autotuner would benchmark those configs, so `define_user_defined_triton_kernel` refuses it and names the kernel. A user kernel with one config, or a plain `@triton.jit` one, still compiles through AsyncCompile, but under `coordinate_descent_tuning=False` and `incremental_autotune=False`. Its `user_autotune` decorator keeps `filename=`, so `coordinate_descent_tuning` in its `inductor_meta` would make `check_autotune_cache` consult the autotune cache, and a cached best config would replace its own. If the compile-time block ever leaves a hoisted kernel with more than one launcher, `generate_and_run_autotune_block` raises rather than emitting a kernel that would tune itself.

## Alternatives considered

- **Skip the compile-time pass and tune on first launch** (the parent's behaviour). That is exactly the nondeterminism described above.
- **Rewrite each kernel's `filename=` to a per-kernel autotune-cache path.** The choice would then depend on a cache file existing next to the artifact, and the kernel would still coordinate-descend when that file is missing.

## Tests

```python
# test_kernels_launch_with_their_compile_time_config, under
# coordinate_descent_tuning=True and max_autotune_pointwise=True
with (
    mock.patch.object(CachingAutotuner, "autotune_to_one_config", runtime_tuning),
    mock.patch.object(CachingAutotuner, "_coordinate_descent_tuning", runtime_tuning),
    mock.patch.object(AutotuneCache, "create", runtime_tuning),
):
    exec(compile(code, path, "exec"), ns)
    self.assertEqual(ns["call"]([x])[0], expected, atol=0, rtol=0)
for name, cfg in ns["KERNEL_CONFIGS"].items():
    (launcher,) = ns[name].launchers
    self.assertEqual(config_to_dict(launcher.config), cfg, name)
```

The test is parametrized over a persistent reduction, a reduction, a pointwise kernel, a bucketize kernel (whose `inductor_meta` is not a literal), and a `torch.cond` whose branch kernels live in subgraphs (run with `x` and `-x`, so both branches launch). It checks that every decorator is `fixed_config` and `KERNEL_CONFIGS` is present. It then runs the module standalone with all three tuning entry points patched to raise, requires bitwise equality with the compiled result, and checks that each kernel's one launcher uses exactly its `KERNEL_CONFIGS` entry. It also wraps `PythonWrapperCodegen.generate_and_run_autotune_block` to capture the tuned scope, and checks that every entry equals the config of the launcher tuning left. Recording a different config (such as `num_warps=1`) fails all five cases, although the module is still self-consistent. Without the decorator rewrite all four cases fail. `test_template_and_combo_kernels_run_standalone` now also runs its module under the same three patches, under `coordinate_descent_tuning` for its matmul template case, and checks that the template keeps its decorator and has no `KERNEL_CONFIGS` entry. `test_compile_time_autotuning_is_on_before_decompositions` checks that under the bare flag `repeat_interleave` with a tensor `repeats` falls back to aten instead of decomposing into a Triton kernel, and it fails without the `compile_fx` default. `test_dynamic_shape_kernel_keeps_its_pinned_config_at_every_size` compiles a reduction with `dynamic=True`, which is tuned once on the size hints, and runs the module standalone under the three patches at three sizes, including the compile-time one. `test_triton_kernels_require_compile_time_autotuning` checks that an unset `autotune_at_compile_time` is turned on and an explicit `False` is refused. `test_user_kernel_does_not_read_the_autotune_cache` runs a plain `@triton.jit` kernel under both flags, checks that neither key is in its meta, and runs the module standalone under the three patches. It fails without the patched meta. `test_user_kernel_autotuned_over_several_configs_is_refused` and `test_multi_kernel_is_refused` pin the other refusals. `_code_for` sets no autotune config, so every readable test goes through the unset default. Without the default, 23 of the readable tests fail. Also, `test_emitted_module_runs_standalone_and_matches_eager` loses its `autotune_at_compile_time=None` variant.

Test Plan:

```
python test/inductor/test_readable_wrapper.py
python test/inductor/test_compile_to_python.py
python test/inductor/test_wrapper_codegen.py
```

test_kernels_launch_with_their_compile_time_config (persistent reduction,
reduction, pointwise, and a torch.cond whose branch kernels live in
subgraphs, all under coordinate_descent_tuning and max_autotune_pointwise)
checks that every decorator is fixed_config and KERNEL_CONFIGS is present,
runs the module standalone with CachingAutotuner.autotune_to_one_config,
_coordinate_descent_tuning and AutotuneCache.create patched to raise,
requires bitwise equality with the compiled result, and checks that each
kernel's one launcher uses exactly its KERNEL_CONFIGS entry. Mutation-checked:
without the decorator rewrite all four cases fail; keeping
coordinate_descent_tuning in the pinned inductor_meta fails them on the
autotune-cache lookup. New refusal tests:
test_triton_kernels_require_compile_time_autotuning,
test_user_kernel_autotuned_over_several_configs_is_refused and

title: [dynamo] Add registration APIs to decouple autocast/ctx-manager from backends
body:
### Summary
torch.compile() hard-coded torch.amp.autocast_mode.autocast and the CUDA/CPU autocast entry points in TorchInGraphFunctionVariable, and AutocastModeVariable.create accepted only those three functions. A PrivateUse1 backend (e.g. NPU) that registers its own autocast entry point could therefore not be traced: the call fell through to a graph break, or hit the "unexpected autocast function" assertion if it reached the ctx-manager handler.

Add lazy registration APIs -- register_ctx_manager_class, register_constant_fold_function and register_device_autocast_entry -- so a backend can extend the set of traceable ctx-manager classes, constant-foldable functions and autocast entry points after torch is imported. The trace path now queries these registries via _get_supported_ctx_manager_classes / _is_constant_foldable / _autocast_entries instead of the module-level sets. With no registrations every query returns the original set, so existing behavior is unchanged; a regression test locks in device_type equivalence for the generic/cuda/cpu paths.

Third-party autocast entry points are routed to
AutocastModeVariable.create, which now looks up the registered device_type for entry points whose signature omits it, so NPU-style autocast is traceable.

The ctx_manager.py half must land in the same PR as the torch.py routing: a standalone routing change would send third-party autocast into the assertion path in create(), so splitting them would create a broken intermediate state.

### Test Plan:
```bash
python -m py_compile torch/_dynamo/variables/torch.py torch/_dynamo/variables/ctx_manager.py test/dynamo/test_ctx_manager.py
python test/dynamo/test_ctx_manager.py CtxManagerTests.test_autocast_third_party_device_type_injection
python test/dynamo/test_ctx_manager.py CtxManagerTests.test_autocast_device_type_equivalence
python test/dynamo/test_ctx_manager.py CtxManagerTests.test_register_device_autocast_entry_validates_args
```

title: Partition the pinned host allocator's free lists by NUMA node behind an opt-in flag
body:
Related to #160420.

In that issue @galv asked for a use case where NUMA affinity in the pinned
allocator actually matters. Here is one, with measurements.

This addresses the reuse problem in that issue's title rather than the
`cuMemCreate` / `CU_MEM_LOCATION_TYPE_HOST_NUMA` mechanism proposed in its body,
so I have not marked the issue as fixed — that call is @galv's to make.

## The setup

One inference process drives 6 A100s on a dual-socket AMD EPYC 7H12: GPUs 0-3
hang off NUMA node 0, GPUs 4-5 off node 1. Each GPU loads several hundred MB to
a few GB of constants through pinned staging buffers. The loader threads are
bound to the node of the GPU they serve.

The node-1 loaders are consistently ~30% slower than the node-0 loaders, *and
they have the least contention* — one loader on node 1 versus two on node 0,
doing identical work:

| | concurrent loaders | median prepare | max |
|---|---|---|---|
| node 0 (cuda:0-3) | 2 | 1065 ms | 1388 ms |
| node 1 (cuda:4/5) | **1** | **1389 ms** | 2067 ms |

## Why binding does not fix it

The binding is correct. The cache defeats it.

I pre-warm the pinned cache from a thread bound to each node, then read the
actual page placement from `/proc/self/numa_maps`:

```
node0 prewarm, 12 x 64MiB:  494.80 ms   pages all on N0 (196608 pages = 768 MiB)
node1 prewarm, 12 x 64MiB:    0.15 ms   pages still all on N0   <- nothing allocated
```

Node 1 allocates nothing: node 0's freed blocks are an exact size-bucket match,
so the slow path is never reached and `cudaHostAlloc` -- which would have placed
the pages on the calling thread's node -- is never called.

This is the part I would emphasise: node 1 does not *sometimes* get remote
memory, it gets remote memory **every time**. No amount of CPU or memory binding
changes that, because no allocation ever happens on node 1 to bind. On this host
a cross-node host-to-host copy runs at 36.8 GiB/s against 116.8 GiB/s local, so
every staged copy through such a block pays 3.2x, plus a second penalty on the
H2D DMA that I have not isolated.

Scope, to be precise: the general statement is about the allocator -- a
node-blind cache in front of it means correct binding does not imply local
memory. Under one process per GPU that never manifests, exactly as the comment
in `CachingHostAllocator.cpp` says, and I am not claiming otherwise. What my
deployment supplies is a case where it does: one process whose threads span two
nodes and share one cache. `torch/numa/binding.py` cannot help there -- it emits
`numactl --physcpubind` with no `--membind` and is organised local-rank ->
device-index, i.e. built around one process per GPU.

I am aware of #185417 and that it was closed. That patch proposed *placement
policy* via `set_mempolicy`, which does overlap what `torchrun` already does.
This change does not do placement policy -- it partitions the *reuse* structure,
which no launcher-level binding can reach.

## The change

Keep one free list per NUMA node in `CachingHostAllocator`, behind an opt-in
`pinned_numa_aware` allocator setting. Off by default.

- An allocation is served from the pool of the node the **calling thread** runs
  on. No change to `Allocator::allocate()` — the interface stays device-agnostic
  and callers need no modification.
- A free returns the block to the pool it came from, recorded on the block at
  allocation time, not to the pool of the freeing thread's node. Otherwise
  blocks drift to whichever node frees most often and the partition decays.
  Note this is the allocating pool's node: with default first-touch it is also
  where the pages are, but an explicit mempolicy or the `host_register` path can
  break that, which is why those combinations are rejected.
- Partitioning, not filtering: `default_pools_[node]` is a direct index, so the
  size-bucket lookup after it is byte-for-byte what it is today. The added work on
  the allocation path is one `GetCurrentNUMANode()`, measured here at **563 ns** --
  `sched_getcpu()` is 8 ns through the vDSO, but `numa_node_of_cpu()` walks the
  per-node cpumasks and costs the rest. That is 46x the uncontended mutex
  acquisition already on this path, so it is not free, though it is invisible next
  to the work it guards: a 64 MiB staging copy is milliseconds. A workload doing
  many small pinned allocations would notice. A `thread_local` cache brings it to
  2.4 ns and is safe -- a bound loader thread does not migrate, and a thread that
  did would only lose locality for itself, since a block's pool is recorded at
  creation and free routing does not consult the calling thread. I have not done
  it here: it is a separate concern from the partitioning and I would rather land
  the structure first. Say the word and I will add it.
  The free path adds a field read.
- No cross-node fallback when the local pool is empty. Falling back would
  preserve exactly the "sometimes fast, sometimes slow, no visible reason"
  behaviour that took me a full day to track down. A fresh 64 MiB pinned
  allocation is ~40 ms, paid once per node per size bucket.
- Pool count is `numa_max_node() + 1`, not the number of nodes, because node ids
  can be sparse.

This builds directly on #167507, which already introduced `MempoolId_t`-keyed
private host pools — the partitioning machinery exists, this adds one dimension
to it.

**Opt-in because of memory, not speed.** Each node keeps its own free list, so
the same sizes may be held more than once; how much is duplicated depends on how
many nodes actually allocate and on how the work is spread. Here it is one extra
copy, 768 MiB cached instead of 384 MiB. `pinned_max_cached_size_mb` limits the
effect for large allocations — a block above that size is freed rather than
cached — but it is a per-block threshold, not a cap on the total.

## Behaviour when the flag is unset

The allocator keeps a single pool and the allocate/free fast paths are
unchanged.

Two qualifications, because I would rather state them than have them found.

Allocate and free now also run an initialization check, which is one acquire load
once the pools are built. And the second commit changes the c10 NUMA topology
queries for every caller, not only for this flag: `GetNumNUMANodes()`,
`GetNUMANode()` and `GetCurrentNUMANode()` used to be gated on
`FLAGS_caffe2_cpu_numa_enabled` and are now gated on NUMA being available. That is
a deliberate widening -- the previous gate conflated "may we move pages" with "may
we ask what the topology is" -- but it is a behaviour change outside this feature.

The one intentional behaviour change in the allocator is independent of the flag:
the first commit fixes per-bucket allocator statistics being shared across pools.
`HostStatsStaged` held the per-bucket vectors in a single instance while the
comment stated they were protected by `pool.free_list_[index].mutex_` — different
pools, different mutexes, same counters. #167507's private pools can already
trigger this today; N concurrent per-node pools would make it routine.

## Known limitations

**Per-bucket `peak` is now summed across pools, so it over-reports.** Before the
first commit the bucket counters lived in one shared vector and `peak` was exact.
They now live per pool and `getStats` sums them, so two pools that never peak at
the same moment still add up. The existing code already sums peaks across buckets
and documents that as an approximation; this adds a second dimension to the same
approximation. Blocks retired from a destroyed pool take the max rather than the
sum, so it cannot grow without bound, but it is not exact.

The clean fix is the other shape: leave the counters shared and give them their
own per-bucket locks, rather than moving them into the pools. That is a smaller
change than what is here and it keeps `peak` exact. I did not do it because it
decides how these counters should be structured as more pool kinds are added, and
that call belongs to whoever maintains this file. Say the word and I will redo the
first commit that way.

**Enabling the flag makes 11 existing tests in `TestCachingHostAllocatorCudaGraph`
fail.** They go through a helper that sets
`pinned_use_cuda_host_register:True,pinned_num_register_threads:8`, which is
exactly the combination the compatibility check rejects. Default-off means CI is
unaffected, but anyone who turns the flag on process-wide and runs `test_cuda.py`
will see them. Rejecting loudly rather than silently degrading to a single pool
was a deliberate choice -- degrading silently reproduces the "sometimes fast, no
visible reason" behaviour this exists to remove -- but the friction is real and I
am happy to be told the other way is preferred.

## Commits

1. Fix per-bucket host allocator stats being shared across pools
2. Gate the c10 NUMA topology queries on availability, not on the placement flag
3. Keep one pinned host free list per NUMA node behind an opt-in flag

(1) and (2) stand on their own; happy to split them into separate PRs if that is
easier to land.

## Validation

Built and tested on the host above. With the flag off, a node-1 allocation takes
0.19 ms, triggers 0 fresh `cudaHostAlloc` calls, and lands 0/65536 pages on the
local node. With it on: 116.50 ms, 4 fresh allocations, 65536/65536 pages local.

New tests in `test/test_cuda.py`, all subprocess-isolated because the setting
latches at the first pinned request. Being straight about what they cover: I
checked them by emulating the feature away -- forcing `numa_max_node()` to 0 so
the allocator keeps one pool while parsing, validation and latching still run --
and only `test_free_routes_by_block_node_not_by_freeing_thread` fails under that.
The other seven constrain the preconditions and the two repaired failure modes,
not the partitioning. Not covered: genuine single-node pool construction, sparse
node ids, the out-of-range fallback, and the rollback path when pool setup throws.

---

*Disclosure per AI_POLICY.md: the measurements above are mine. I used AI
assistance to organise them into this description and to review the
implementation, and I have read and verified the code and the numbers myself.*

title: Optimize all-gather copy-in with a flat parameter buffer
body:
FSDP2 currently packs parameter shards into a contiguous communication buffer on every `foreach_all_gather`.

This PR places eligible sharded parameters in a single contiguous flat storage during lazy initialization. During all-gather copy-in, FSDP copies this flat buffer directly into the rank-local slice of the all-gather output.

This preserves the existing in-place all-gather contract while replacing per-parameter packing with a single contiguous copy. Under mixed precision, the same copy also performs the conversion from the original parameter dtype to `param_dtype`, avoiding a separate cast buffer.

The fast path:
- Checks and caches eligibility during lazy initialization.
- Preserves parameter object identity when rebasing DTensor storage, so existing optimizer references remain valid.
- Uses an O(1) readiness check in the all-gather path.
- Falls back to the existing path for CPU offload, meta parameters, non-uniform dtypes, FSDP pre/post-all-gather extensions, compiled autograd, and parameters that cannot be safely rebased.
- Preserves the existing in-place all-gather input/output aliasing.
- Does not change the existing copy-out path.

Per-all-gather local copy count:

| Configuration | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| No mixed precision | 1 foreach copy | 1 contiguous copy |
| Mixed precision | 2 foreach copies | 1 contiguous cast copy |

The collective test classes mix device-generic, accelerator-common, and backend-specific proof targets in single classes. Splitting them by hardware classification makes the test intent explicit and allows future device matrices to pick up the appropriate subsets without changing existing distributed admission.

#198338 extracts the class split and hw_classification labels from this PR as a separate structural change. After #198338 lands, rebase this PR on it so the device parameterization and Triton admission changes can be reviewed here on their own.

title: [DCP] Support dynamic thread_count auto-tuning in DCP writers
body:
Closes #193804

This change introduces dynamic auto-tuning of write `thread_count` in Distributed Checkpoint (DCP) writers (`_FileSystemWriter`, `FileSystemWriter`, and `FsspecWriter`)

## AI Generated Summary

1. **Dynamic `thread_count` Auto-Tuning**:
   - `_FileSystemWriter` now supports dynamic auto-tuning of IO threads when `thread_count=None`.
   - The optimal concurrency is determined dynamically per save invocation in `_calculate_optimal_thread_count(plan)` based on:
     - Available CPU cores.
     - Number of write items in the `SavePlan`.
     - Total tensor payload size divided by `min_size_per_thread`.
     - Capped at `max_threads`.

2. **Cloud Storage Optimization (`FsspecWriter`)**:
   - `FsspecWriter` now defaults to `thread_count=None` (triggering auto-tuning by default for remote/cloud checkpoints).
   - Configured with `min_size_per_thread=1GB` to avoid connection thrashing and GIL contention on small checkpoints while automatically scaling parallel upload streams on multi-gigabyte models.
   - Allows users to configure explicit `thread_count`, `max_threads`, and `min_size_per_thread` overrides.

3. **Local Storage Behavior (`FileSystemWriter`)**:
   - `FileSystemWriter` maintains default `thread_count=1` (preserving standard single-threaded local disk IO by default).
   - Users can opt in to auto-tuning by passing `thread_count=None`.

## Test Plan

- Added unit and roundtrip tests in `test_file_system_checkpoint_cpu.py`:
  - `test_calculate_optimal_thread_count`: Validates thread calculation across various payload sizes and verifies clamping against thread/item limits.
  - `test_filesystem_writer_save_and_load_auto_tuned`: Verifies end-to-end saving and loading with `FileSystemWriter(thread_count=None)`.
- Added unit and roundtrip tests in `test_fsspec.py`:
  - `test_fsspec_writer_thread_count_auto_tuning`: Verifies default auto-tuned saving to `memory://` filesystem and explicit parameter overrides.
- Verified state dict equivalence between single-threaded and multi-threaded auto-tuned checkpoints.

title: [Feature Refactoring] Remove hardcoded cuda default in _gen_rank_device and _alloc_tensor
body:
## Summary

`_gen_rank_device` and `_alloc_tensor` in `torch/distributed/checkpoint/optimizer.py` defaulted `device_type` to `"cuda"`, which hardcodes a CUDA assumption for out-of-tree backends. This PR makes the default device inferred from `torch.accelerator.current_accelerator(check_available=True)`, falling back to `"cpu"` when no accelerator is available, and adds unit tests for the new behavior.

## Changes

- `torch/distributed/checkpoint/optimizer.py`:
  - Add `_infer_default_device_type()`, which returns the current accelerator's device type or `"cpu"` when none is available.
  - Change `_gen_rank_device(global_rank, device_type="cuda")` to accept `device_type: str | None = None` and infer the default via `_infer_default_device_type()` when not provided.
  - Change `_alloc_tensor(props, size, device_type="cuda")` to accept `device_type: str | None = None` and infer the default the same way.
  - Existing callers that pass an explicit device type (`pg_device_type`, `dp_pg_device_type`) are unchanged.
- `test/distributed/checkpoint/test_optimizer.py` (new):
  - Add `TestOptimizerDeviceDefaults` (`hw_classification = HardwareClassification.GENERIC`) covering explicit CPU, accelerator-less fallback to CPU, default following a mocked accelerator (XPU), and `_alloc_tensor` default/explicit paths.

## Test Plan

`python test\distributed\checkpoint\test_optimizer.py --hw-classification GENERIC -v`

title: Keep RNG ops working, and rank-agnostic, under compile_on_one_rank
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #196154
* #196153
* __->__ #196152
* #196940
* #196939
* #196938
* #196150
* #196151
* #197585

Every RNG op failed to compile under compile_on_one_rank -- rand, randn, randint
and so dropout too:

  RuntimeError: prims::inductor_seed() Expected a value of type 'Device'
                for argument 'device' but instead found type 'Node'

replace_random and replace_randint run on the joint graph, where a factory op's
device operand is still a coor current_device() node: respecialize_current_device_nodes
does not concretise those until post_grad. Both handlers take that operand
straight off the matched node, so a graph node reached inductor_prims.seed(),
whose schema declares Device and cannot accept one.

Resolve the node where a real device is genuinely needed, and only there:

  - get_device(), which feeds inductor_prims.seed()
  - fuse_seed_creation_pass, when it builds meta["val"] for the fused seed --
    the graph argument beside it keeps the node, which is what makes the fused
    seed rank-agnostic

Anything else that turns out to be a graph node now raises rather than being
silently mishandled.

That alone leaves the seed's device baked, because fwd_only -- the tracer behind
every replace_by_example -- disables compile_on_one_rank wholesale. That is right
for a pattern template, which is only ever matched against, and wrong for a
replacement, which is spliced into the user's graph and so bakes a rank-specific
device into it. Split the two: fwd_only keeps the feature live when tracing a
replacement, and the fourteen template call sites are unaffected.

The RNG path is now device-agnostic in the joint graph:

  inductor_seeds_default = prims.inductor_seeds.default(1, current_device_default_1)

where it previously read device(type='cuda', index=0).

title: Drop the device index from the fx graph cache key under compile_on_one_rank
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #196154
* __->__ #196153
* #196152
* #196940
* #196939
* #196938
* #196150
* #196151
* #197585

Every rank compiled the same graph and then missed on every other rank's cache
entry, so no compiled artifact was ever shared. The index reaches the key through
exactly one component -- example_inputs' TensorMetadata:

  [lfqb4cez...] example_inputs[0]: TensorMetadata(..., device=device(type='cuda', index=0), ...)

Nothing else contributes one. In particular the graph hashed alongside it does
not: the key is built in _compile_fx_inner before _recursive_post_grad_passes
runs, so it sees the AOT graph, where devices are still current_device() nodes.
Measured on a 16-GPU CooR job, 4730 device-bearing key lines per rank, all of
them example_inputs, and zero from gm.

Strip it in extract_tensor_metadata_for_cache_key, whose stated job is removing
fields not needed for caching, and which already does this for storage_offset
and storage_bytes. Gated on the accelerator being the current one, so cpu
tensors and non-CooR compiles keep their index -- outside CooR several devices
can legitimately be live and must not collide.

The full key is now byte-identical across devices under CooR, and still
correctly distinct without it.

test_inductor_compiled_on_one_device_runs_on_another asserted a cache *miss* as
a deliberate tripwire for this change -- its comment asked that landing a
device-agnostic key trip the test rather than silently widen it. It now asserts
the hit. That comment also flagged CompiledFxGraph.device_idxs as a second
requirement for reuse; the reused artifact was checked to run on the reusing
rank's own device and to be numerically correct, so no change is needed there.

title: [test] Reuse device meshes across FSDP2 ND-mesh subtests
body:
test_2d_mlp_with_nd_mesh and test_3d_mlp_with_nd_mesh build a global mesh and pass it to their subtest helpers, but each helper overwrote it with a freshly built mesh, so every subtest created new NCCL communicators. test_shard_placement_fn_tp_ep rebuilt its meshes in every subtest even though they depend only on tp_degree and dp_replicate.

On RCCL every communicator keeps a ~40 MB proxy-ops segment per rank in /dev/shm until the test's processes exit, so each of these tests exceeded a 10 GiB /dev/shm on 8 GPUs and failed with ENOSPC.

Use the mesh that is passed in, and build the tp_ep meshes once per configuration. Peak /dev/shm on 8x MI300X at this commit: 2D 16.1 -> 1.3 GB, 3D 21.4 -> 1.6 GB, tp_ep 20.5 -> 8.8 GB.

title: Make tensor device observations rank-portable under compile_on_one_rank
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #196154
* #196153
* #196152
* #196940
* #196939
* #196938
* #196150
* __->__ #196151
* #197585

Dynamo specializes tensor device metadata before make_fx runs. Under
compile_on_one_rank, baking the current accelerator index into a guard, an FX
constant, or Tensor.get_device() makes the artifact rank-specific: another rank
can either recompile unnecessarily or silently observe the tracing rank's index.

Classify an indexed accelerator as runtime-relative only when it is the current
accelerator under CooR. x.device uses a dedicated variable that keeps the
accelerator type static and resolves index-dependent observations at runtime.
Tensor guards still check the exact index at this commit; #196150 relaxes them
to check against the runtime current device using the same classification.
Tensor.get_device() uses the same coor::current_device_index SymInt operator as
x.device, whose fake implementation leaves the index unbacked until execution.

An exact index guard would preserve eager specialization but defeat CooR by
creating one artifact per rank. Returning only an index-less device works for
factory and .to() passthrough but loses observable index semantics. The runtime
index representation preserves both: device passthrough remains portable, while
arithmetic reads the executing rank's index and data-dependent control flow
graph-breaks rather than specializing to the tracing rank.

The index observation is cached per tracer, not per graph. A higher-order op
traces each subgraph with its own tracer, and a proxy created under a sibling
cannot be lifted into this one -- both branches of a torch.cond reading
x.device.index otherwise trip the root-tracer assertion in
lift_tracked_freevar_to_input.

torch.device(d) copies d: the result is equal to it but a distinct object, so
the call hands back a fresh rank-relative device rather than d itself, and the
device= keyword form is accepted as well. Handing back a distinct variable is
what keeps `torch.device(d) is d` False the way it is eagerly, so identity
comparison is taught that two of these are never the same object -- the same
rule a bound method already follows, and the same reason `x.device is x.device`
is False.

Equality reports one equal to an explicit cuda:N whenever N is the running
rank's index, so its hash has to agree with every cuda:N. Under CooR both it and
a constant torch.device hash as the index-less device, so all devices of one
type share a bucket and equality decides: two rank-relative devices are the same
key (which is what _group_tensors_by_device_and_dtype, and so
clip_grad_norm_, needs), and against an explicit cuda:N the key comparison reads
the runtime index -- a data-dependent error under fullgraph, a graph break
otherwise, the same as `x.device == torch.device("cuda:N")`. Refusing to hash
was the alternative, but it made clip_grad_norm_ fail to compile under CooR.

CompileOnOneRankUnsupported, for a construct CooR cannot express at all, is
raised by later commits in the stack; it propagates whether or not graph breaks
are allowed, which is why it is its own type rather than an Unsupported or a
UserError -- convert_frame soft-fails both of those.

The tensorless index operator is assigned a CPU lowering device because
FallbackKernel otherwise has no tensor from which to infer one.
