title: Guard tensors against the current device index under compile_on_one_rank
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #196154
* #196153
* #196152
* #196940
* #196939
* #196938
* __->__ #196150
* #196151
* #197585

A TENSOR_MATCH guard records a tensor's device type in its DispatchKeySet and
its device index separately. Under compile_on_one_rank, an input on the current
accelerator should use a rank-relative index guard so that another rank can
reuse the compiled artifact. The device type stays exact, and an input on a
non-current accelerator is refused rather than guarded (see below).

Nothing here guards a device value that Python reads back. Under CooR the index
carries no information -- every accelerator tensor is on the current device --
and the preceding commit makes that explicit by handing back an index-less
"cuda" from x.device, so a read cannot observe the compiling rank's index in
the first place. Adding an exact guard for those reads would defeat the point:
it pins the artifact to the one rank whose device it recorded, turning the
divergence into a recompile rather than preventing it.

The relative-versus-exact decision has two halves. Which tensors qualify is
derived: it turns only on whether the tensor is on an accelerator, the same
answer on every rank, so a guard rebuilt from a state loaded elsewhere reaches
it without consulting the saving rank -- whose device is the one thing a reload
must not read. Whether the relaxation applies at all is recorded, as
compile_on_one_rank on the saved graph state, because that half is not
portable: loading rebuilds the guard through the same builder, so a relaxed
guard reloaded with the setting off would come back pinned to the saving rank's
index and reject the device it was saved to accept, and an exact one reloaded
with it on would come back relaxed and accept a device it was saved to reject.

What makes the derived half hold is refusing the case that would otherwise
differ: an input on an accelerator other than the current one cannot be made
rank-portable, so tracing now rejects it, in wrap_to_fake_tensor_and_record.
The make_fx backends already refused such a graph via
_coor_check_current_accelerator, but Dynamo builds tensor guards before any
backend runs, so an eager-backend compile reached the guard with a device only
the tracing rank has.

The recursive-dict-tag fast path keeps a TensorCheck snapshot of its own, and
an unchanged tag lets it answer without running the TENSOR_MATCH leaf, so that
snapshot has to be taken in the same relative form. Pinned, it accepts a
parameter left behind on a device the leaf rejects. The root guard manager
carries the mode for that path to read. It shows up only with
use_recursive_dict_tags_for_guards on, and only while the tag holds: busting
the tag forces the leaf to run and the guard rejects correctly again.
clone_manager copies the mode too, so a cloned root snapshots the same way.

Checking a relative guard needs the current accelerator index. Cache that value
once per root guard evaluation so guard sets containing thousands of tensors do
not make thousands of runtime device queries. The recorded-index path stays
call-free: TensorCheck short-circuits rather than resolving a current device it
would not use.

TensorCheck holds the choice in one field -- an optional index, unset for "the
current one" -- rather than an index plus a flag deciding whether to read it.
Unset means the current accelerator, never "any device": both forms compare the
tensor's index against something. The pybind default now matches the C++
constructor's, so out-of-tree callers of add_tensor_match_guard still compile.

Guard mismatch diagnostics report both the runtime current-device index and the
actual tensor index. The exact-index path also casts DeviceIndex to int before
formatting, fixing the pre-existing behavior where its int8_t representation
was emitted as a character.

Cover the refusal directly, and keep pinning that the runtime guard rejects a
tensor on a non-current device -- relaxing the index must not mean ignoring it.
The dict-tag fast path gets a case of its own, since it answers without the
leaf, and the serialization test covers a load under the opposite setting in
both directions. The get_device test compiles with fullgraph and counts frames,
because the original code object's cache entries would miss the resume frames a
graph-breaking implementation compiles under their own code objects.

```shell
python test/dynamo/test_guard_manager.py
python test/dynamo/test_guard_serialization.py
python test/dynamo/test_modules.py
python test/dynamo/test_subclasses.py
python test/distributed/tensor/test_compile_on_one_rank.py

```

title: [export_python] precompile: check dtype and device of tensor-subclass inputs at load
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #193901
* #193900
* #193899
* #198257
* #198256
* #198255
* #198254
* #198253
* #198252
* #193898
* #198277
* #198276
* #198275
* #198247
* #198246
* __->__ #198245
* #198311
* #198274
* #193974
* #193973

**Problem.** The artifact records a dtype, a device and a shape for every tensor
input and checks them on each call, but it recorded `None` for all three when the
input was a traceable wrapper subclass (e.g. DTensor), and the generated driver
skipped the whole check for such a leaf. Skipping the shape made sense: a
subclass goes through AOTAutograd's flatten path, so its outer shape is not the
dense shape the inductor artifact bakes. Skipping dtype and device did not. The
outer dtype is exactly what AOTAutograd specializes on, so a float64 subclass
handed to a graph built for float32 came back as reinterpreted bytes with no
error, and a CUDA subclass was handed to a graph built for CPU.

**Fix.** `_dense_dtype` and `_dense_device` now record a value for any
`torch.Tensor`, subclass or not, and the driver's per-input loop in both the
eager and inductor forwards skips only non-tensors; a `None` shape now skips
only the shape comparison, while dtype and device are still compared. The
`_dense_shape` docstring spells out what is still unguarded (a subclass's inner
shapes), and the capture comment on tracing with grad enabled now states the
specialization it implies and why the ambient grad mode is not used instead.

```python
code, cache = torch.compiler.precompile(fn, dtensor_f32)  # captured as float32
run = torch.compiler.precompile.load(code, cache)
run(dtensor_f64)  # now raises the dtype mismatch instead of returning garbage
```

Test Plan:

```
python test/test_precompile.py
```

No new tests; the existing dtype, device and DTensor subclass tests pass
unchanged, and the change only widens which inputs reach the existing dtype and
device checks.

title: [inductor] Wildcard symbolic size-list entries in retraced patterns
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #198320

The HUD compilers dashboard lost ~20% speedup and gained 3-5 s of compile
time on every BERT-family HuggingFace model under the cudagraphs_dynamic
config after #195383 relanded (9b6e45278f). Static configs and non-BERT
models were flat.

#195383 validates every pattern-matcher match by re-tracing search_fn
with the matched inputs and matching the resulting specific pattern,
built with fx_to_pattern(match_node_meta=True). In that mode size lists
are wildcarded elementwise and the op's output shape is pinned by an
expected_meta check instead, but _wildcard_size_list kept PatternExpr
entries literal. Under a symbolic batch, matmul's decomposition reshapes
q/k to [s0*heads, seq, head_dim], so the re-traced _sfdp_pattern_29
contains a sym-expr node CallFunction(operator.mul, KeywordArg('arg0_1'),
12, _users=4) inside its view size lists and matches it structurally,
users count included. The user graph has a single mul(arg, 12) sym node
shared by the views of all 12 layers, so the specific match failed with
"multiple_users" for every layer, SDPA fusion was silently dropped, and
the unfused softmax kernels cost the extra compile time. Static shapes
never produce such a node, which is why only the dynamic config moved.

_wildcard_size_list now also receives the raw fx size-list args and
requires every entry (an int, or a sym node's meta["val"]) to be -1 or
statically equal to the traced output dim, the rule already applied to
ints. When that holds the whole list is wildcarded, sym nodes included;
expected_meta still pins the output shape, so a mismatched size is
still rejected and the wrong-output cases #195383 fixed stay fixed. The
alternative of relaxing the users check on sym nodes would still match
their spelling (mul vs sym_size chains) and was not pursued. The sym
KeywordArg bindings the dropped nodes provided are not needed: check_fn
unflattens only the static argnames and re-traces the replacement from
the fake args. The fix is scoped to size lists: a shared sym node used as
a scalar SymInt argument (slice bounds, say) or in a stride list would
still be matched structurally, but no registered pattern does that.

Test Plan:

New regression test with two attention layers sharing the batch dim, run
in inference and training so both the fwd_only and joint_fwd_bwd

title: Functionalize mutations in deferred local_map
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #185043

Deferred local_map builds its joint forward/backward graph from an already captured local body while functionalization is suspended. Mutation nodes can therefore survive into partitioning, and side-effect-only Triton mutation HOPs can be dropped entirely under FakeTensor execution. A raw joint trace can also fail when an in-place update changes a tensor that an earlier operator saved for backward.

Materialize a forward-only graph first so call_method, mutable ATen, out=, Python wrapper, and mutation-HOP forms are visible. For supported non-invoke bodies, functionalize that forward before AD tracing, using an explicit empty make_fx decomposition table so detach boundaries survive into the later backward. Bodies containing opaque Python callables stay on the AD-aware path so a hidden custom autograd function keeps its backward semantics. Only the exact torch package namespace is treated as internal, so third-party packages such as torchao do not accidentally take the pre-AD path.

invoke_subgraph needs Python-mode functionalization but saves operands for lazy backward construction. Give inspection and joint traces fresh cache identifiers, and use stride-preserving operand clones only while building its mutation-bearing joint. After custom autograd and nested HOP backward logic has expanded, functionalize the canonical joint before partitioning. Effectful or still-unsupported HOP combinations fail explicitly instead of silently miscompiling.

Pre-functionalizing every body was rejected because it can erase custom autograd boundaries, while post-joint-only functionalization can hit saved-tensor version checks before it gets a graph. The split path preserves AD semantics while normalizing mutations early whenever that is safe.

Fixes #167568

title: [CUDA] Fix borrowed reference handling in memory snapshot
body:
## Summary

`PyTuple_GetItem` returns a borrowed reference. `THCPModule_memorySnapshot` passed tuple elements from both accepted argument forms to owning `THPObjectPtr` wrappers, which decremented their reference counts when the wrappers were destroyed. This can leave the input tuple pointing at a freed object.

We first saw a crash while repeatedly creating CUDA `MemPool` objects and taking pool snapshots. It appeared at pool ID `(0, 257)`: IDs through 256 were masked by immortal small integers in the tested Python 3.12 runtime. The same crash reproduced with PyTorch's default allocator and no NCCL registration. With snapshots disabled, 512 fresh pools completed cleanly. A direct call to `torch._C._cuda_memorySnapshot((0, non_interned_id))`, without creating a pool, changed that ID object's reference count from 3 to 2.

Use borrowed `PyObject*` pointers for the tuple entries; the input tuple remains alive throughout these checks and conversions. Add an isolated subprocess regression test for the two- and three-item argument forms so a bad decrement cannot corrupt the main test process.

## Validation

- `git diff --check origin/main..HEAD` and Python syntax compilation of `test/test_cuda.py`.
- Rebuilt the affected PyTorch 2.10 vendor source on GB200 with CUDA 13.1 and the same two-item correction. The direct probe changed from a 3→2 reference count on the original binary to 3→3 on the patched binary.
- The patched binary completed 512 fresh `torch.cuda.MemPool` create/allocate/snapshot/destroy lifecycles through pool ID 512 with a clean process exit.

The vendor source accepts only the two-item form, so this binary validation does not exercise current main's three-item branch. The PR adds a regression test for both forms, but the three-item test has not been run against a CUDA-enabled current-main build.

title: [inductor] Skip addmm decomposition for zero alpha or beta
body:
## Issue

Fixes #196596

## Summary

The Inductor `addmm` decomposition materializes both scaled terms as
`alpha * out + beta * self`. This does not preserve eager zero-scalar behavior
when an operand contains NaN or inf, since `0 * NaN` is still NaN.

The two scalars have different semantics:

* `beta == 0` is documented: "If beta is 0, then the content of input will be
  ignored, and nan and inf in it will not be propagated" (`torch/_torch_docs.py`).
* `alpha == 0` has no equivalent documented guarantee. Its behavior depends on
  the BLAS implementation: an MKL build skips the GEMM and returns a finite
  result, while a build configured with `USE_EIGEN_FOR_BLAS=ON` multiplies
  through and returns NaN for the same input.

Return `NotImplemented` when either scalar is zero, generalizing the existing
CUDA `beta == 0` bailout. This avoids encoding zero-scalar behavior in the
decomposition and instead preserves the eager behavior of the active backend on
the default fallback path.

An alternative would be to keep the CPU decomposition for `beta == 0` and skip
only the bias term, as the core `baddbmm` reference decomposition does. I kept
the bailout instead to make the fix small and avoid adding separate zero-scalar
semantics to each decomposition branch; `alpha == 0` would still require a
fallback.

Known gap, left for a follow-up: under `max_autotune`, a Triton template can win
and its epilogue computes `acc * alpha` and `bias * beta`
(`torch/_inductor/kernel/mm_common.py`), so the NaN can reappear. The CPP GEMM
template has the same issue for `alpha`, although it already skips the bias
epilogue when `beta` is zero.

## Tests

`test_addmm_zero_scalar_matches_eager` asserts that the decomposition returns
`NotImplemented` and that the compiled result matches eager. This holds for
both tested BLAS behaviors.

`test_addmm_zero_beta_drops_nan_bias` additionally asserts the stronger
backend-independent invariant that no NaN from `input` reaches the output when
`beta == 0`, since that behavior is part of the documented `torch.addmm`
contract.

On CPU, 8 of the 12 new cases fail without the change. The other four use the
`(4, 1, 4)` shape, which exercises the non-CPU `k == 1` decomposition branch
but does not decompose on CPU. CUDA and XPU numerics were not tested locally.

## Checklist

* [x] Passes lint (`spin fixlint`)
* [x] Added/updated tests
* [ ] Updated documentation (not applicable)
* [ ] Included benchmark results (not applicable)

## BC-breaking?

No

title: [inductor] Don't write an in-place foreach op straight into a buffer it reads elsewhere
body:
Fixes #198033

`register_foreach_inplace` lowers `_foreach_add_(xs, ys)` as the out-of-place op followed by `mutate_to(x, result, unsafe_alias=True)`. With `unsafe_alias`, `realize_into` gives the pointwise that computes `result` the layout `MutationLayoutSHOULDREMOVE(x)`, which is only safe when `result` reads `x` at the element it writes. `torch._foreach_add_([x], [x.flip(0)])` reads the mirrored row in the kernel that writes it: wrong at every size on CPU, a race on CUDA that shows at 1024 x 1024.

This checks the reads of the pointwise against its write before aliasing. When a read of the target is at another index, the result is realized into a buffer of its own and copied, the way `x.add_(x.flip(0))` is already lowered. An optimizer step reads each parameter where it writes it, so it still writes in place with no extra buffer.

Test plan: `test_inplace_reads_self_elsewhere` in test_foreach.py, which fails without the change. On 2.14 with CUDA (RTX 4070), test_foreach.py is 600 passed, and test_compiled_optimizers.py is 804 passed with and without the change, with the same one pre-existing failure (`test_S429861`).

title: Preserve rank-relative devices in Dynamo device contexts
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #196154
* #196153
* #196152
* #196940
* #196939
* __->__ #196938
* #196150
* #196151
* #197585

Tensor device observations use a runtime-relative device under
compile_on_one_rank. Device context constructors previously required a Python
constant, so passing x.device either failed during tracing or tempted callers to
freeze the compiling rank's index.

Represent these contexts explicitly as CurrentDeviceContextVariable. CooR gives
a rank a single accelerator, so entering the current device is a no-op and no
index reaches the graph.

That no-op is sound only while nothing moves the current device mid-frame, and
two paths could. Both are now refused. Entering a device context with an
explicit index is refused because, with a no-op enter,
`with torch.cuda.device(1)` wrapped around a rank-relative context did not
switch back on entry and silently allocated on the wrong GPU under
fullgraph=True. That includes the compiling rank's own index: the artifact runs
on every rank, so `torch.cuda.device(0)` compiled on rank 0 would name the wrong
GPU everywhere else. Calling set_device (cuda, xpu, mtia, or
accelerator.set_device_index and its deprecated set_device_idx alias) while
tracing is refused because a no-op exit restores nothing, so the move would
leak past the region and leave every rank-relative device in the frame denoting
the wrong GPU. The refusal is unconditional, even for the device the rank is
already on, so whether a frame compiles doesn't depend on which rank compiled it;
set_device outside compiled code, e.g. the usual set_device(local_rank) at
startup, is unaffected. set_device_idx is marked skipped in trace_rules because
the warnings.warn in its deprecation wrapper graph-breaks, which ran the wrapped
set_device_index eagerly without ever reaching the check.

An index-less constant device (e.g. `torch.device("cuda")` or None), when the
context manager matches the rank's accelerator type, becomes a
CurrentDeviceContextVariable as well, rather than resolving through
GenericDeviceVariable.create. That covers the index-less form Dynamo's own
reconstruct emits at a graph break, and is what keeps a resumed frame portable:
create() resolves the index at trace time, so tracing the resume frame baked in
the compiling rank, and since that artifact is shared across ranks every rank
ran the resumed region on the compiling rank's GPU.

The alternative to refusing set_device was to keep real exchange nodes and make
their operand rank-relative, preserving eager's restore-on-exit semantics. That
is more machinery to serve a call that violates CooR's single-accelerator
premise anyway, so refusing it is the simpler contract.

Test Plan:

```shell
TORCHINDUCTOR_COMPILE_THREADS=1 python test/distributed/tensor/test_compile_on_one_rank.py
```

74 passed, covering the rank-relative context, its reconstruction across a graph
break on a device other than the compiling one, and both new refusals (including
the compiling rank's own index and each set_device variant but mtia).

Dynamo regression coverage for the shared SkipFunctionVariable and device
context paths:

```shell

python test/dynamo/test_functions.py
python test/dynamo/test_ctx_manager.py
python test/dynamo/test_trace_rules.py
python test/dynamo/test_streams.py
```

body:

After tensor devices became runtime-relative under compile_on_one_rank, Dynamo
could no longer pass x.device through the stream constructor's constant-only
example path. Converting it to the tracing rank's device without retaining its
origin would instead reconstruct the stream on the wrong rank.

title: Anchor a property descriptor's guard source at the type
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #196154
* #196153
* #196152
* #196940
* #196939
* #196938
* #196150
* #196151
* __->__ #197585

`object_generic_getattr` computes one instance-anchored source and hands it to
`_resolve_descriptor_get` for every kind of descriptor. That anchor is wrong
for a `property`: the descriptor lives on the type, and `PropertyVariable`
derives its `fget` source from it, so the guard reads `L['obj'].attr.fget` --
which evaluates the getter and then asks the resulting value for `.fget`:

    AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'fget'

Reaching it takes a `property` on an object Dynamo wraps as a
`ConstantVariable`, which in practice means `torch.cuda._CudaDeviceProperties`:

```python
props = torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0)
torch.compile(lambda x: x + props.multi_processor_count)(torch.randn(2, device="cuda"))
```

Point the source at the descriptor `mro_lookup` actually returned. Naming it
`type(obj).attr` is not enough: that reads back through `type.__getattribute__`,
where a data descriptor on the metaclass beats the class chain, so a metaclass
`property` of the same name reproduces the very same `.fget` error one level up.
Index the owning class's `__dict__` instead, walking the MRO to find it and
guarding that the classes ahead of it still do not define the name.

Only the `property` branch moves: `staticmethod` and `classmethod` keep the
instance anchor, since reading those through the type unwraps them. A
pure-Python property resolves through `UserDefinedObjectVariable` and never gets
here, and `torch.finfo` / `torch.iinfo` expose getset descriptors rather than
properties.

That MRO walk already existed three times over -- in
`AutogradFunctionVariable._get_raw_attribute_source` and in both
`get_source_by_walking_mro` methods -- so it becomes one `mro_attr_source` next
to `mro_lookup`, and the callers keep only what differs: their extra guard and
what a miss means. Three discrepancies had to be settled to share it. The
absent-guard loop runs `range(idx)` everywhere now, so the `user_defined`
callers guard MRO index 0 the way `misc` already did -- otherwise setting the
attribute on `type(obj)` later moves the owner while the guard still reads
`__mro__[idx]`. `mro_source_cache` is keyed on the owning class rather than the
descriptor: one descriptor object can sit in several unrelated classes, and a
source through one of them does not notice the attribute being reassigned on
another. Keying on the owner still lets instances and subclasses that reach the
same owner share one source, so they do not pick up an OBJECT_ALIASING guard.
And entry 0 is spelled as the class itself only after checking that it is the
class -- every MRO CPython computes puts it there, but a metaclass overriding
`mro()` can not, and now that index 0 is guarded the mismatch would fail a guard
on the frame that created it.

`TestConstantTypeProperty` covers the `common_constant_types` path: a plain
property, one shadowed by a metaclass descriptor, one inherited from a base,
one shadowed on the subclass after the first compile (which has to recompile),
and one on a class whose metaclass reorders `__mro__`. The
`_CudaDeviceProperties` case moves to `TestConstantTypePropertyAccelerator`, so
both classes carry a `hw_classification` and survive `--hw-classification`.
Two tests in `test_repros.py` pin the cache key from both sides: a descriptor
shared by unrelated classes recompiles when one of them reassigns it, and two
instances reaching the same class attribute get no OBJECT_ALIASING guard.

Test Plan:

```shell
python -m pytest test/dynamo/test_user_defined_object.py
python -m pytest test/dynamo/test_misc.py test/dynamo/test_repros.py \
    test/dynamo/test_functions.py test/dynamo/test_autograd_function.py
python -m pytest test/distributed/tensor/test_compile_on_one_rank.py
lintrunner
```

title: [BE] Move MetalShaderLibrary cache guard out of the class
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.18.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #197837
* #197836

The guard that landed in #167541 uses `std::recursive_mutex`, that changes  `sizeof(MetalShaderLibrary)` and therefore breaks ABI with existing  out-of-tree C++ extensions, and recursive calls were made from other methods within the same class. 
Make it a file-static `std::mutex` in OperationUtils.mm, where every accessor that touches library caches are defined. 

Dropping recursion means untangling the two chains that nested:

- `hasFunction` called `getFunctionNames`, which locks. It now checks the populated flag under the lock, computes the names unlocked, then reacquires to  fill the set, re-testing the flag in case another thread got there first.
- `getCachedKernelFunctionPtr` called `getLibrary` + `getLibraryPipelineState`,
  both of which lock. It now looks up under the lock, builds the kernel unlocked
  and reacquires to insert; `try_emplace` keeps whichever thread won and the
  loser's kernel is dropped.

`getPipelineStateForFunc` never nested: `getLibraryPipelineState(getLibrary(), fname)` evaluates the argument before the call, so those locks are sequential.

No behavior change intended; this is the cleanup discussed on #167541.
Authored with the assistance of Claude Code.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

title: [inductor] Give require_stride_order a stride order in copy_strided
body:
Fixes #198332

The lowering of `prims.copy_strided` sorts the dims by stride, which gives the fill order, and passes that to `require_stride_order`, which takes the stride order (the rank of each dim). The two are the same when the permutation is its own inverse and differ otherwise: for a 3-d tensor with its last two dims transposed, strides `(30, 1, 6)`, the buffer came out as `(5, 20, 1)`. With dynamic shapes on CPU that layout led to a kernel that writes past another buffer (`x.index_fill(...)` on a transposed input followed by a reduction, see the issue).

This uses `ir.get_stride_order(stride)`.

Test plan: `test_copy_strided_keeps_the_requested_strides` in test_torchinductor.py checks the buffer's strides in the output code; it fails without the change on CPU and CUDA. On 2.14 with CUDA (RTX 4070), with the change and without: test_torchinductor.py GPUTests on strides, copies, views, index_fill, lerp and mutation (518), and the OpInfo tests of index_fill, index_copy, index_add, lerp, copy and as_strided on CUDA float32 (44), with no new failure.

title: [Test] Add has_sufficient_memory() hook to DeviceTypeTestBase
body:
## Summary

This PR adds a `has_sufficient_memory()` hook to `DeviceTypeTestBase` and updates `largeTensorTest()` to use it when available.

It also introduces `test_size_overrides` to allow device-specific test bases to override declared test sizes.

## Motivation

`largeTensorTest()` currently relies on `_has_sufficient_memory()` to determine whether a device has enough available memory for a requested allocation size. `_has_sufficient_memory()` currently contains hardcoded backend-specific memory queries for built-in device types such as CUDA/XPU/MPS/CPU.

Available memory querying is fundamentally a device-level capability and is useful for device-generic testing infrastructure.

Additionally, out-of-tree backends may need to override the memory requirements declared by `largeTensorTest()` to accommodate backend-specific memory constraints.

This PR introduces a reusable `has_sufficient_memory()` hook on `DeviceTypeTestBase` so device-specific test bases can customize memory reporting behavior.

## Changes

- Add `has_sufficient_memory()` hook to `DeviceTypeTestBase`
- Implement the hook for CPU/CUDA/MPS/XPU test bases.
- Update `largeTensorTest()` to use the hook when available while preserving the existing fallback logic for compatibility.
-  Add `test_size_overrides` to allow device-specific test bases to override memory requirements declared by `largeTensorTest()`. 
- Add OpenReg test cases to verify the memory hook and test size overrides.

title: [dynamo] Replay random.Random draws on the live object instead of baking trace-time constants
body:
## Issue

Fixes #196437

## Summary

Dynamo snapshotted a `random.Random` argument's `getstate()` at trace time and
replayed every draw from that frozen snapshot under a TYPE_MATCH-only guard, so
any cache hit (e.g. the 4th shape in a `dynamic=True` sequence) returned the
compile-time draw and clobbered the object's state via a stale `setstate()`.
Such draws are now recorded as replay-on-source entries so `__gen_rand_values`
calls the method on the live runtime object (mirroring the existing
module-level `random.*` replay design); `seed`/`setstate` still pin
trace-time-deterministic behavior, and the stale write-back is skipped when
draws replayed live. See the issue for the full analysis.

title: [dynamo] Wrap observed exception arguments
body:
## Summary

`raise_observed_exception()` may receive `args` forwarded directly from a real Python exception via `exc.args`. These arguments are not necessarily strings or `VariableTracker`s.

For example, `UnicodeEncodeError.args` contains integer values for the start and end offsets. Previously, `raise_observed_exception()` converted only string arguments through `SourcelessBuilder`, allowing raw integers to reach `ExceptionVariable`. This caused Dynamo to fail while formatting the observed exception with:

```text
AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'debug_repr'
```

Convert all observed exception arguments through `SourcelessBuilder.create()`. `SourcelessBuilder` already preserves existing `VariableTracker`s and wraps supported Python values appropriately.

A focused regression test covers an observed `UnicodeEncodeError` containing non-string arguments.

Related to #195901 (`test_builtin.py::TestType::test_type_doc`).

After this change, `TestType.test_type_doc` progresses past the reported `debug_repr` crash and reaches the separately tracked unsupported class-level `setattr()` path at `A.__doc__ = doc`. Therefore, the CPython expected-failure marker for the full test remains in place.

title: [Feature Refactoring][dynamo] Device-agnostic repro generation in after_aot for out-of-tree backends
body:
## Summary

`torch/_dynamo/repro/after_aot.py` hardcodes CUDA in four places, which blocks out-of-tree accelerator backends from using the repro tooling: generated repro scripts only do `import torch` (so a PrivateUse1 backend fails when the script recreates tensors on that device), the repro header calls `_cuda_system_info_comment()` (CUDA toolchain info only), `repro_minify` pins subprocesses with `torch.cuda.device_count()` + `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`, and a helper infers the carrier device with `tensor.is_cuda`. This PR makes all four device-agnostic with zero new public API, reusing the `arg.device.type != "cpu"` inverse check already used elsewhere in this file. All probing happens at call time — no import-time side effects (this module sits on the torch_npu import chain via `torch/_inductor/debug.py`, so import-time purity is mandatory).

## Changes

- Added a module-private helper `_infer_repro_device_type(args)` that returns the device type of the first non-cpu tensor argument (or "cpu").
- The repro header system info keeps `_cuda_system_info_comment()` verbatim for cpu/cuda and falls back to generic `getattr`-based collection for other accelerators (`torch.version.<dt>`, `is_available`, `device_count`, `get_device_name`). Every failure degrades to comment text — debug tooling must never break repro generation.
- Added `_oot_backend_imports(device_type)`: injects `try: import torch_<backend>` into the generated script only when the device type equals the registered PrivateUse1 backend name (`torch._C._get_privateuse1_backend_name()`); built-in devices inject nothing.
- Added `_minifier_env_variables(args)`: resolves the visibility env var through a small device-type mapping (currently `{"npu": "ASCEND_RT_VISIBLE_DEVICES"}`; `TODO(#189137)` — switch to the future DeviceInterface API when it lands). CPU, cuda and any unmapped device type keep the historical `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` lines verbatim; `repro_minify` now calls it.
- Extended `test/dynamo/test_after_aot.py` with a new `TestAfterAotDeviceDecoupling` class (`@instantiate_parametrized_tests`, `hw_classification = HardwareClassification.GENERIC`, 13 tests including a `@parametrize`-driven mapping test and an `hpu` unmapped-type fallback case). Tests call the production symbols directly; mocks are used only for determinism (patching `torch.npu`, `torch._C._get_privateuse1_backend_name`, `torch.cuda.device_count`).

| device | repro header info | generated script | minifier env |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| cuda | `_cuda_system_info_comment()` (byte-identical) | unchanged (no injection) | `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` (byte-identical) |
| cpu-only | unchanged | unchanged | unchanged |
| npu | generic: `torch.version.npu` (if provided), device count, device name | `try: import torch_npu` | `ASCEND_RT_VISIBLE_DEVICES` |
| other PrivateUse1 | generic collection | `try: import torch_<name>` | historical fallback |

Every in-tree backend (cuda/cpu/xpu/mps/mtia) lands on the verbatim fallback path — cpu-args and cuda-args repros are byte-identical before/after this patch (A/B diff verified on the validation boxes).

## Depends on

None. All APIs used (`torch._C._get_privateuse1_backend_name()`, `torch.cuda.device_count()`, `getattr(torch.version, <dt>)`) are already in trunk.

## Not changed

- `_cuda_system_info_comment` in `debug_utils.py` is untouched and remains the collector for cpu/cuda repros. When the debug_utils device-agnostic entry point lands, this module can switch to it with a one-line change (follow-up).
- `_dynamo/device_interface.py` and the inductor registration paths are untouched.
- The unused `_build_symbolic_wrapper` helper's `a.is_cuda` is left as-is (dead code, see the NOTE in source) — identified during review and moved out of scope for this PR.
- The mapping constant is a `TODO(#189137)` placeholder for `visible_devices_env()`.
- `torch_npu` requires no changes: the helpers only use standard `torch.npu.is_available/device_count/get_device_name`, and `_get_privateuse1_backend_name()` already covers PrivateUse1.

## Test plan

- NPU (Ascend 910B3 x8, torch 2.13.0a0+gitfad7424 + torch_npu 2.13.0): probe `generate_compiler_repro_string(gm, [npu_tensor])` on base -> no `import torch_npu`, header shows `no GPU info collected`; after patch -> injection present + `# npu device count: 8` + `# npu device 0: Ascend910B3`. Runner -> OK (13 tests). `test_debug_utils.py` regression -> 48 passed / 4 failed with the failure set byte-identical to the unpatched base (pre-existing, see Notes). cpu-args repro byte-identical before/after (A/B diff).
- CPU (venv_cpu, `cuda=False`): runner -> OK (13 tests); `test_debug_utils.py` regression -> 36 passed.
- CUDA (node-5-15, 4x A100-SXM4-80GB, CUDA 12.4): cuda-args repro byte-identical before/after the patch (`CUDA NO-OP VERIFIED`); runner -> OK (13 tests); `test_debug_utils.py` regression -> 67 passed.
- CI (lint / unittest / dynamo shards).

## Notes (pre-existing failures, not introduced by this PR)

1. `test/dynamo/test_debug_utils.py`: 4 cases fail identically on the unpatched runtime tree. Two root causes, both in the torch_npu patch layer: (a) `TestInductorConfigOverrideIntegrationCPU` x2 — one fails with `TypeError: patch_inductor_wrapper.<locals>.new_call() got an unexpected keyword argument 'config_patches'` (trunk's compiler wrapper now passes `config_patches=`; torch_npu's patched `new_call` is stale), the other hits an import-time `RuntimeError: 0 active drivers ([]). There should only be one.` from `torch_npu/_inductor/config.py` initializing the triton driver inside the patched cudagraph check; (b) `TestBackendOverrideIntegrationNPU` x2 — `KeyError: 'npu'` from `device_op_overrides_dict` (no OOT registration channel; upstream RFC #189137 proposes these registration interfaces). None are touched by this diff. Ownership: (a) torch_npu, (b) the #189137 RFC scope. Not fixing here to keep the diff scoped to `after_aot.py`.

Running a generated npu repro end-to-end (`get_args`) hits a SyntaxError: torch_npu's runtime patch of `InputWriter.tensor` emits kwargs containing slashes (`origin_format_/ND=True, ...`), which are not valid Python identifiers. title: [export_python] inductor: keep the AsyncCompile lifecycle only when a readable graph uses it
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #193901
* #193900
* #193899
* #198257
* #198256
* #198255
* #198254
* #198253
* #198252
* #193898
* #198277
* #198276
* #198275
* #198247
* #198246
* #198245
* #198311
* __->__ #198274
* #193974
* #193973

**Problem.** Under `readable_wrapper`, Triton kernels are hoisted into the module as ordinary code, so a Triton-only graph never calls `async_compile` -- yet every readable module still carried the `AsyncCompile` import, the `async_compile = AsyncCompile()` binding, and the `async_compile.wait(globals())` / `del async_compile` pair.

**Fix.** The wait/del now goes through `write_preamble_line` keyed on `async_compile`, like the import and the binding already did, so all four lines appear exactly when something else in the module uses `async_compile`.

**Summary.** In the parent commit the import and the binding were already deferred preamble lines keyed on `async_compile`, but the wait/del was a plain `splice` into `prefix`, which the usage scan reads. That unconditional `async_compile.wait(globals())` counted as a use of `async_compile`, so it kept the binding and the import alive in every readable module, even one where no line ever called an `AsyncCompile`. This commit routes the wait/del (and its two blank separator lines) through `write_preamble_line` too, so during the scan it reads as absent like every other preamble line, and the whole lifecycle survives only when another line references `async_compile` (a C++ kernel's `async_compile.cpp_pybinding(...)` or a user `@triton.jit` kernel's `async_compile.triton(...)`, in the root or in any subgraph). The decision is made once, on the final text of the root module, because a kernel defined in a subgraph binds through the root's `async_compile` and only the root waits on it. It also leaves the compile-time autotuning block out of readable modules, and default codegen is unchanged, since the default `write_preamble_line` emits every line.

## What a readable module contains

For a Triton-only graph (`test_async_compile_is_dropped_when_no_backend_needs_it`):

```python
def fn(x):
    return (x * 2).relu()

x = torch.randn(256, device="cuda")
_, code = _code_for(fn, x, readable_wrapper=True)

# parent: the module still carries
#   from torch._inductor.async_compile import AsyncCompile
#   async_compile = AsyncCompile()
#   ...
#   async_compile.wait(globals())
#   del async_compile
# now:
assert "AsyncCompile" not in code
assert "async_compile" not in code
```

For a graph with a C++ kernel (`test_async_compile_survives_when_a_backend_needs_it`), the kernel cannot be hoisted -- its text is C++ and producing the value needs a compiler invocation -- so the lifecycle stays, exactly once. The decision is per-graph, not per-mode:

```python
def fn(x):
    return (x + 1).relu().sum(0)

_, code = _code_for(fn, torch.randn(1024), readable_wrapper=True, cpu_backend="cpp")
assert "async_compile.cpp_pybinding(" in code
for line in (
    "from torch._inductor.async_compile import AsyncCompile",
    "async_compile = AsyncCompile()",
    "async_compile.wait(globals())",
    "del async_compile",
):
    assert code.count(line) == 1
```

A user-defined `@triton.jit` kernel is the one Triton kernel that is still an `async_compile.triton(...)` source string, so it keeps the lifecycle alive too (`test_async_compile_survives_for_a_user_defined_triton_kernel`):

```python
from torch.testing._internal.triton_utils import add_kernel

def fn(x):
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    add_kernel[(4,)](x, x, out, x.numel(), BLOCK_SIZE=64)
    return out

x = torch.randn(256, device="cuda")
expected, code = _code_for(fn, x, readable_wrapper=True)
assert code.count("= async_compile.triton(") == 1
assert code.count("async_compile = AsyncCompile()") == 1
assert code.count("async_compile.wait(globals())") == 1
# and the module runs standalone and matches eager
```

## How the wait/del joins the preamble table

```python
# parent: a plain splice into prefix, which the usage scan reads as a use
def write_async_compile_wait(self) -> None:
    self.prefix.splice("""

        async_compile.wait(globals())
        del async_compile
        """)

# now: preamble lines keyed on async_compile
def write_async_compile_wait(self) -> None:
    # The two blank separator lines are gated too, so a dropped wait leaves no gap.
    for line in ("", "", "async_compile.wait(globals())", "del async_compile"):
        self.write_preamble_line(self.prefix, ("async_compile",), line)
```

Every preamble line reads as absent during the usage scan, so neither the binding nor the wait/del can witness itself as a use of `async_compile`. The import is keyed on `async_compile` rather than `AsyncCompile` for the same reason: its only user is the binding, which the scan does not see, so the import lives and dies with the binding.

## Why the root module decides, not a codegen flag

A flag set during codegen would go wrong across subgraphs. A kernel defined in a subgraph binds through the root's `async_compile`, and a subgraph writes only its no-op `write_async_compile_wait` and leaves the lifecycle to the root. The readable subgraph gets that no-op by MRO, since the readable class does not override `write_async_compile_wait`. The scan already covers `subgraph_definitions`, so a C++ kernel in any branch keeps the root's lifecycle alive (`test_cpp_kernels_in_root_and_subgraphs_run_standalone`):

```python
def fn(x):
    y = (x + 1).relu()
    pred = y.sum() > 0
    return torch.cond(pred, lambda t: (t * 2).sin(), lambda t: t.cos(), (y,))

x = torch.randn(64, 128)
expected, code = _code_for(fn, x, readable_wrapper=True, cpu_backend="cpp")
assert code.count("= async_compile.cpp_pybinding(") >= 3   # root + one per branch
assert code.count("async_compile.wait(globals())") == 1     # only the root waits
ns = {"__name__": "_readable_artifact"}
exec(compile(code, "<readable_artifact>", "exec"), ns)
torch.testing.assert_close(ns["call"]([x])[0], expected)  # runs standalone, matches eager
```

## The compile-time autotuning block is dropped too

With `triton.autotune_at_compile_time`, inductor prepends the tuning code to the module as an inert `r"""..."""` string, kept as a debugging aid. It is the single largest thing in a small artifact, and it is also the last place the module mentions `async_compile.triton(`, so leaving it in would keep a string form of every kernel next to its hoisted definition. `_compile_to_module_lines` now skips it when the wrapper is the readable one:

```python
# graph.py
readable = isinstance(self.wrapper_code, ReadablePythonWrapperCodegen)
if config.triton.autotune_at_compile_time and not readable:
    ...  # prepend the tuning block, as before
```

The `autotune_at_compile_time` variant of the standalone Triton test changes accordingly:

```python
# parent: exactly one string-form kernel survived, inside the tuning block
self.assertEqual(code.count("= async_compile.triton("), 1 if autotune_at_compile_time else 0)
# now
self.assertNotIn("async_compile.triton", code)
```

## Default codegen

Nothing changes outside readable mode. The default `write_preamble_line` emits every line, so the default wrapper writes the same wait/del as before, and the tuning block is still prepended for every other wrapper.

Test Plan:

```
python test/inductor/test_readable_wrapper.py
python test/test_precompile.py
```

4 new tests: that the AsyncCompile lifecycle is dropped from a Triton-only
graph, that it is kept exactly once for a C++ one and for a graph calling a
user-defined @triton.jit kernel (still a source string, so it stays in the usage
scan; the latter also runs standalone), and that a CPU torch.cond
with C++ kernels in the root and both branches execs standalone and matches
eager. The autotune_at_compile_time variant of the standalone test now asserts
that no `async_compile.triton` survives in the module.

This commit was authored with the assistance of an AI coding agent.

title: [Feature Refactoring] Decouple FlexGEMM runtime CUDA-specific device guards
body:
## Motivation

`torch/_inductor/kernel/flex_gemm/runtime.py` hardcodes CUDA in two places, which prevents third-party (PrivateUse1) accelerators from reaching the FlexGEMM runtime:

1. `normalize_c` rejects any C tensor that is not CUDA (`if not broadcast_C.is_cuda`).
2. The external-stream context is built with `torch.cuda.stream(torch.cuda.ExternalStream(...))`.

## Approach

- **Condition guard replacement**: `normalize_c` now takes the GEMM's device type and validates that C lives on that device (a consistency/capability query instead of a hardcoded CUDA check). CUDA behavior is unchanged: the accepted set of C tensors is identical (`device.type == "cuda"` for CUDA GEMMs).
- **Type generalization**: the stream context is created through `torch.get_device_module(a.device).stream(...ExternalStream(...))` instead of `torch.cuda.*`.

## Testing

- `normalize_c` exercised on CPU: matching device type accepts and broadcasts, mismatching device type raises with both device names in the message, `C=None` / `beta=0` passthrough unaffected.
- `py_compile`, `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` clean.

title: Replace `Linear` `inner_product` calls with `matmul`
body:
## Summary

Replace direct inner-product calls in MKLDNN Linear with matmul calls for forward. Backward is left as inner-product.

oneDNN already attempts to redirect eligible inner-product operations to matmul on both AArch64 and x86. Calling matmul directly removes this intermediate inner-product dispatch step and allows the appropriate matmul implementation to be selected immediately.

This changes the MKLDNN Linear path on both AArch64 and x86, so input and validation from the x86 stakeholders is requested before merging.

title: [cuda graphs] Automatic nn.Module FQN annotation in Inductor cudagraph trees
body:
This PR implements Issue #186026 .

The problem it solves is that when cuda graph is enabled it is difficult to map the kernels back to the operators which created them.  Since cuda graph makes it so a single kernel launch triggers multiple GPU kernels we lose information about the origin of those kernels.  Then the mapping is complicated further when torch.compile is enabled.  The further away we get from eager execution, the harder it is to map kernels back to their original operators. 

This PR takes advantage of a feature in Cuda 13.1 (cudaGraphNodeGetToolsId ) which assigns unique ids to each kernel.  Then it leverages the mark_kernel() function on the inductor compile side which can bind the kernel names at compile time to the cuda graph kernel at runtime.  When Pytorch profiler or nsys profiler is used, they can be post processed offline in order to get the graphNodeId.  This id can be joined on the same nodeId which is recorded at compile time.

An important side effect is that no additional profiler instrumentation is required beyond just sampling the Cuda Kernel events.  This is important for runtime performance, the profiler won't incur additional latency when this feature is enabled.

title: [no-ci] [precompile] Make DynamoTracer the default tracer and settle the docs
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #198217
* #198227
* #198138
* #198216
* #198137
* #198215
* #198136
* #198214
* #198243
* #198135
* #198213
* #197993
* #198284
* #198283
* #198223
* #198211

**Problem.** `capture()` still defaults to `MakeFxTracer()`, the single non-strict trace, even though the Dynamo front-end is served and covers everything the make_fx form accepts; and the module docstring of `torch/_precompile.py`, the tracer paragraph of Note [precompile programming model] and the docs still describe the reference stack (`accumulate`, an installed mode, source-rendered subgraphs, a tracer that "currently raises NotImplementedError").

**Fix.** Flip the default to `DynamoTracer()`, drop the `setdefault("tracer", DynamoTracer())` the Dynamo tests no longer need, and rewrite the docstring, the Note paragraph, the API reference and the user guide to describe the surface as it is.

**Summary.** With both front-ends served, `capture()` defaults to `DynamoTracer()`: it takes as many calls as the caller makes, keyword arguments included, and refuses nothing a `MakeFxTracer` capture would have accepted, while the make_fx form stays available for the single non-strict trace with its explicit contract. Until this commit `capture(step, artifact_path=..., cache_path=...)` meant a make_fx capture that accepted exactly one positional call and refused a second, so a caller who wanted the multi-call Dynamo capture had to ask for it with `tracer=DynamoTracer()`. Now the bare call is the Dynamo capture and `tracer=MakeFxTracer()` is the explicit opt-in, which is the direction the two tracers' contracts point: the default should be the one that refuses less. The module docstring of `torch/_precompile.py` and the tracer paragraph of Note [precompile programming model] now describe the surface as it is -- `capture`, `save`, `load`, the two tracers, the standalone Dynamo artifact and its grad-mode contract -- in place of the reference stack's text they carried (`accumulate`, an installed mode, source-rendered subgraphs), and the API reference and user guide show the multi-call capture. The Dynamo tests rely on the default; the make_fx tests already pass `tracer=MakeFxTracer()` explicitly, so no test changes meaning.

## Where this fits

The stack replaces the callable `torch.compiler.precompile(fn, *example_inputs)` (trace once on inputs passed up front, pair returned in memory) with a caller-driven context manager: `capture(fn, artifact_path=, cache_path=)` is entered with a `with` block, the caller calls it on as many example inputs as they like (each graph break and recompiled variant is folded in), the `(python_code, cache)` pair is written to the two files on exit, and `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` serves it in a fresh process. The end-to-end example and the PR-by-PR map live in #197993's "The new API, end to end" section. This is the top of the stack: `DynamoTracer` becomes the default tracer, so `capture()` is multi-call out of the box, and the docs describe the finished API.

## The default flips

Parent: the signature names the make_fx tracer as the default, and the docstring calls it "(the default)".

```python
def capture(fn, *, artifact_path, cache_path,
            tracer: MakeFxTracer | DynamoTracer = MakeFxTracer(),
            backend: str = "inductor", training: bool = False) -> Capture:
```

Now: the default is the Dynamo tracer, and the "(the default)" marker moves from the `MakeFxTracer` sentence of the docstring to the `DynamoTracer` one and onto `DynamoTracer`'s own class docstring.

```python
def capture(fn, *, artifact_path, cache_path,
            tracer: MakeFxTracer | DynamoTracer = DynamoTracer(),
            backend: str = "inductor", training: bool = False) -> Capture:
```

What a caller observes, with `step` a module-level function of an importable module:

```python
with torch.compiler.precompile.capture(
    step, artifact_path="m.py", cache_path="m.cache"
) as cap:
    y1 = cap(model, x1)
    y2 = cap(model, x2)   # parent: refused, make_fx takes exactly ONE positional call
                          # now: another guarded variant of the Dynamo capture
    cap.save()            # optional checkpoint of what ran so far

# The single non-strict trace is still there, asked for by name:
with torch.compiler.precompile.capture(
    step, artifact_path="fx.py", cache_path="fx.cache", tracer=MakeFxTracer()
) as cap:
    y = cap(model, x1)    # exactly one call, under the Note's contract
```

The flip is safe in one direction only, which is why it is this direction: the Dynamo capture takes every call a make_fx capture would have taken (and keyword arguments besides), whereas a make_fx default refuses the second call of every loop. Nothing about either tracer's behaviour changes here; only which one the bare call picks.

## The module docstring says what the module does

The docstring at the top of `torch/_precompile.py` was carried over from the reference stack and still described `precompile.accumulate(...)` rewriting the artifact after every call, `training` as a knob shared by both tracers, a Dynamo artifact that installs onto live code objects with a `load()` context manager that "unloads on exit what load() installed", and a `require_*` paragraph phrased around "multi-graph capture keeps all live guards". This commit replaces that with the surface as built:

```python
"""... ``precompile.capture(...)`` returns a capture that writes a ``(python_code, cache)``
artifact to disk when the ``with`` block exits, or whenever ``cap.save()`` is called
inside it; ``load`` reloads it from those two files.

    with torch.compiler.precompile.capture(
        step, artifact_path="model.py", cache_path="model.cache"
    ) as cap:
        for x in loader:
            out = cap(model, x)         # runs step(model, x), returns its result
            cap.save()                  # optional checkpoint of what ran so far
    f_c = torch.compiler.precompile.load("model.py", "model.cache")
    out = f_c(model, x)                 # pass the model again at runtime
```

The `DynamoTracer` paragraph now states the artifact's actual contract: it records every frame Dynamo compiles while the calls run (entry, graph-break continuations, recompiled variants) with one guard tree per variant, inlines the transformed bytecode and guard trees into `python_code` (pickled, rehydrated at load), and dispatches among the variants at call time, RAISING on a call no variant covers. The artifact is STANDALONE and installs nothing, so `fn` must be a module-level function of an importable module, an unreachable frame is refused at write time, and the artifact is locked to the producing Python version and torch build. Grad mode is a `GLOBAL_STATE` guard, a `.backward()` in `fn` graph-breaks and re-runs at serve time through the live autograd engine, unserializable guards are reported in `PrecompileSummary.dropped_guards` rather than checked, and the `require_*` gates refuse known coverage gaps and RISKY drops by default. The `MakeFxTracer` paragraph keeps its explicit contract and absorbs the `training=True` and autocast sentences that used to sit in the shared paragraph, since they are make_fx-specific. The `backend` paragraph names both lowering paths (`compile_to_python` for make_fx, the bundled AOTAutograd cache entry for Dynamo) and says the loaded runnable's enter and exit are no-ops for these standalone artifacts.

## The Note's tracer paragraph stops saying "planned"

Parent, at the bottom of Note [precompile programming model]:

```python
# tracer: the capture front-end, orthogonal to backend. "make_fx" (default) is a
# non-strict trace and is the only tracer implemented today -- everything above (the
# invariants, the contract) describes its behavior. "dynamo" is planned (a Dynamo-based
# front-end that analyzes Python rather than specializing to one traced path) and
# currently raises NotImplementedError.
```

Now the paragraph names both dataclasses, marks `DynamoTracer` as the default, and says which invariants belong to which tracer: invariants 1, 2, 3 and 6 are the make_fx contract, while under Dynamo a call outside the captured variants is REFUSED by the guards rather than silently served and unserializable guards are reported rather than checked.

## The docs show the multi-call capture

`docs/source/torch.compiler_api.md` and `docs/source/user_guide/torch_compiler/torch.compiler.md` swap the `lambda model, x: model(x)` example (a lambda is not a module-level function, so the standalone Dynamo artifact would refuse it) for a module-level `step` and two calls, and the API reference explains the two tracers in one sentence before listing `DynamoTracer` ahead of `MakeFxTracer`:

```python
# step is a module-level function: def step(model, x): return model(x)
with torch.compiler.precompile.capture(
    step, artifact_path="m.py", cache_path="m.cache"
) as cap:
    y1 = cap(model, x1)
    y2 = cap(model, x2)  # a recompile or graph break becomes another variant

f = torch.compiler.precompile.load("m.py", "m.cache")  # in a fresh process
y = f(model, x1)
```

## Tests

`TestPrecompileDynamoCapture._capture` in `test/test_precompile.py` drops its `kwargs.setdefault("tracer", DynamoTracer())`, so every Dynamo test now exercises the default the way a user hits it. The make_fx classes are untouched: `TestPrecompileCapture._capture` already pins `kwargs.setdefault("tracer", MakeFxTracer())`, and `test_a_dynamo_pair_does_not_mix_with_a_make_fx_pair` passes `tracer=MakeFxTracer()` explicitly for its make_fx pair, so the flip does not change which tracer any existing test runs under.

Test Plan:

```
python test/test_precompile.py
python test/dynamo/test_precompile_package.py
lintrunner -a torch/_precompile.py test/test_precompile.py docs/source/torch.compiler_api.md docs/source/user_guide/torch_compiler/torch.compiler.md
```

title: [no-ci] [precompile] Add save() checkpoints and summary() to Dynamo captures
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #198217
* __->__ #198227
* #198138
* #198216
* #198137
* #198215
* #198136
* #198214
* #198243
* #198135
* #198213
* #197993
* #198284
* #198283
* #198223
* #198211

**Problem.** A Dynamo capture wrote its artifact only when the `with` block exited cleanly, so a job that died mid-loop left nothing on disk, and there was no way to read the coverage or guard report the session had built up.

**Fix.** `_DynamoCapture` gains `save()`, which checkpoints everything captured so far to the same two files without ending the capture, and `summary()`, which returns the session's `PrecompileSummary` inside the block and after it.

**Summary.** A Dynamo capture that dies mid-loop left nothing on disk, because the artifact was rendered and written only on a clean exit. `_DynamoCapture.save()` now renders and writes everything captured so far to the same `artifact_path` / `cache_path` pair without ending the capture, so each call re-renders and rewrites both files and a job that dies between saves leaves the last checkpoint loadable, while a gate refusal or a write failure raises and writes nothing partial with the capture still open. Exit writes only when there are calls the last save did not cover, tracked as the call count the last write saw, which starts at `-1` so a block that never called still raises the nothing-captured error rather than writing an empty artifact. Calls and saves share the capture's one lock, so a `save()` never snapshots the capture mid-compile, and a `save()` from inside `fn` is refused. `summary()` exposes the session's `PrecompileSummary` -- coverage, recompilation, failure and guard information for everything captured so far -- readable inside the block and after it, including after a gate refusal, since the refusal is raised only after teardown.

## Where this fits

The stack replaces the callable `torch.compiler.precompile(fn, *example_inputs)` (trace once on inputs passed up front, pair returned in memory) with a caller-driven context manager: `capture(fn, artifact_path=, cache_path=)` is entered with a `with` block, the caller calls it on as many example inputs as they like (each graph break and recompiled variant is folded in), the `(python_code, cache)` pair is written to the two files on exit, and `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` serves it in a fresh process. The end-to-end example and the PR-by-PR map live in #197993's "The new API, end to end" section. This PR adds `cap.save()` checkpoints and `cap.summary()` (coverage, recompiles, dropped guards) to the multi-call `DynamoTracer` capture from #198138.

## save() checkpoints mid-block

The parent wrote once, from `__exit__`. `save()` is the same `_write()` -- `snapshot_artifact(**self._gates)` then `_write_artifact` -- callable from inside the block, behind the same three refusals a call has (not entered or already exited, inside `fn`, nothing captured yet):

```python
with capture(step, artifact_path=artifact, cache_path=cache, tracer=DynamoTracer()) as cap:
    cap.save()                 # PrecompileError: nothing was captured ...
    cap(model, x2)
    cap.save()                 # renders + rewrites m.py and m.cache with the first call
    cap(model, x3)             # recompiled variant; not on disk yet
# exit: the block has a call the last save did not cover -> both files rewritten
```

Each `save()` rewrites both files from scratch, so the checkpoint after `x2` and the final artifact after `x3` differ. A `require_*` gate refusal or an `OSError` from the rewrite raises out of `save()` as a `PrecompileError`; `_write_artifact` leaves the previous pair in place, so the last good checkpoint is still loadable and the capture stays open for more calls or another `save()`.

`test_save_checkpoints_mid_block` pins this: the pre-call `save()` raises `"nothing was captured"`, the checkpoint after the first call is read back, and the artifact after exit is not byte-equal to it.

## Exit writes only what the last save did not cover

Exit tracks the call count the last write saw:

```python
# __init__
self._saved_calls = -1          # not 0: a block that never called is still dirty at exit

# _write, after _write_artifact succeeds
self._saved_calls = self._calls

# __exit__: parent wrote on every clean exit
if exc[0] is None:
# now
if exc[0] is None and self._calls > self._saved_calls:
```

So a block whose last `save()` covered every call writes nothing at exit, a block with calls after the last `save()` writes a final checkpoint, and a block that never called (`_calls` is 0, above the `-1` start) still reaches the `"nothing was captured"` error instead of writing an empty artifact. A block that raised still writes nothing, as before.

## summary() inside and after the block

```python
with capture(step, artifact_path=artifact, cache_path=cache, tracer=DynamoTracer()) as cap:
    cap(model, x2)
    cap(model, x3, scale=0.5)
    summary = cap.summary()
summary.complete           # True
summary.frames             # 2: the entry and its graph-break continuation
summary.resume_functions   # 1
summary.guarded_codes      # >= 3: a variant per call the guards told apart
```

`summary()` is `self._map(self._session.summary)`, so `PackageError` / `RecompileError` surface as `PrecompileError` like every other session call. It is readable after a gate refusal too, because `__exit__` holds the refusal and re-raises it only after teardown:

```python
with self.assertRaisesRegex(PrecompileError, "captured call raised"):
    with capture(step, ...) as cap:
        cap(model, x2)
        with self.assertRaises(RuntimeError):
            cap(model, torch.randn(2, 5))
        cap.summary().complete     # False: the raised call is a coverage gap
# nothing written: neither m.py nor m.cache exists
```

The dropped guards move from being documented as an artifact list (`DROPPED_GUARDS`) to being reported through `Capture.summary`; the artifact still lists the same slots:

```python
with capture(single, ...) as cap:
    cap(model, x2)
    summary = cap.summary()
"MODULE_MATCH" in summary.dropped_guard_types   # the default filter drops the model identity guard
summary.kept_guards                             # non-empty
summary.risky_dropped_guards                    # ()
for guard_type, source in summary.dropped_guards:
    assert f"[{guard_type!r}, {source!r}]" in open(artifact).read()
```

`test_dropped_guards_are_reported_in_the_summary_and_the_artifact` reads the default filter's drops from the summary and checks the artifact lists the same `(guard_type, source)` slots; `test_the_strict_gate_refuses_dropped_guards` keeps the `DynamoTracer(require_no_dropped_guards=True)` refusal on its own. `test_graph_breaks_and_recompiles_round_trip_in_a_fresh_process` and `test_a_raised_call_is_refused_at_exit_and_writes_nothing` gain the summary assertions shown above.

Test Plan:

`test_save_checkpoints_mid_block` checkpoints after the first call and checks the exit rewrite after the second; `test_dropped_guards_are_reported_in_the_summary_and_the_artifact` reads the default filter's drops from the summary and the artifact; the round-trip and raised-call tests gain their summary assertions.

title: [MPS] Use atomic counters for histc
body:
## Summary

Replace the per-element temporary used by MPS `histc` with an atomic Metal
histogram. The new implementation uses threadgroup counters for histograms that
fit within an 8 KiB local-memory budget and global counters for larger bin
counts.

The current path materializes a tensor with shape `[input.numel(), bins]`. For
one million float32 elements and 256 bins, this is a 1 GiB temporary. The new
path uses a 2 KiB global count tensor and 1 KiB of threadgroup memory per active
threadgroup.

Counts are accumulated as int64 using the existing
`c10::metal::AtomicType<long>` helper, then copied to the requested output
dtype. Since `histc` is unweighted and each update adds the exact integer value
one, atomic update order does not affect the result.

## Performance

Apple M1, float32, 256 bins:

| Elements | Current MPS | This change | Speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1,024 | 50.017 ms | 0.0664 ms | 752.7x |
| 65,536 | 49.905 ms | 0.0714 ms | 698.6x |
| 1,048,576 | 82.225 ms | 0.1996 ms | 412.0x |

These numbers are specific to the tested M1 and workload.

## Testing

```text
python test/test_ops.py TestCommonMPS -k histc
python test/test_ops.py TestCommonCPU -k histc
```

The common OpInfo samples cover floating-point and integer dtypes, empty input,
single-bin histograms, large-bin global counters, and narrow ranges. Additional
checks covered contiguous and non-contiguous inputs, non-contiguous `out=`, and
the threadgroup/global boundary. The changed files also pass lintrunner.

title: Add tiled CUDA kernel for dense 2D transpose copies
body:
Addresses #113560.

`t().contiguous()` on CUDA goes through the generic TensorIterator elementwise kernel, which can't coalesce both the read and the write of a transpose. This adds a shared-memory tiled kernel for copies that TensorIterator reduces to a 2D transpose, including sources with a row pitch larger than the row (narrowed or strided outer dims).

## Kernel

- 128-bit global loads and stores for aligned 1-, 2- and 4-byte elements. Byte and halfword copies are packed into 32-bit words, shared memory transposes the words, and `__byte_perm` handles the 4x4 / 2x2 transpose inside each word.
- 64x64 tiles for vectorized fp32, 128x128 and 64x64 for packed byte and halfword copies.
- The scalar tiled kernel is kept as a fallback when pointer alignment, dimensions or row pitch rule out wide accesses, and for 8-byte elements.
- The grid-stride loop over tile rows is only compiled in when `tiles_y` exceeds `maxGridSize[1]`. Running it unconditionally cost 10-48% on Hopper for shapes that never needed it.
- Dispatch cutoff is 256 KiB for vectorized 1- and 2-byte copies, 4 MiB otherwise.

## Results

GB200, fixed 256 MB transposes, against a plain contiguous copy as the ceiling:

| dtype | tiled GB/s | contiguous copy GB/s |
|---|---|---|
| fp32 | 5910-6191 | 6168-6220 |
| fp16 | 5615-5660 | 5578-5660 |
| uint8 | 4816-5011 | 4855-5023 |

RTX 4060 (sm_89): fp32 goes from 127 to 225 GB/s against a ~230 GB/s bus limit. Vectorization is neutral there since the scalar kernel was already bus-bound, and the 256 KiB cutoff shows no regression against the generic path (within noise at 256-512 KB, 1.1-2.95x from 1 MB up).

## Tests

`test_copy_transpose_tiled` covers uint8/fp16/bf16/fp32/fp64/complex64 across square, non-square and non-multiple-of-32 shapes, plus narrowed and strided sources, all bitwise. `test_copy_transpose_tiled_rejects` covers broadcast and dtype-converting sources. Additional tests cover the dispatch boundary, alignment fallbacks, pitched rows and large-h grid-stride iteration.

Vectorized path and tile sizing by @ngimel.

title: Make the aten.polar ref functional so it can be used as a decomposition
body:
Summary:
`torch._refs._conversions.polar` is registered as a decomposition for `aten.polar` but has never been usable as one. It builds its result and then writes the parts into it:

```
result = torch.complex(abs, angle)
result.real = abs * torch.cos(angle)    # -> aten.copy_
result.imag = abs * torch.sin(angle)    # -> aten.copy_
```

A decomposition is inlined into a graph that must stay functional, so those two assignments become `aten.copy_` nodes writing into intermediates and `assert_functional_graph` rejects the graph during AOT capture. This has been true since the ref was added in #100345, and stays latent because `aten.polar` is not in `core_aten_decompositions()`: Inductor calls the ATen kernel rather than the ref.

This computes both parts first and builds the result from them -- same value, no mutation. The dtype validation stays on the inputs, which the old body got from `torch.complex(abs, angle)`; checking the products instead would let `cos`/`sin` promote an integral input to float and accept a dtype polar rejects. That check is now shared with the `complex` ref.

`aten.polar` has no DTensor sharding rule, so its output placement follows the decomposition: `cos`/`sin` redistribute the angle, and the magnitude stays Partial through the linear `mul` and `complex`. Two Partial inputs now give `Partial(sum)` rather than `Replicate()`, which is correct and saves a collective; `test_misc_ops_with_no_sharding_rules` is updated.

`aten.polar` is deliberately not added to `core_aten_decompositions()`; a backend that wants it can register it.

The `complex` ref has the same mutation-style body and is left alone: rewriting it as `view_as_complex(stack(broadcast_tensors(real, imag), -1))` gives equal values but an aliasing result where eager returns a fresh tensor, failing nine ref tests on `_is_view`. A non-aliasing formulation is a separate change.

Authored with an AI assistant.

Test Plan:
# OpInfo

Covers both conversion refs, including the error-case test that pins the input dtype checks.

```bash
buck2 test @//mode/opt fbcode//caffe2/test:test_ops -- --regex 'conversions_polar|conversions_complex'
```
https://www.internalfb.com/intern/testinfra/testrun/30399297522083552

35 passed, 8 skipped, 0 failed. An earlier revision of this change validated the dtype of the *products* rather than the inputs; `test_python_ref_errors__refs__conversions_polar_cpu` caught it with `AssertionError: Exception not raised`, because `cos`/`sin` promote an integral input to float.

# DTensor

```bash
buck2 test @//mode/opt fbcode//caffe2/test/distributed/tensor:decompositions
```
7 passed. `test_misc_ops_with_no_sharding_rules` asserted `Replicate()` for `polar` on two `Partial()` inputs, which was a property of the old decomposition. Probing each step shows the new placement is correct: `cos(Partial) -> Replicate` (non-linear, so the angle is redistributed first), `mul(Partial, Replicate) -> Partial(sum)` and `complex(Partial, Partial) -> Partial(sum)` (both linear), giving `polar(Partial, Partial) -> Partial(sum)`.

# Using the ref as a decomposition: before and after

Registering the ref for `aten.polar` in the Inductor decomposition table and compiling `torch.polar`.

**Before**, every case failed. On CPU, for `float32`, `float64`, 0-d and broadcast shapes:

```
BackendCompilerFailed: AssertionError: n=copy__1, n.args[0]=imag,
placeholders={arg1_1, arg0_1}
```

raised from `assert_functional_graph`, reached via `aot_dispatch_base_graph` during AOT capture. The same on an NVIDIA A100, for `float32` and `float64` -- the tracer names the lane view differently, same defect:

```
BackendCompilerFailed: AssertionError: n=copy__1, n.args[0]=select_1,
placeholders={arg1_1, arg0_1}
```

**After**, every case passes. CPU: `float32`, `float64`, 0-d, broadcast. A100: `float32`, `float64`, `float16` (`complex32`), 0-d, broadcast -- the CUDA path also exercises Triton codegen. On the A100 the ref matches eager `torch.polar` for `float16`/`float32`/`float64`, and still raises `RuntimeError` on mismatched dtypes and `NotImplementedError` on integral inputs.

With no decomposition registered, `torch.polar` compiles fine on both devices before and after: nothing depends on the ref today, which is why this went unnoticed.

# New test

`test_polar_ref_is_functional` in `caffe2/test/test_decomp.py`, which has no fbcode target and runs in OSS CI. Its body was executed against both the old and new bodies to confirm it discriminates rather than passing vacuously: the old traces to two `aten.copy_` nodes, the new to none, with numerics matching `torch.polar`.

Differential Revision: D121287139

title: Make largeTensorTest's host-memory check cgroup-aware
body:
`_has_sufficient_memory` gates CPU-side allocations on `psutil.virtual_memory().available`, which reads `/proc/meminfo` and therefore reports the **host's** memory. In a container that is not the ceiling the OOM killer enforces.

On a CI pod capped at 41GiB but scheduled onto a 64–768GiB node, the gate sees hundreds of gigabytes free and admits tests that cannot possibly fit:

```python
@largeTensorTest("180GB", "cpu")  test_pool3d_large_size_int64
@largeTensorTest("64GB", "cpu")   test_warp_softmax_64bit_indexing
@largeTensorTest("30GB", "cpu")   test_invalid_input_csr_large
```

Each then allocates until the cgroup kills it, so a test written to *skip* on small machines instead takes down the shard with a bare SIGKILL. Which of them run depends on which node the pod landed on, which is why these read as flaky.

This clamps the figure to what the cgroup will actually allow — cgroup v2 `memory.max`/`memory.current`, falling back to the v1 pair. Where the cgroup is uncapped (`"max"` on v2, the ~2^63 sentinel on v1, or the files absent) the helper returns `None` and the psutil value stands, so bare-metal runs and containers without a memory limit behave exactly as before.

Verified the helper against all four shapes:

| case | result |
|---|---|
| 41GiB limit, 8GiB used | 33GiB |
| v2 uncapped (`max`) | `None` → psutil |
| v1 uncapped sentinel | `None` → psutil |
| usage > limit | `0`, not negative |

Found while migrating the 1-GPU CUDA jobs to smaller OSDC runners (#197326), where six such tests accounted for 23 of 31 failures — but the bug is not specific to that change: any containerised runner with a memory limit below its host's has always been affected.
